threads.subject: Working remotely in Canada for a foreign employer -- REP-2018-1502--
threads.question:
Dear Sir / Madam,
A new partner is looking to bring groups of clients to Canada (Vancouver). His new venture is to have Swiss employees of Swiss firms come for 3-6 months in Vancouver to work remotely for the same Swiss employer while taking English classes and experiencing a new way of life. We understand that there won't be any violation of the work laws since the employees will be working for the same employer in Switzerland and won't a threat to the Canadian labour market. However, he has requested a confirmation of what section in IRPR referred to the ability of visitors to continue to work remotely for a foreign employer while in Canada.
Could you please confirm if there is any specific regulation that confirms the above?
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Thank you!
Lnfomndion
threads.answer:
Hello,
Sincere apologies for the delayed response -thank you for your patience.
Please kindly note that R 186 (A) and R 187 (1)(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) refers to the ability of a foreign national to work in Canada without a work permit as a business visitor.
According to IRPR, a business visitor to Canada is a foreign national who is described in subsection (2) or who seeks to engage in international business activities in Canada without directly entering the Canadian labour market only if, •The primary source of remuneration for the business activities is outside of Canada; and
- The principal place of business and actual place of accrual of profits remain predominately outside Canada.
Please refer to R 186 and 187 of IRPR for additional information, DIVISION 3: Work without permit
Moreover, when traveling to Canada, it is recommended that the clients bring with them the necessary documentation to prove that they are not entering the Canadian labour market. If the client indicates that they will be working while visiting Canada, the POE officer may have questions.
Thank you!

threads.subject: Query re work permit extension/change of conditions approval notice and ability to work to new employer-- REP-2018-2015 --
threads.question:
Hi.
Where a FW applies for work permit extension which includes a change of employer to a new employer, can that person start working for the new employer upon receiving the confirmation in the portal that the work permit extension/change has been approved, or must they wait for the actual work permit to be received in hand? Does IRCC have a position on that?
Thanks
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
nmigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés ation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION 1: Where a FW applies for work permit extension which includes a change of employer to a new employer,
RESPONSE: If a Foreign Worker decides to change their employer (change their employment), they must apply for a new work permit. A new work permit is required when there is a change in employer, occupation/NOC or work location. It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185].
QUESTION 2: can that person start working for the new employer upon receiving the confirmation in the portal that the work permit extension/change has been approved, or must they wait for the actual work permit to be received in hand.
RESPONSE 2: In order to work in Canada, a foreign national must either be working under the authorization of a work permit, or be work permit exempt. A work permit, as defined in the IRPR, is "a written authorization to work in Canada issued by an officer to a foreign national." Therefore, in order for a foreign national to work under the authorization of a work permit, they must have been issued their work permit and not simply have had their application approved.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Sent: Novemper 9, 2018 12:39 PI ## Hello,
I was wondering if I could get your thoughts on something we plan on doing in support of having thesis-based graduate students have the option to work full time during spring/summer terms.
At our institution, the, undergraduate and course-based graduate students don't have to have any registration or take courses during spring/summer, we can easily determine that that period of time (May-August) can be considered an "official break" thus allowing them to work full time off campus (assuming they had
maintained full time registration in prior winter and following fall terms).
nmigration, Refugees
The confusion has been around thesis-based graduate students who have to maintain full-time registration status by registering in during spring and summer while they work on their research. These students don't attend classes during spring/summer during that time since their courses are usually available in fall and winter terms.
Historically, this period was also considered an "official break" since even thesis-based students were not required to maintain registration during that period of time (as is currently the case with course-based students).
Since the IRCC definition of a "Regularly Scheduled Break" states that "To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLl's academic calendar (for instance, winter and summer holidays, Reading Week). Each regularly scheduled break should not be longer than 150 days. The maximum cumulative duration of scheduled breaks is 180 days per calendar yea"
We have usually advised thesis-based graduate students that they should not work more than 20 hours/week during spring and summer because of a lack of "definition" on our university calendar clearly identifying this period to be an official break causing a clear disadvantage for thesis-based graduate students who are only working on their thesis/research during this time and not really taking any classes.
Given this background I wanted your opinion on the following:
If we were to clearly identify spring/summer terms to be considered official academic breaks, would this satisfy the IRCC definition above thus allowing ALL international students the opportunity to work full time off campus if they choose to do so during that period?
We are thinking of adding a definition onto our website along with the other immigration information which we currently have ... something to the effect:
"For immigration purposes, spring and summer terms (May through August) are considered regularly scheduled breaks for the majority of our graduate and undergraduate academic programs regardless of whether the student chooses to register in courses or not during that time".
Please let me know what your thoughts are on this or if you need further clarification?
Thanks!
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
## Good day,
We apologize for the delayed response,
As per current guidelines: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/students/work-off-campus.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/students/work-off-campus.asp); Students must hold full-time status during the academic session prior to, as well as subsequent to, their scheduled break. If an institution allows for back-to-back scheduled breaks, thus creating a break period longer than 150 consecutive days, students are only eligible to work off campus during the first 150 consecutive days. They cannot work for the entire break if it is longer than 150 consecutive days. Taking into account all regularly scheduled breaks, students may only work off campus on a full-time basis for a total of 180 days during each calendar year. It is up to each designated learning institution as to what they consider to be the dates of their scheduled breaks.
Some intensive programs may not have scheduled breaks. Students participating in such programs may work a maximum of 20 hours per week during the entire program of study.
For your information, there are no legal restrictions preventing students from working on-campus in addition to working the maximum 20 hours per week off-campus.

Si l’erreur au lieu de travail apparaît sous les conditions, il faut demander une modification aux conditions figurant sur le permis de travail.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Can you please advise how to deal with an Express Entry application wherein an applicant has unaccompanying children and is unable to provide much information about them, aside from names and dates of birth (has been estranged from them for many years). It is our understanding that a Statutory Declaration can be provided to show that the applicant has no contact or information and therefore has been unable to have them complete medical requirements which means that they cannot be sponsored at any point in the future. But, we seek your confirmation that this will be acceptable?
We also seek your advice on how to deal with entries in the Express Entry system if we have no information for the children. For example, we have no passport information and so are unable to complete any ID details How do we proceed in this regard?
Answer:
It is strongly recommended that the applicant attempt to make contact with the dependent child in order to acquire all the relevant documents and medical exam results. If the applicant is still unable to provide the required documents such as a passport/travel document or National ID, then at the least a birth certificate must be submitted in order to establish familial relationship and the identity of the dependent child. It is also highly suggested to provide a statutory declaration with the application.
There is a section during the submission of the application where you will be required to enter a valid passport/travel document or National ID with document number. You may submit an expired passport for the non-accompanying child, however a future expiry date will have to be entered in order to continue in the system. If a passport or National ID is not forthcoming, then enter the data for another government issued ID with document number along with a future expiry date (this may include the birth certificate if the applicant was unable to obtain another government issued ID). Please also provide a letter of explanation for the lack of proper documents and medical results.
This does not guarantee that the application will be accepted as it will be assessed on a case by case basis by an IRCC agent.
We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.subject: Query re Travel History question for eAPR application and trips BETWEEN country of origin and residence; and
threads.question:
Greetings.
The eAPR travel history question asks the adult applicant to list trips the applicant "has taken outside his/her country of origin or of residence in the last ten years (or since his/her 18th birthday if this was less than ten years ago).
Include all trips: tourism, business, training...."
1. Does an applicant have to list trips BETWEEN the country of origin and the country of residence, or is that not needed as such a trip would not be outside those two countries? An example to illustrate –French citizen born in France (so France is the country of origin) and the person holds a Canadian work permit and has resided in Canada since January 1, 2017 since transferred from France to Canada. Can you confirm that if the applicant had trips between Germany and Canada AFTER January 1, 2017 that those would NOT need to be listed in the eAPR travel history? The wording of the questions suggest that you do NOT have to list trips between the country of origin and residence but we want IRCC to confirm that.
2. If the applicant above had obtained a second citizenship (say United Kingdom) before moving to Canada from France (so they had two passports/two citizenships) does the applicant have to list trips between the country of the second citizenship and Canada after January 1, 2017? In other words, is “country of origin" only the country they were born in and have had citizenship in since birth, or does it mean “country in which he/she holds citizenship(s)” for the purpose of the travel history question?
Thanks.
L'nformtondenvedisuanation
threads.answer:
### where dual citizenship is held-- REP-2018-1890--
Dear
Please note that the applicant has to report all trips outside his/her country of origin or residence during the last ten years or since his/her 18th birthday. In other words, while the applicant is residing in Canada, he/she has to lists all trips outside Canada, even when travelling to their country of origin or to another country where they have citizenship.
If your client was residing in France prior to January 2017, he/she would have to list all travel outside France even if the travel was to another country within the European Union (e.g., Germany) or to another country where they have citizenship (e.g. a
country in United Kingdom).
In addition, if an applicant travels to a country where he/she is a citizen but where he/she does not reside at the time of
travel, they would have to list the travel to that country.
We hope this information is helpful.
Regards,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Questions Regarding International Students-REP-2018-1250 -
threads.question:
Dear officer,
I would like to get some clarification on the three situations below.
1. If the international student held a valid secondary study permit and submitted the application to extend/change condition to a post-secondary study permit, can the student start the post-secondary program before the condition change application is approved?
2. In the event of the student receive the notification of approval for their co-op work permit but lost the hard copy in the transit, can the student start the co-op term giving that the student already applies for a replacement?
3.In the event of the student receive the notification of approval for their co-op work permit but not yet receive the hard copy, can the student start the co-op term?
4. Pursuant R215 (1) (c), the work permit holder can apply for study permit inside Canada. Would working holiday work permit count to R215(1)(c)?
Thank you in advance for your time and effort.
ation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello
Please accept our apology for the late response to your enquiry. Please find below response to your questions:
1. If the international student held a valid secondary study permit and submitted the application to extend/change condition to a post-secondary study permit, can the student start the post-secondary program before the condition change application is approved? Response: Under current guidelines, no, an international student who holds a valid secondary study permit, and who submitted an application to extend/change condition to a post-secondary study permit, cannot start the post-secondary program before the condition change application is approved. Note that if a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada
2. In the event of the student receive the notification of approval for their co-op work permit but lost the hard copy in the transit, can the student start the co-op term giving that the student already applies for a replacement? Response: The student would still have the status of being able to work in Canada. However, depending on the requirements of the employer, they would not be able to prove their status until they receive their replacement co-op work permit.
3. In the event of the student receive the notification of approval for their co-op work permit but not yet receive the hard copy, can the student start the co-op term? Response: Note that the notification itself is not the co-op work permit. The student would then not be able to prove their status unless they have the co-op work permit hard copy (the hard copy would also have the validity dates of the co-op work permit). Also, the student would only be able to work within the validity dates of their co-op work permit.
4. Pursuant R215 (1) (c), the work permit holder can apply for study permit inside Canada. Would working holiday work permit count to R215(1)(c)? Response: The type of work permit you get for Working Holiday is an open work permit. This would fall under R215(1)
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Query re eTAs and cancellation of eTAs upon becoming a permanent resident/PR -- REP-2018-1838--
threads.question:
This query is regarding the cancellation of an eTA when a foreign national becomes a permanent resident of Canada.
1) when is an eTA delinked or cancelled when a foreign national who has an eTA on his or her passport becomes a PR either through (a) landing at a port of entry, or (b) attending an in Canada interview to obtain PR status [those two things are broken down in case there is a difference in treatment]?
2) If the foreign national has more than one passport with an eTA, does the eTA only get delinked or cancelled on the passport that the foreign national used in the PR application and when landing to become a PR, or are eTAs on other passports that the foreign national has also delinked or cancelled? For example, someone holding a UK and an Italian passport, but they used the
L'information divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accès àlinformatior UK Passport in the PR application, and provided a copy of the Italian one with the PR application. They land and become a PR using the UK passport. Both passports have eTAs on them – does the eTA on the Italian passport get cancelled by IRCC or CBSA after the person becomes a PR?
3) Does IRCC have a policy or directive regarding cancelling eTAs when a foreign national becomes a PR and if so, can it be provided?
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day,
Any eTA associated to the client's immigration file will be cancelled by an officer once their permanent resident status is confirmed.
An eTA can only be held by foreign nationals; once a foreign national becomes a Canadian permanent resident (PR), they are no longer eligible to hold such a document. Legislation stipulates that the permanent resident visa is a required document for a foreign national seeking to establish permanent residence (A20(1)(a), R50) and, on the contrary, an eTA is an entry requirement for a foreign national seeking to enter Canada and remain on a temporary basis (A11(1.01) and R7.1). IRCC's longstanding position is that once a foreign national becomes a PR, their PR visa is 'spent', and, if they previously held a TR document (eTA or temporary resident visa), it is no longer valid. Neither a PR visa nor a temporary resident visa or eTA can be
used by a PR to enter Canada after landing.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR) receive an electronic authorization counterfoil (e-foil) that will allow them to board a flight to Canada to land as a permanent resident. The legislation requires permanent residents to prove their status to be allowed entry to Canada by producing a permanent resident card. Once they have become a PR, they will be required to pres ent a PR Card or a Permanent Resident Travel Document (PRTD) to be allowed to board subsequent flights to Canada.
Kind regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Work Permit Condition --REP-2019-0658--
threads.question:
#### Dear Immreps,
I am seeking confirmation that a change of position within the same NOC Code will not require a change of occupation on the work permit if the work permit contains a condition that the states the worker is not authorised to work in any occupation other than stated.
Thanks so much.
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION: a change of position within the same NOC Code will not require a change of occupation on the work permit
ANSWER: It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker –
i.e. employer, occupation orlocation.
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must:
- be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary
mmigration, Refugees
Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker.
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1)of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the
increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMlA-exemption.
Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it
may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must
receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change.
If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer. Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and
provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for
compliance purposes.]
Thank you kindly

threads.subject: Level of studies, students transitioning from ESL to Academic Programs --
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am requesting clarification in a few grey areas we are facing in assisting our students at Vancouver Island University (VIU). VIU has high school for International students and transitioning to University level studies requires the student to have a new Study Permit to continue at the University.
As per IRPR Section 215 (1) (f, i) and 216 (1) (a) students transitioning from secondary level to university level and must be accepted and may extend their study permits within Canada.
Questions:
1. Can high school graduate on valid study permit continue their studies on implied status (from secondary to University level) while waiting for a new Study Permit for the University level?
Yes. A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have implied status as a temporary resident during that period. If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
However, please note that the conditions of the study permit would remain the same (ex: work conditions).
mmigration, Refugees
2. High school students on visa (eTA) who studied less than six months would they apply for study permit outside of Canada? If so, would they benefit from biometrics exemption?
Foreign nationals in Canada without a study permit who are studying at the preschool, primary or secondary level may apply for a study permit from within Canada as per [R215(1)(f)(i)]. More information can be found at the following link: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.html)
There is a temporary public policy exemption for in-Canada applicants. More specifically, foreign nationals who are eligible to apply from within Canada would normally provide their biometrics as part of an application or request for
a temporary resident visa (TRV) a work permit or study permit a temporary resident permit permanent residence
However, since there is currently no biometric service delivery network within Canada, these applicants are exempt from the biometrics requirement until such time as the public policy is lifted. Applicants who apply from within Canada, but whose applications are not eligible to be processed from within Canada, are not covered under this public policy exemption. Those applicants are required to leave Canada in order to submit their biometrics as part of their application. For more information: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/identity-management/biometrics/exemptions.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/identity-management/biometrics/exemptions.html)
We also continuously face challenging situations when ESL students successfully complete their program and transition to concurrent Academic Programs of study. We have sometimes cases that ESL student's spouse was issued open Work Permit and waiting time for Academic Programs start is up to 9-11 months. We would appreciate clarifications to the following questions:
1. Can ESL student who have successfully graduated from a language program and are waiting to start an Academic Program work off campus up to 150 days (between programs)?
Students are not eligible for the off-campus work permit program if they are registered in an ESL/FSL course. Even if they have completed their program, they remain restricted to the conditions of their current study permit. The students can submit an application to change conditions, extend their stay or remain in Canada as a student.
Depending on the student's eligibility, they may be able to work off-campus if they obtained a new study permit for their academic program. More information on off-campus work can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html)
2. Spouses of ESL Program who holds open work permit, are they eligible to start working while Principal Applicant is still in ESL program?
Yes.
Also, number of our graduate programs have Internships at VIU. Often student's Coop Work Permit is not issued at Port of Entry. We encourage them to apply for Coop Work Permit online before they start their Internship. We have following questions in this regard:
1. Can student start Internship by substituting Study Permit work authorization if student applied for Coop WP online?
Off-campus work authorizations are not a substitute for internships requiring a coop WP. If the student is authorized to work off-campus, they can work for any employer for up to a maximum of 20 hours per week. However, to be eligible to work off-campus, the student must be enrolled in full-time studies.
For more information: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html#fulltime-status
2. Can student flagpole for Coop Work Permit if needs urgently to start his/her Internship?
Foreign nationals may apply for a work permit on arrival at a port of entry (POE) in Canada if they are exempt from the requirement for a temporary resident visa and their job falls within the International Mobility Program (ex: Coop work permits).
Sincerely,
Zare.Atabak

threads.subject: Spousal Open Work Permit Validity -- REP-2018-1589
threads.question:
From Hello,
I’m writing to clarify the specific circumstances in which a spousal open work permit (issued to the spouse of a full time student) would be considered invalid, and in particular, whether an officer can impose conditions that would render a work permit invalid in circumstances not described in R209.
It is my understanding that spousal work permits only become invalid upon expiry (or if a removal order becomes enforceable), regardless of the status of the study permit holder spouse, per R209. This has also been confirmed in recent correspondence with IRCC. However, lately we have been seeing some spousal work permits issued at the POE that have included the following comment under the “Remarks/Observations”: "**Note: Open work permit only valid while spouse is a full time enrolled student at a designated learning institution**"
mmigration, Refugees
This does not appear to be consistent with R209 and it does not appear that R185 includes authority for an officer to impose a condition that alters when a work permit would become invalid. And, even if an officer can impose such a condition, the statement referred to above is not being included as a condition (i.e.: noted under the “Conditions" section of the work permit) but rather as a remark, so it does not appear to fall under the authority of R185.
Questions:
1) Does the inclusion of such a comment on an open work permit render the work permit invalid once the spouse (study permit holder) is no longer enrolled as a full time student at a DLI?
a. If so, does the spousal open work permit holder also benefit from the 90 day bridging period allotted to study permit holders, so that they can transition to a subsequent status (i.e.: work permit extension or visitor extension)?
2) If this comment holds no authority, can the open work permit holder continue to use their work permit until its expiry (as per R209), even with the comment included?
a. Should they apply for an amendment of their document to remove the comment?

threads.answer:
Good day,
We apologize for the delayed response.
This is in response to your question regarding the validity of an open work permit issued to the spouse of an eligible foreign student under R205(c).
As per R183 and R209, a work permit becomes invalid when it expires or when a removal order that is made against the permit holder becomes enforceable. As such, the validity of the spousal work permit is independent of their spouse's study permit, meaning the spousal work permit will remain valid until the indicated expiry date. If the work permit holder should wish to renew their spousal work permit and they would need to either qualify themselves for an employer-specific work permit or seek a visitor record as their spouse is no longer a full-time student at a DLI.
If the work permit holder would like the remark provided below to be removed from their work permit, they would need to submit a new application including the fees. In this situation, this change would not meet the requirements of an amendment request.
To note if a study permit holders chooses to no longer actively pursue their studies at a DLl while in Canada, the study permit holder may be in non-compliance of their study permit conditions as per R220.1 (1) and must change their status or leave Canada.

Co-op work permit program for post-secondary international students is intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLl) in Canada. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
The work that student will be undertaking is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. If the practical component of student's studies is an essential part of their program, i.e. the student will not be able to complete their studies and receive their degree without completing the practical component of their studies, then the student is eligible to apply for a coop work permit.
Since it appears that the students in theprogram have the option to choose another course instead of undertakingandcourses, these courses don't appear to be an essential part of their program, and thus wouldn't qualify for a co-op work permit program. threads.answer:
Hello,
This is in response to your query of January 21st, in which you were seeking guidance on what name to use for the work permit application form.
For Immigration and Citizenship lines of business, based on the Naming Procedures: Name Structures and how to record them in GCMS, if an individual only has either a given name or surname, the name should be recorded in the surname field as the primary identifier and the given name field should be left blank. This complies with International Civil Aviation Organization Standards on Machine Readable Travel Documents, Part 4, which indicates that although primary identifier (surname) and secondary identifier (given names) are mandatory, if there is no secondary identifier, the field is to be left blank. The MRZ is the main area that should be relied upon to establish the client's primary name, even if a passport is non- compliant with ICAO standards. In cases where the issuing state has included the full name in the same field of the MRZ, the names should not be arbitrarily broken down in to various names and inserted into distinct fields of GCMS. threads.question:
Subject: Minors applying for citizenship Dear Sir/Madam, Can you please clarify the content in the below link? [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility/minors.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility/minors.html) Under the question: Have been physically present in Canada 3 out of the last 5 years It shows "No" if Minor (under age 18) has a Canadian parent or a parent who is applying for citizenship at the same time As per the above, it means that if a parent lives in Canada and meets the residency obligations can apply for Citizenship with his permanent residence minor child who is not living in Canada and did not meet the residency obligations. In other words, a permanent residence minor child has no obligations to meet the 3 out of 5 years presence in Canada in terms of applying for citizenship with his/her parent(s). I appreciate if you send more clarification on that matter.
Lnfomn
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Thank you for your inquiry. As indicated in the link you are referring to, there are currently two pathways to citizenship for minors (under 18) – subsection 5(1) and subsection 5(2). The requirements for minor applications submitted under subsection 5(2) are not the same as those submitted under subsection 5(1) and vice versa – key differences between these subsections are captured in the chart below:
Applying under subsection 5(1) Apply under subsection 5(2)
For minors without a Canadian parent For minors with a Canadian parent OR who don't have a parent applying for OR who have a parent applying for citizenship at the same time as them citizenship at the same time as the
Minor required to meet residence Minor not required to meet residence requirements (physical presence and requirements income tax, if applicable)
Minors who have a Canadian parent to apply for citizenship on their behalf OR minors who are applying for citizenship at the same time as their permanent resident parent(s) are intended to apply under subsection 5(2). Under this subsection, there is no obligation for the minor applicant to meet physical presence (physically present in Canada 3 out of the last 5 years prior to their citizenship application). With this being said, the minor is required to be a permanent resident of Canada and must not have lost this status or have any unfulfilled conditions related to that status (inclusive of meeting all residency obligations).
To address your specific question, if a parent lives in Canada and meets the residence requirements of Canadian citizenship, the minor child is not required to meet any physical presence obligations if they are applying under subsection 5(2). However, all minors must maintain their permanent resident status until they are granted citizenship as well as take the oath of citizenship, if 14 years of age or older.
Let us know If you have any other questions or require further clarification.
Thanks!
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Proof of Settlement Funds might include detailed bank statements for the previous six months but must include a letter from one or more banks presenting "the average or the balance for each month ending." The applicant should try to ensure that officers have sufficient information to determine that funds are legally accessible to the foreign national for their free and exclusive use to support settlement upon arrival.
2- In extenuating circumstances, a letter of explanation may help officials with their assessment of an applicant's settlement funds. Ultimately, the applicant must satisfy the officer that funds are available and transferable, unencumbered by debts or other obligations, and sufficient to support initial establishment in Canada. Applicants are advised to provide as much detail as possible. Proof in the form of official letters or statements from financial institutions confirming available savings or investment account balances, bank drafts, money orders and similar financial instruments are the clearest evidence of such funds.
3-The applicant must provide proof the spouse's funds are available to assist with settlement and can be accessed by the principle applicant at any time, especially where the spouse is non-accompanying. The proof could be in the form of funds held in a joint account with the spouse, or a letter of commitment from the spouse the funds will be readily available to the principle applicant.
For any debts: Proof of settlement funds should include sufficient evidence the funds are unencumbered by dept. Proof could be in the form of a letter from lending institutions and any other evidence available such as statements from credit institutions.
The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient proof of funds to satisfy an IRCC reviewing officer making a decision on the application.
For further information please refer to the following links: Proof of Settlement Funds
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Co-op Work Permits or On Campus Work -- REP-2019-0743
threads.question:
Hello ImmReps,
I hope this email finds you well.
We have two questions about the Co-op Work Permit category:
1) If an international student chooses to add a compulsory co-op placement to their program of study, does this render the student eligible for a co-op work permit?
2) If the location of work for a co-op placement is on-campus, can the international student work in that co-op placement on the basis of their valid study permit, without a separate co-op work permit? Or is a separate co-op work permit required despite the location of work?
Thank you and best regards,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Please see response to your questions
1) If an international student chooses to add a compulsory co-op placement to their program of study, does this render the student eligible for a co-op work permit?
Co-op for post-secondary international students is intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLl) in Canada. In other words, they would not complete their program without completing the co-op work portion. By choosing to add a co-op placement, it appears that the co-op placement is not an essential part of that program. If a similar program is offered without the requirements of a co-op placement, the co-op placement is not then an essential part of that program of study.
2) If the location of work for a co-op placement is on-campus, can the international student work in that co-op placement on the basis of their valid study permit, without a separate co-op work permit? Or is a separate co-op work permit required despite the location of work?
There's no hour limitation for on-campus employment. This work may contribute to a co-op requirement provided they observe the work authorizations on the study permit.
NOTE: if the work to be undertaken is in an occupation in which the protection of public health is essential, as described in the following guidelines ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/standard-requirements/medical-requirements/exam/who-must-submit- immigration-medical-examination.html), the applicant must wait until their co-op work permit has been issued before they may begin work.
IRCC would still encourage that students in co-op programs apply and hold a co-op work permit, in case if they find co-op employment off-campus and their co-op work commitments surpass 20 hours/week.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Thank you,

Minimum requirements
Skilled work experience Skilled work experience means you've worked in 1 of these National Occupational Classification (NOC) job groups:
- Managerial jobs (skill type 0)
- Professionai jobs (skill levei A)
- Technical jobs and skilled trades (skil level B)

threads.subject: Visitor Record Remark Enforceability -- REP-2019-0746
threads.question:
From Dear ImmReps,
We are following up on our correspondence below, as we have not yet received a response.
When there is a Remark on a Visitor Record that says “Must Confirm Departure at the Port of Entry”:
1) If the individual leaves Canada at any time during the validity period of their Visitor Record, is this Condition seen to have been met?
2) If the individual submits a Visitor Record Extension application from within Canada before the Visitor Record expires, is the individual still obligated to depart Canada, or can they remain in Canada and benefit from implied status as a visitor?
Thank you in advance for your assistance.
Kind regards,
Lnformon
threads.answer:
Good day,
If a foreign national is required to confirm their departure at a port of entry, as may be indicated on a Visitor Record, the foreign national is required to present themselves to a CBSA officer at a port of entry PRIOR to leaving Canada.
If a foreign national applies to extend their stay before their current status expires, they are required to depart Canada either: a-before the expiry of the new Visitor Record, or b-immediately following the refusal of the extension application.
If the extension application is refused, the foreign national is subject to the conditions on the original Visitor Record and is required to confirm their departure with a CBSA officer prior to leaving Canada. If the extension application is approved, the foreign national should abide by any conditions detailed in the remarks section of the new Visitor Record.
Please note, The typical service standard for responding to an enquiry is 20 business days.
Thank you, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

As you may know, in order for IRCC to provide a permanent resident (PR) card to a PR, they must provide their address in Canada, as per section 58(1) of the Immigration and Refugee
In order to allow the Department to provide a permanent resident card, a permanent resident referred to in paragraph 53(1)(a) must provide to the Department, within 180 days
On occasion, an officer at an IRCC office or Canadian point of entry may accept an address of a paid representative, service provider, or relative, depending on the circumstances. threads.subject: Adding a Spouse to a pending CEC application --REP-2018-1973
threads.question:
Hello,
If an applicant with a pending CEC application gets married, can you please clarify the process of adding the spouse (whether accompanying or not) and how the CRS points will be adjusted in the Express Entry system.
Thank you for your prompt attention.
Best,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Dear M:
To add a spouse after an e-APR has been submitted, the applicant would need to send a Webform to inform IRCC. The applicant will then be contacted regarding additional documents and fees. Based on the documentation provided by the applicant, the officer will determine whether applicant's score will be recalculated.
The Ministerial Instructions list the MEC for Express Entry. Applicants must meet the MEC to be accepted into the Express Entry pool and must also meet the MEC when they are issued an ITA and when they submit their e-APR.
If an applicant's situation changes in the time between when they receive an ITA and when they submit their e-APR to such a degree that their qualifications fall below the MEC, the application must be refused under section A11.2. The officer will also consider whether the application should be refused for not meeting the minimum requirements of the federal program to which they are applying or for misrepresentation.
If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is equal to or higher than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application will not be refused under section A11.2, as long as the applicant's supporting documentation corroborates their claims and they continue to meet the MEC for Express Entry, including the requirements of the program
under which they were invited to apply.
If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is lower than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application will be refused under section A11.2 for not having maintained the qualifications that would justify the ITA.
Please note that the onus is on the applicant to satisfy an officer that they meet all the requirements.
We hope this information is helpful.
Regards,

threads.subject: travail entre la fin des études et la demande de PTPD --REP-2019-0599
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Un étudiant étranger termine sa formation le 1er décembre 2018. La lettre de son établissement d’enseignement confirmant la fin de sa formation lui est remise le 2 décembre 2018.
Il demande un PTPD le 4 janvier 2019.
L’étudiant en question avait-il le droit de continuer de travailler, ne serait-ce qu’à temps partiel, entre le
1er décembre 2018 et le 4 janvier 2019 ?
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Merci
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Pour répondre à votre question, lorsque l'étudiant reçoit une confirmation écrite de son établissement d'enseignement indiquant qu'il a terminé son programme, il n’est plus autorisé à continuer à travailler au Canada, puisqu'il ne répond plus aux critères d'admissibilité énoncés à l'alinéa R186v). Il doit présenter une demande pour changer son statut (p. ex. changement pour un statut de visiteur) ou quitter le Canada avant que son permis d'études ne devienne invalide, conformément à l'article R222.
Conformément à l'alinéa 186w) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR), les étudiants ayant terminé leur programme d’études peuvent travailler en attendant qu'une décision soit rendue à l'égard de leur demande de permis de travail s'ils étaient inscrits à plein temps dans un établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) à un programme postsecondaire de formation générale, théorique ou professionnelle, et s'ils ont respecté le maximum d'heures de travail autorisé.
Ceci dit, un étudiant ayant reçu une confirmation qu'il a complété son programme d’études et qui n’est pas en attente de décision à l'égard d’une demande de permis de travail n’est pas autorisé à travailler au Canada.
Cordialement,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Implied Status Work to Study Permit and Non-Credit Short Courses --REP-2019-0677
threads.question:
# Hello,
I am a RISIA working at the and I have a question I was hoping to get a response. If an individual originally on a work permit applied for a study permit before the work permit expired and they are authorized to stay as a temporary resident by law until a decision is made [R183(5)], would this person be able to start studying a short term non-credit course that was less than 6 months in length before receiving approval of their study permit? I am understand that it's explained on the IRCC website that "if you come to Canada on a work permit and then apply for a study permit, you must stop working when your work permit expires and cannot start studying until you receive your study permit", as well as "if you don't have a study permit: you can apply for a study permit from inside Canada, but you can't start
ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
your program until you get the permit", but I'd like to know if this applies for a student taking 1 course for upgrading which is 4 months in length and a non-credit course.
Thank you for your time.
Best regards,
nmigration, Réfugiés nd Citizenship Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months).
Holding a study permit for short-term courses may allow students to apply later, from within Canada [R215(1)(a)], to renew or change the conditions of their study permit for further studies. Study permit holders may also be eligible to participate in work programs that are available to international students [R186(f) and R205].
With the exception of exchange programs, even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit.
While a foreign national may attend a short-term course or program without a study permit at a non-DLl, they may not be
issued a study permit to attend courses at a non-DLI [R216(e)].
For more information, please visit our webpage on who needs a study permit: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-)
refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study- permits/who-needs-study-permit.html
We hope this information is useful to you.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I am wondering whether it is possible for someone currently in Canada on a post-graduation (open) work permit to apply for a study permit. Will they both be valid at the same time, or will the study permit will invalidate the post-graduation work permit?
I believe one will invalidate the other, but I would like your confirmation. If they are both valid at the same time, what will be the conditions of the work permit?
I am asking this question because I came across this question/answer stating that those with study permits can also apply for an IEC work permit and use both at the same time:
[http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum-934&top=25](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum-934&top=25) Although my question is not about IEC, I am wondering about this issue since I came across that question. Please kindly verify.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
There is no legal restriction to a temporary resident holding a study and work permit simultaneously. The issuance of one permit does not automatically invalidate a previously issued permit.
Each permit application is based on the information provided by the foreign national for that application. A temporary resident may legally hold more than one permit at a time if the processing officer is satisfied that the person meets the requirements of the program they are applying under.
The onus, as always, remains on the applicant to establish that they are a bona fide temporary resident who will leave Canada following the completion of their studies and/or work.

threads.subject: In-Canada CL Sponsorship Question--REP-2019-0815-
threads.question:
Good morning,
Does a young couple have to both be inside Canada when they submit a SCLIC In-Canada Sponsorship application? Specifically, does the applicant have to be in Canada at the time of submission?
I know a Canadian sponsor can be residing abroad as long as she will be living here when the applicant becomes a PR. I know an applicant can be in Canada without valid status at the time of submission. I'm now wondering if the applicant has to actually be in canada at the timeof the submission? Can submit their In-Canada Sponsorship Application (and OWP application) prior to moving back to Canada?
This particular couple currently lives in New Zealand and are planning on moving to Canada in the summer. I'm wondering if they can submit their In-Canada application prior to the move back to Canada?
Page 3381
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your enquiry.
Applicants submitting applications under the in-Canada class and the open work permit pilot must be in Canada to apply.
To be eligible under the Spouse or Common-law Partner in Canada (SCLPC) class a sponsor and applicant must be residing together in Canada. This is a primary requirement of the SCLPC class, and it is set out in section 124(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Ce:
Good day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. Question:
We are seeking your guidance on whether an individual would receive the 200 CRS points based on their arranged employment if: The individual has a valid job offer (meeting the definition of a valid job offer) under the Express Entry system; Has been working in Canada in a NOC Ojob on a work permit that is exempt from needing an LMIA and is currently working for an employer specified on the work permit, has more than one year of full-time work experience and has a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after the issuance of the permanent resident visa; and An error was made on the individual's work permit stating a NOC 0 occupation instead of a NOC 00 occupation, however, an amendment has been submitted to amend the NOC code from a NOC 0 to a NOC 00 occupation retroactively (covering the whole duration of their work permit).
In this situation, will this individual be able to obtain the 200 CRS points? Response:
In order to obtain 200 points for Qualifying Offer of Arranged Employment, at time of decision the IRCC reviewing officer must be satisfied the PA meets the requirement pursuant to the Ministerial Instruction (MI's), under s29(2)(a)(iii). The applicant must hold a work permit on which is indicated the name of the employer who provided arranged employment for an occupation under a skilled NOC 00. In addition, the applicant works for that employer and must have worked for one-year continuously in Canada for that same employer on a full-time or equivalent part-time basis. Also, as stipulated under R82(1) of IRPR, the arranged employment must be for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one-year after the applicant is issued a permanent residence visa.

[http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2002-227/page-19.html#docCont](http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2002-227/page-19.html#docCont)

threads.subject: Work without a Work Permit while on a Work Permit ---REP-2018-2033-
threads.question:
Good Morning Madame/Sir,
Could you please tell me, if a foreign national is in Canada with an employer specific Work Permit and has been asked by that employer to do something that is not within the scope of employment on the Work Permit but would fall under the category of Work without a Work Permit, is the foreign national then required to leave and re-enter Canada to obtain approval to do such activities, or can the foreign national conduct such activities without going through that process? If so, is there any other process that they would have to go through to ensure compliance?
Thank you for your time.
Sincerely,
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
L'nformaonduuedoislsinftion
threads.answer:
Hello,
Answer: It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing additional duties, thereby increasing weekly hours, and a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker-i.e. employer, occupation or location. Or, if the change in working conditions negatively impacts the worker, such as reduction in hours or salary, then a new Offer of Employment and a new work permit would be required before the change takes effect, otherwise the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend duties, hours or salary information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
mmigration, Refugees
Additional points to note:
An increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same” wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMlA-exemption. Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered. In that case, a new Offer of employment and new work permit may be required. In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties outside of the original NOC, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer. Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers
Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those
requirements for compliance purposes.]
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: FOR REVIEW AND APPROVAL: TRAVEL OUTSIDE CANADA OF A PERMANENT RESIDENT WHO USED TO BE A CONVENTION REFUGEE--REP-2018-1887
threads.question:
Good afternoon Sir/Madam:
This question is related to avoiding cessation of protection and not related to residency obligation.
I have a client who used to be a convention refugee and he now has become a permanent resident in Canada. He is an engineer who has received an offer of employment from an oil service company that operates in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Sudan, Guinea and Zimbabue (A multinacional company that has offices in various countries, not originally a Canadian company). My client will request his travel document because he does not want to have his Besides the conditions related to his residency obligation, does he have any other conditions that will prevent him on taking this job offer?
We request clarification given that he used to be a convention refugee and now he will require to enter Canada every
mmigration, Refugees 1*1
Informatn disosddefomtionAc L'nformtonduveduaatio 45 days, to stay 45 days and then leave again for another 45 days. My client does not want to jeopardize is residency in Canada or be the subject of a cessation of refugee protection because he is no longer continuously remaining in canada, as his family will remain in Canada.
Thank you very much for your consideration herein,
Yours,
threads.answer:
Good day,
If your client wishes to travel in order to go work outside of Canada, he has to apply for a Refugee Travel Document, which is recognized as a valid travel document and can be used to travel to other countries. Your client should also contact the consulate or embassy of the countries where he will be travelling to work in order to determine if he will also need a visa to enter these countries.
As for the return to Canada, since your client holds permanent resident (PR) status, he will need his Refugee Travel Document as well as a valid PR card to re-enter Canada. If he is not in possession of a valid PR card but still decides to travel abroad, your client will have to apply from outside Canada for a permanent resident travel document (PRTD) and demonstrate that he meets the residency obligation.
Please note that your client should no longer use or apply for a passport from his home country. In addition, if your client was to travel to his country of origin, he could be the subject of a cessation of refugee protection (and possible revocation of his PR status), as it may be considered that he voluntarily re-availed himself of the protection of his country of nationality.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: - FW: DUI law changes---REP-2019-0610
threads.question:
Good day,
I am in urgent need of receiving clarification and documentation directly from IRCC on the matter of the DUl law changes as of December 18, 2018. There was much information prior stating that DUl offence (among others) would become serious criminality on or after this date.
However there is no information now.... The online Canadian criminal code is contradictory ( the effective date is Dec
6, 2018) but the last modified date is Dec 19, 2018. The online CCC is not listing s. 255 as serious criminality for offences. Please advise IRCC's stance on DUl law- are DUI's serious or minor criminality. This is a major issue for admissibility to Canada and there is no public information.
I hope my inquiry is clear.
Thank you,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello
We apologize for the delayed response to your query. We trust that the response below will allow you to better instruct your clients on matters related to the recent amendments to the Criminal Code by the provisions of Bill C-46.
Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, serious criminality is a category of criminal inadmissibility that applies to both permanent residents and foreign nationals. It can be triggered by the maximum possible sentence or the actual sentence imposed, i.e.: •People who have been convicted of an offence inside Canada that has a maximum possible sentence of 10 years or more, or who have been convicted (or committed) an equivalent offence outside Canada; or, People who have been convicted of an offence in Canada for which the person received an actual sentence of more than six months. Under the new impaired driving rules, the maximum penalty for most impaired driving infractions has increased from five to 10 years (where no bodily harm or death occurs). As a result, most impaired driving offences could lead to a finding of inadmissibility for serious criminality under Canada's immigration laws. We are aware that the online version of the Criminal Code may not reflect the changes brought by Bill C-46, however;
they came into force on December 18th, 2018. For more information, please visit:
[http://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/42-1/bill/C-46/royal-assent#enH492](http://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/42-1/bill/C-46/royal-assent#enH492)
To note, criminality is a category of inadmissibility for offences that do not meet the thresholds for serious criminality (including offences with a maximum possible sentence of less than 10 years). It applies to foreign nationals only.
Impaired driving offences committed on or after December 18th, 2018 are considered serious criminality, while offences committed prior to this date may be considered criminality.
For additional information on the implications of Bill C-46 on inadmissibility assessments, please visit the questions and answers section of our website: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=152&top=8](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=152&top=8)
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I'm waiting for my post-graduation work permit. Can I

●You can leave Canada and return, as long as your visa or Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) is still valid.

Implied status [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/implied-status-extending-stay.html
Temporary resident : Implied status (extending a stay)
This section contains policy, procedures and guidance used by staff. It is posted on the Department's website as a courtesy to stakeholders.
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to
have implied status as a temporary resident during that period.
If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
Implied status and travelling outside Canada
A temporary resident with implied status who has left Canada may be allowed to
- re-enter Canada as a temporary resident, pending a decision on the renewal of their application to study or work in Canada, provided they are temporary resident visa (TRV)-exempt, as per section R190, or on a multiple-entry visa.
They may not resume work or study in Canada until their application for renewal has been granted. Those not able to resume work must satisfy the border services officer that they have sufficient means of support.
It should be noted that this applies to foreign nationals who are TRV exempt, as per paragraph R190(3)(f), and to those with multiple-entry visas. Temporary residents from TRV-required countries who have implied status and are seeking re-entry to Canada following a visit solely to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon are still considered to be TRV exempt, as per subparagraph R190(3)(f)(ii). In this case, their period of authorized stay is extended, pending a decision. This interpretation of the legislation is consistent with the Federal Court decision of De Brito v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration);
- apply for a new work or study permit at the port of entry (POE), provided they have a right to do so under the IRPR.
Temporary residents from TRV-required countries who are on implied status and are seeking re-entry to Canada following a visit solely to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon may apply for a new or subsequent work permit at the POE, as they fall under the exception of subsection R198(1).
Note: It is strongly recommended that, at the POE, the temporary resident present documentary proof of their application (copy
of their application, copy of the fee payment receipt, etc.) for an extension as a visitor, student or worker.
If the foreign national must res ume work or study, they can apply for a new work or study permit at the POE, but only if they are authorized to do so under the IRPR.
Best Regards,
Lnfomn

threads.subject: Question for Express Entry -- REP-2019-0792
threads.question:
Hello,
We have a question in regards to Express Entry.
Our client has a work permit for a company in Canada to work as the Chief Executive Officer. He also owns a 41.46% share of the parent company, and subsequently, for the company in Canada.
Please advise if we would be able to count this as Canadian work experience, or if it would be considered as self-employment in Canada, and as such, would not qualify for points under Canadian work experience.
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
The assessment of an individual's employment status is undertaken on a case-by-case basis, considering their particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer.
As per paragraph 15(7)(b) of the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System and paragraph 87.1(3)(a) of the Regulations, periods of self-employment do not count for purposes of points for 'Canadian work experience' under the CRS or meeting the work experience requirement under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed. Under the CEC, self-employment will not be included in calculating the period of work experience.
IRCC officers consider various factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed. You may wish to provide any of the information/documentation listed below in support of your client's application:
- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work; whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work; the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and any other relevant factors, such as written contracts; Any other documentation including bank statements, third party references, invoices, etc., if applicable
An applicant may choose to request a ruling from the CRA to have their employment status determined. Such a ruling will state whether, in the view of the CRA, a workeris an employee or self-employed, and whether or not that worker's employment is pensionable or insurable. A worker may request a ruling by sending a letter or completed Form CPT1, Request for a Ruling as to the Status of a Worker under the Canada Pension Plan and/or the Employment Insurance Act to their tax services office. This ruling may thereafter be submitted to IRCC to supplement a PR application.
Please note that the onus is on the applicant to prove that he/she was not self-employed during their period of qualifying work experience in Canada.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your questions, please see our responses below.
Question 1) If an individual starts a program of studies at a DLl university as part-time, but then switches to full time studies: Do they need to revise the study permit? Answer: Study permit holders who are currently part-time and wish to study full-time may do so without making an application to amend their permit.
Question 2) If yes to 1, how can they do this? Should they make an application to amend their permit? Answer: See question 1.
Question 3) When they switch to full-time, and make any requisite amendments to their study permit, will they then be able to pursue off campus employment? Answer: The study permit holder may work off campus once they are studying full-time and if their study permit has given the appropriate work authorizations.
If a study permit does not have conditions relating to off campus work, they may request an amendment only if the individual was eligible to work off campus at the time of application. If an individual was not eligible to work off campus at the time of application, they would need to apply for a new study permit and demonstrate that they meet the requirements for off campus work.
We hope this information was of assistance.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
