Hello,
Thank you for your enquiry.
Applicants who submit an application under the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class must live with their sponsor in Canada, maintain temporary resident status in Canada and be subject to a sponsorship application. These legislative requirements which are found under section 124 of the Regulations must be met throughout processing. Periods away from each other of short and limited duration such as vacations or business trips are generally not viewed as a period living apart. However, the circumstances of each application is assessed on its own merits, and the sponsor and applicant must be able to satisfy an officer that they are continuously living together in Canada.
Couples applying as common-law partners must be able to establish that they have been living with their partner for at least 12 consecutive months in a marriage-like relationship to be eligible under the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class. The requirement for common-law partners to cohabit in a conjugal relationship for at least one year is stated in section 1(1) of the Regulations. As previously mentioned, applicants must continuously live together in Canada to be eligible.
Please refer to the Complete Guide, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, and the Program Delivery Instructions.

threads.subject: Rétablissement de statut et 150 jours de congé d'études-besoin de clarification règlementaire -REP-2019-0649-
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Nous avons quelques étudiants dans la même situation et nous voudrions avoir des clarifications règlementaires de votre
mmigration, Refugees
part.
Les étudiants avec des permis d’études expirant au 31 août 2018 et ayant envoyé leur demande de renouvellement depuis l’intérieur du Canada à la mi-août ont reçu leur réponse de la part d’IRCC à la fin octobre – début novembre suite aux longs délais de traitement d’IRCC. Pendant cette période ils étaient en statut implicite et nous avons pu conserver leur inscription, mais, afin de respecter les règlements d’immigration et nos obligations avecle Ministère d’Éducation du Québec, celle-ci a été annulée immédiatement dès qu’ils ont reçu leur refus.
Les étudiants ont envoyé leurs demandes de renouvellement de permis d’études avec rétablissement de statut suite au refus, c’est-à-dire, autour de la mi-novembre 2018. Le site d’IRCC affiche que vous travaillez en ce moment sur les demandes reçues le 6 novembre 2018. Cependant, certains étudiants ayant envoyé leur demande avant n’ont toujours pas de réponse et pour ceux l’ayant envoyé autour du 12-15 novembre elles ne sont bien sûr pas encore traitées.
À la date limite d’inscription à laquelle les étudiants doivent avoir leurs documents d’immigration en règle (CAQ et permis d’études) est le 18 janvier 2019 pour cette session, soit, vendredi prochain. Cette date ne peut pas être reportée, car nous devons respecter les règlements du Ministère d’Éducation du Québec qui nous obligent à vérifier cela. Étant donné les longs délais de traitement d’IRCC, il est fort probable qu’une partie de ces étudiants ne puissent pas non plus être inscrits à cette session d’hiver 2019.
IRCC a publié le 7janvier dernier des clarifications concernant l’évaluation des conditions liées à un permis d'études. À la lumière de la situation décrite ci-dessus, nous voudrions savoir :
1. Est-ce que le délai de 150 jours pour un « congé d’études » s’appliquerait dans ces cas de figure?
Selon nous, cela serait totalement inéquitable, car c’est une situation hors du contrôle de l’étudiant et causée par les délais de traitement d’IRCC (et du MIDI pour ce qui est des renouvellements des CAQ en été 2018). Cela dit, si la réponse est oui,
2. À partir de quel moment le délai commence à compter parmi ceux indiqués ci-dessous?
a. La date du premier jour de cours de la session régulière à laquelle l’étudiant n’a pas été inscrit (dans le cas de figure présenté, fin août 2018)
b. La date du refus de permis d’études
c. À partir du 91 jour de l’émission du refus (car l’étudiant a 90 jours pour faire sa demande de rétablissement de statut)
d. Tout autre
3. Est-ce que cette situation les rendrait inadmissibles au programme du permis de travail post-diplôme?
Nous comprenons que les clarifications sont nouvelles et que notre demande exige peut-être des vérifications, mais ce sont des cas réels et une réponse rapide de votre part serait grandement appréciée. Cordialement,
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Nous regrettons le délais de réponse à votre question.
Le respect des conditions liées au permis d’études est évalué pour la période de validité du permis d’études seulement. Le délais de 150 jours ne s’applique donc pas lorsqu'un permis d’études est expiré.
Vous trouverez de plus amples renseignements surle statut implicite au lien suivant: [https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-guides/bulletins-guides-](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-guides/bulletins-guides-) operationnels/residents-temporaires/visiteurs/statut-implicite-prolongation-sejour.html
Prolongation
- Si la prolongation est approuvée, la date de délivrance inscrite sur le document est la date à laquelle la décision a été prise. Les commentaires dans la section réservée à cet effet devraient préciser que le demandeur a conservé son statut en vertu du paragraphe R183(6).
- Si la prolongation est refusée, le demandeur conserve son statut jusqu'à la date à laquelle la décision est prise.
- Si la prolongation est rejetée (incomplète), le demandeur conserve son statut jusqu'à la date d’expiration indiquée sur le document de résidence temporaire.
Remarque : Si une deuxième demande de prolongation est envoy ée après une première demande et que la décision prise relativement à la première demande a été :
- approuvée, alors le nouveau statut s’applique.
- refusée et que le permis original était toujours valide lorsque la deuxième demande a été reçue, alors le demandeur conserve son statut implicite jusqu'à ce qu'une décision soit prise relativement à la deuxième demande, et le demandeur est sans statut à partir de la date du refus de la deuxième demande.
- refusée et que le permis original était expiré lorsque la deuxième demande a été envoyée, alors le demandeur n’a pas le statut implicite et est considéré comme étant sans statut. (Puisque son permis original était expiré, le demandeur doit présenter une demande de rétablissement. La deuxième demande sera donc retournée au demandeur parce que les frais de rétablissement étaient manquants.) rejetée parce qu'elle n’était pas complète, alors la demande est renvoy ée au demandeur. On considère que la demande n’a jamais été reçue, le statut implicite n’est pas octroyé et le demandeur conserve son statut jusqu'à l’expiration du document de résidence temporaire.
Cordialement, La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Canadian interests

threads.answer:
Ce:
Hello,
Correct, completion of studies refers to a successful graduation of studies. A study permit holder who drops out of their program of study or who takes a break in their program is not considered to have completed their studies. As such, R222(1)(a) does not apply and the study permit remains valid. Although the study permit does not become invalid, as per as per R220.1(1), the study permit holder in Canada is still subject to the following conditions:
- they shall enroll at a designated learning institution and remain enrolled at a designated learning institution until they complete their studies; and
- they shall actively pursue their course or program of study.
Any break in studies which is outside of a regularly scheduled break (e.g., the summer break) would be not be treated in the same way as a regularly scheduled break. Officers would be assessing whether the study permit holder is in compliance with the above study permit conditions during a break in studies which falls outside of a regularly scheduled break.
Information on how an officer assesses student compliance with conditions can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/assessing-conditions.html

threads.subject: [CPD-2019-0150] s.5(2) application for minors without a Canadian parent --REP-2019-0849
threads.question:
Section 5(2) of the IRPA clearly indicates citizenship shall be granted to any permanent resident who is THE MINOR CHILD OF A CITIZEN. It says nothing about minors whose parents are PRs applying for citizenship at the same time.
However, every guide on CIC's website clearly indicates that a minor child applying for citizenship under s. 5(2) can be a child whose parent is also applying for citizenship OR has a Canadian parent. i.e. there is no requirement that one parent be a citizen.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/application-canadian-citizenship-minors.html-specifically](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/application-canadian-citizenship-minors.html-specifically) says this form is for an application under subsection 5(2) intended for minors who are PRs of Canada who are applying at the same time as their parent OR who already have a Canadian parent.
mmigration, Refugees
More specifically, CiC's website clearly indicates that the 1095 day requirement is not a requirement for minors applying
under 5(2).). [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-)
citizen/eligibility/minors.html This PDF document reiterates that: [https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/pdf/minors-applying-citizenship.pdf](https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/pdf/minors-applying-citizenship.pdf)
If a PR parent applies for citizenship alongside their PR minor child (with no Canadian parent), does the minor child have to comply with the 1095 day residency requirement?
If a minor child has to apply under 5(1) even though they have a parent applying for citizenship at the same time, it is clear by 5(3)(b)(ii) that the 1095 day requirement can only be waived on compassionate grounds by the minister.
Lnfomn
threads.answer:
Greetings,
Thank you for your query. These are two separate categories of grant applications.
If minor children apply for citizenship under subsection 5(2), and are applying concurrently (or not) with a parent, they are not subject to the physical presence requirement. A minor child may apply under subsection 5(1) (a minor 5(1) application) with or without their parents, in either case they are subject to the physical presence requirement. A waiver of this requirement can be requested and will be assessed by the delegated decision maker.
Please note that under subsection 5(2), there is no requirement for a minor applicant to have a Canadian parent at the time of application for citizenship however, parentage to a Canadian parent must be established in order for the minor to be granted citizenship.
In answer to your specific question: If a PR parent applies for citizenship alongside their PR minor child (with no Canadian parent), does the minor child have to comply with the 1095 day residency requirement? -Not if the PR parent applies under subsection 5(2) of the Act for the child.
I hope this will be helpful to you.

Good afternoon;
Recently, I have received a few queries about the ability for a student to work Off-Campus as self-employed.
I have reviewed the 2018 Annotated Immigration and Refugee Protection Act of Canada, as
well as the Temporary Resident Program Instructions, the Employer Portal overview, IMP and
TFWP program instructions.
I have not been able to find anything that prohibits self-employment for students.
Unfortunately, the only reference to self-employment for a student I could find was in terms
of "On-Campus" work ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-)
citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-on-campus.html ). I assume that the self-employed work referred to in this case would be as a tutor or coach to other students. The queries I have received are from foreign nationals that want to work off-campus as self-employed. Given that a student would not require an Offer of Employment or LMIA, I cannot see a strict reason that would prohibit self-employment (outside of CRA requirements).
If self-employment is permitted as a student, would a holder of the Post-Graduate Work Permit be permitted self-employment? Again, the PGwP does not require an Offer of Employment, so there would be no need for an employer portal.
Although there are some FAQs about self-employment on work permits, it appears that these references are to the federal self-employed cultural benefits stream, or as part of the start-
formation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
up visa program.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our website for the requirements to work off campus as an international student. Provided the student meets the requirements along with the conditions on their study permit that authorizes them to work off campus, the student is permitted to be self-employed.

If yes, are there any criteria, such as initial legal entry, etc.?

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Can a foreign national who is not allowed to work in a country outside of Canada, but who has nevertheless acquired dully documented work experience (pay stubs, contracts, attestations, tax declarations) have that work experience be taken into account under the FSWP and Express Entry? If yes, are there any criteria, such as initial legal entry, etc.?
Answer:
The applicant's status abroad while accumulating work experience does not form a part of the minimum requirements for FSW nor the requirements in the Ministerial Instructions. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that they meet the minimum requirements of FSW and the requirements in the MI's, even though the applicant did not have the required status to perform the work abroad. In addition, there is no hindrance in the Express Entry systems in creating a profile or submitting an application based solely on the issue of the applicant's status in a foreign country.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Question Regarding International Mobility Program, Change of Conditions--REP-2019-0638-
threads.question:
Hello,
I have the following question regarding an LMIA Exempt Offer of Employment:
submitted and filed, an LMIA Exempt Offer of Employment through the Employer Portal. The request filed in the Portal was for a Visiting Professor for 12 months with no financial compensation from An LMIA Exempt Application Number was received and the Visiting Professor applied for an obtained a work permit to come to Since arriving at
the hosting unit would like to provide a monthly living allowance to the Visiting Professor.
Can you please advise if a living allowance can be provided within the current LMIA Exempt Offer or if a new LMIA Exempt
Offer and work permit are required before a living allowance can be provided?
Thank you.
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day,
Apologies for the delay in response.
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker –
i.e. employer, occupation or location.
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not
required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same” wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMlA-exemption. Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment
mmigration, Refugees
as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it
may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer. Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.]

Mail received time: Mon, 4Mar 2019 09:09:42
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
In order to get transferability points for Education, more points are awarded for those who have Two or more post-secondary program credentials AND at least one of these credentials was issued on completion of a post-secondary program of three years or longer.
Question for Principal Applicant: If an individual has only had a Masters from a accredited US university assessed and the Masters requires a bachelor's degree, is the individual required to obtain an ECA for both the master's and the bachelor's degree or is an ECA for the highest credential assessment sufficient?
If the ECA for the Master degree states that an admission requirement is a bachelor degree, is the assessment different? Or is an ECA for the underlying bachelor's degree still required to obtain the transferability points?
Question-For a spouse: a Maximum of 10 points is possible for the Master's degree (or professional degree). Therefore, I would assume an ECA for just the master's would be sufficient.
Answer:
The principal applicant earns the same CRS points with a Master's degree OR for two post-secondary degrees where at least one of those credentials was obtained upon the completion of a post-secondary degree of three years or longer. Therefore, an ECA for only the highest level of education would be sufficient to receive the maximum CRS points under "Skill Transferability".
In addition, the principal applicant is not required to obtain an ECA for the Bachelor's degree due to the admission requirement indicated on the ECA for the Master's degree.
For the spouse, an ECA for only the highest level of education is required to receive the maximum CRS points under Level of Education".

Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Bridging Open Work Permit (BO WP) Eligibility for Applicant under the New Interim Pathway for Caregivers--- REP-2019-1014--
threads.question:
Hello,
The IRCC website here states the following:
You may be eligible for a bridging open work permit if:
- you applied for permanent residence
- your current work permit expires in 4 months or less
- you have valid status on your work permit •you are currently in Canada
Assuming a foreign national meets the above-mentioned requirements, would that foreign national be eligilbe for a BOWP if they submit their PR application under the new Interim Pathway for Caregivers?
The list of programs on IRCC's website does not include the new Interim Pathway:
You can only qualify if you applied to one of these permanent residence programs:
- Federal Skilled Worker Program.
- Canadian Experience Class,
- Federal Skilled Trades Program,
- Provincial Nominee Program,
- Caring for Children Class, or
- Caring for People with High Medical Needs Class.
Moreover, the public policy (here) regarding the Interim Pathway does not appear to address the question of BOWP eligibility.
Thank you,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Dear
Applicants under the Interim Pathway for Caregivers are eligible to obtain an open work permit under R207(d) for public policy considerations. The open work permit will be issued under LMIA exemption A70 for applicants in Canada if the meet all the necessary requirements.
To be eligible for an open work permit, the applicant must:
- be in Canada and must intend to reside in a province or territory other than Quebec;
- be authorized to work in Canada on a work permit other than a Live-in Caregiver Program work permit OR;
- be on implied status, if you have applied for a renewal of your work permit other than a Live-in Caregiver Program work permit; OR,
- be eligible for restoration of status, and held a work permit other than a Live-in Caregiver Program work permit as your most recent work permit.
- be the principal applicant on an application for permanent residence (APR) under the Interim Pathway for Caregivers;
- have received a positive eligibility assessment on your paper APR under the Interim Pathway for Caregivers.
For further information, please consult the IPC PR Application Guide 0103 - Appendix D-Maintaining your status and eligibility for an open work permit in Canada.
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
We apologize for the delayed response.
This is in response to your enquiry of minor foreign national's, on a visitor status in Canada, eligibility to apply for a study permit from inside Canada.
Please note, R215(1)(f)(i) refers to a visitor who is studying at the preschool, primary or secondary level. As the minor in this case is not studying in Canada, they wouldn't be eligible to apply for a study permit from inside Canada as per R215(1)(f)(i).
Furthermore, as per R215(2), a family member may apply for a study permit from within Canada if they are the family member of a foreign national who currently resides in Canada and holds a valid study or work permit. Otherwise, the minor would need to apply for a study permit from outside Canada.
When applying for a study permit, the parents or legal guardians must prove the minor child will have the care and support they need during their stay in Canada. Minor children under the age of 17 must either:
- come with their parent or legal guardian or
- have a custodian in Canada

threads.subject: Clarification on New PGWP Application Rules---REP-2019-0964
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry regarding PGWPP updated instructions. Please find below response to your questions:
1. If the student misses the 90 day window, a) do they apply to restore their status to student (within 90 day restoration period), b) and apply for the PGWP at the same time? c) Is this done online? d) or do they apply to restore status and when approved, apply for the PGWP? Response: If a student's study permit will expire prior to their application for PGWPP and they intend on remaining in Canada, they are advised to apply for a visitor status. Furthermore, at the time of the PGwPP application approval from overseas, an eTA or a visa will be issued as well to enable the applicant to travel back to Canada. threads.question:

threads.subject: Eligibility to File a new Sponsorship Application under Family Class --REP-2019-0899-
threads.question:
Dear IRCC Immigration Representatives,
I am looking into the following issue and I would like to receive clarification.
Fact Scenario:
nmigration, Refugees
This questions involves whether a new sponsorship application can be made. A previous sponsorship application was submitted by a previous representative on behalf of client to sponsor a spouse under family class in Canada. A fairness letter was received indicating that the sponsor was not eligible because the application was submitted within 5 years of the sponsor's landing as a permanent resident. Upon receipt of fairness letter, a request was made by previous representative to consider the application under H&C grounds and the sponsorship application was noted to have been cancelled and converted into a H&C application and forwarded to the applicable office.
The 5 year ineligible period for the sponsor has now passed. The H&C application is still pending for the spouse.
Questions:
Can the sponsor file a new application to sponsor the spouse? Specifically, with respect to question 6 under Sponsor Eligibility Assessment on Form IMM 1344, would the fact that the previous sponsorship application was cancelled and converted into an H&C application be considered a final decision on the application?
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Dear Sir:
Thank-you for your query.
Our understanding from the information you have provided is that the permanent residence application of your client's sponsored spouse has been converted to an H&C application and forwarded it to an office designated to process H&C applications. In such cases, the application is no longer a family class application, meaning there is no longer a sponsorship component, and the sponsor is not prohibited from submitting a new sponsorship application for their spouse, under paragraph 10(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPA), which states:
Multiple applications
No sponsorship application may be filed by a sponsor in respect of a person if the sponsor has filed another sponsorship application in respect of that same person and a final decision has not been made in respect of that other application.
Please note, however, that if the original application has not been converted to an H&C application, ie. that is still being processed as a family class sponsorship application the sponsor would be prohibited from submitting a new sponsorship application for their spouse under R10(5) because a final decision on the original application has not been rendered.
If your client were to submit the a new sponsorship application, the 5-year sponsorship bar would be moot if more than 5years has passed since becoming a permanent resident.
Trust this addresses your concerns.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: CUSTODY OF CHILDREN AND THE IMM5604E--REP-2019-0906--
threads.question:
Dear ImmReps,
My name is Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant (ICCRC #
I have a lady who was divorced from her ex-husband in 2015. The divorce certificate from the Court indicates the Custody Right of the daughter belongs to her.
She has not kept contact with her estranged husband since then, and absolutely has no ideas where is his whereabout.
The lady is going to file the Spousal Sponsorship application. The IMM5533 checklist requires her to submit the IMM5604 E- Declaration from Non-accompanying Parent/guardian for
Minors Immigrating to Canada.
I have research OP Manuals and have not found IRCC's position on this matter. We have the divorce certificate with her having the full-custody right of her daughter, and the Affidavit from the lady confirming that she has been tried her best and unable to locate her estranged husband. Is it sufficient?
We thank you very much for your help and assistance. We truly appreciate that.
Sincerely yours,
nmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day,
Custodial matters can be complicated and IRCC assesses these issues on a case-by-case basis. As a rule, onus is on the applicant to provide evidence that they have full, uncontested custody of a dependent child. If the parent and child are seeking to come to or remain in Canada permanently, the accompanying parent must normally be in possession of official documentation verifying that the non-accompanying parent has no claim to custody nor any objection to the removal of the child from the country of origin. This ensures that processing the dependent child for permanent residence will not violate the terms of any custodial agreement or arrangements nor contradict any international family law.
The Document Checklist IMM 5533 provides information on the requirements for minor children on p.6, Section 3 “Additional Information about Children”. It provides the following instructions on custody issues for minor children:
any child(ren) under 18 will be issued an immigrant visa as part of this application, and your sponsor is not their other legal
parent, you must complete the Declaration from non-accompanying parent/guardian for minors immigration to Canada
(IMM5604) form ([http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/pdf/kits/forms/IMM5604E.pdf](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/pdf/kits/forms/IMM5604E.pdf)) for each child, and submit a copy of an identity document for the parent who signed the declaration. The parent's signature must appear on the identity document. If you are divorced or separated from that parent, you must also include a copy of any related custody agreements demonstrating that the child is free to move to Canada. If the other parent is deceased, provide a copy of his/her death certificate. If you are unable to provide documents showing that your child's other parent has no objection to your child's immigration, you must provide a detailed explanation. You do not need to submit this if your child is not accompanying you and will not be issued a visa.
The Family Class Program Delivery Instructions for Dependent Children provide instructions on custody issues. These instructions state that applicants who have included in their application children who are subject to custody orders must provide proof that they are allowed to remove the children from the area of jurisdiction of the court. These instructions are available on IRCC's website at [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/non-economic-classes/dependent-children.html#dependantType.
In the specific case you described, we recommend you submit a copy of any related document showing custody agreements, such as the divorce certificate detailing custody arrangements, and the affidavit of the applicant explaining why she is unable to provide documents showing that the other parent has no objection to the child's immigration to Canada.
An officer must review the full circumstances of the case to decide whether to proceed to process a dependent child for permanent residence where written confirmation of no objection from the other biological parent cannot, for all practical
purposes, be obtained.
We hope this answers your question.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I kindly request clarification regarding the below requirements under Canada-European Union (EU) Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) – Contractual service suppliers and independent professionals (work permit required/LMIA exemption codes T47 and T43):
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/international-free-trade-agreements/canada-eu/contractual-service-providers.html
Specific criteria for independent professionals
Independent professional means a self-employed professional who has a contract to supply a service to a Canadian consumer.
In addition to the general criteria listed above, as an independent professional, the applicant must also:
- be engaged in the supply of a service on a temporary basis as a self-employed person
- possess at least six years of professional experience in the sector of activity which is the subject of the contract as
of the date of submission of an application for entry into Canada
Example: A self-employed Italian management consultant seeks entry to Canada to provide services to a technology company under the terms of a pre-arranged contract.
My question relates to who must submit the required offer of employment through the IRCC Employer Portal and pay the $230 employer compliance fee if the self-employed foreign national has a contract with an entity in Canada who would like to engage his services on a temporary basis but for their client in Canada. Would it be the entity that has the contract with the FN or the end client who receives the service? It should be noted that part of the direction and supervision come from the company in Canada who contracts the FN, and part – from the end client in Canada.
Also, please advise what “a copy of a signed contract between the service provider and the Canadian service consumer” means in the above context so it is clear between whom the signed contract should be as there are typically several layers of contractual obligations in many instances. Please also note that in many business scenarios companies in Canada have a vast client base, however, the contract is typically drawn between the Canadian entity who contracts the foreign national and not between the end client and the foreign national. Good day, Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox with your question. Please find further clarifications
regarding the education requirements below:
In order to be eligible under the Caring for People with High Medical Needs program, applicants must meet all the eligibility criteria as established in the Ministerial Instructions. In regards to the education requirements, applicants must have obtained:
a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies, or
•a foreign diploma, certificate or credential, along with an equivalency assessment-issued within five years before the date of application -that indicates that the foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies.
As per subsection 73(1) of the Regulations, "Canadian educational credential" is defined as, "any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions." Therefore, the education would not be eligible unless the applicant completes and receives the education credential as it is defined in s.73(1). Additionally, please note that s.73(1) explicitly says that an equivalency assessment applies to a foreign diploma, certificate, or credential. In order for a student (including exchange students) to be eligible to work off campus, they must

threads.subject: International students who work as Uber/Lyft drivers --REP-2019-2276-
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I have three questions regarding international students who work for Uber and/or Lyft. The concern of many students I had consultation with was how 20 hours of work is defined for an Uber/Lyft driver.
1. When they are available to pick up customers (in traffic, waiting to be called) they are online on the app. Do the hours they are online also count as the hours they work? Or are they considered to be working only during the hours they have a customer in their cars?
2. Uber sends CRA the gross earning and kilometers of each driver, not the times they are online looking for customers or the times they have customers in their cars. This is recorded in the app but not shared with the government. (This is what Uber told one of the students I talked with, attached is an example he sent me) In this case, how will the government know whether the student exceeded 20 hours or not if Uber is not sharing the hours data? Would it be a good idea to submit the hours they work for Uber during an Express Entry application, assuming it could be asked?
3. Many students use Uber and Lyft at the same time to increase their prospects, and this means that they are online on both apps at the same time. Do you think this would be an issue? Would they look as if they worked for 40 hours instead of 20? Do you think this is something that needs an upfront explanation in an Express Entry application in case of the risk of being found inadmissible due to unauthorized work?
Thank you.
Best regards,
nmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Ce:
Hello,
Please find the responses to your questions below:
Question 1: When they are available to pick up customers (in traffic, waiting to be called) they are online on the app. Do the hours they are online also count as the hours they work? Or are they considered to be working only during the hours they have a customer in their cars?
Response 1: These hours would not count towards the hours they work. The time that would count towards their hours worked would be from the time the trip is confirmed to the time the trip is completed.
Question 2: Uber sends CRA the gross earning and kilometers of each driver, not the times they are online looking for customers or the times they have customers in their cars. This is recorded in the app but not shared with the government. (This is what Uber told one of the students I talked with, attached is an example he sent me) In this case, how will the government know whether the student exceeded 20 hours or not if Uber is not sharing the hours data? Would it be a good idea to submit the hours they work for Uber during an Express Entry application, assuming it could be asked?
Res ponse 2: Yes, if Uber does not provide the hours the Uber drivers worked to the drivers, the drivers should keep track of their own hours and not exceed 20 hours per week and provide this information with the application. If Uber releases the hours worked this could be submitted during an Express Entry application. Please keep in mind the onus remains on the applicant to provide detailed explanation and upload supporting documentation that substantiates the information provided in the application and explaining the work hours situation in order for reviewing IRCC officers to make a decision.
Question 3: Many students use Uber and Lyft at the same time to increase their prospects, and this means that they are online on both apps at the same time. Do you think this would be an issue? Would they look as if they worked for 40 hours instead of 20? Do you think this is something that needs an upfront explanation in an Express Entry application in case of the risk of being found inadmissible due to unauthorized work?
Response 3: This should not be an issue as the time that would count towards their hours worked would be from the time the trip is confirmed to the time the trip is completed. (not when they are on the app waiting to confirm a pick up). Please keep in mind the onus remains on the applicant to provide detailed explanation and upload supporting documentation that substantiates the information provided in the application and explaining the work hours situation in order for reviewing IRCC officers to make a decision.
If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Thank you

threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
QUESTION: Does this mean the FW has to apply for Restoration of Status AND Extension of Work Permit to continue working in Canada?
OR
Does the FW only have to apply for Extension of Work Permit to continue working in Canada given that his work permit is
technically still valid until next year.
RESPONSE: This statement: The expiry date on your work permit is linked to the expiry on your passport. If you got a new passport because your old one was expiring, then your work permit will also expire at the same time, means that the work permit will never be issued longer than the passport validity. For example, if the passport validity is until August 15, 2019, the work permit will generally be valid to August 14, 2019. Therefore, if the foreign national is renewing their passport in July 2019, they should also expect to renew their work permit as it will also be expiring at the same time.
If a foreign national obtains a new passport several months before the expiry of their present passport and work permit, the work permit will remain valid until its actual expiry date as per section 209 of the IRPR. For example, the passport is valid to August 15, 2020 and work permit is valid to August 14, 2020. The foreign national obtains a new passport in August 2019. Their work permit would remain valid, linked to the cancelled passport, until August 2020. This is why the first part of the answer in the Help Centre question states: Keep your old passport. If you plan to travel outside Canada, bring both your old and new passport with you. You'll need your valid work permit when you come back.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Taking two 1-year post graduate certificate programs--REP-2019-2350--
threads.question:
Hello Imm Rep Box,
My question is as follows, thank you for your guidance.
If someone takes two 1-year post graduate certificate programs, can they be eligible for a 3-year post graduation work permit?
If the answer to the above question is yes, is there any requirement that after the 1 st program is completed, how soon the 2nd
program has to be started? Thank you.
Can they be eligible for a 3-year PGWP if they take the two programs simultaneously, one being in full time basis during the day, and 2nd one being part time taking evening classes? Thank you very much!
Regards!
threads.answer:
Good morning,
This is in response to your August 27 enquiry regarding PGWP eligibility.
Question: If someone takes two 1-year post graduate certificate programs, can they be eligible for a 3-year post graduation work permit?
Answer: When combining the length of two programs of study, the length of the work permit will combine the length of each program (each program of study must meet all PGWPP eligibility requirements and be at least 8 months in length). If the combined length is 2 years in length or longer, the work permit may be valid for up to 3 years.
Question: Is there any requirement that after the 1st program is completed, how soon the 2nd program has to be started?
Answer: When combining two programs of study for the purposes of considering PGWP validity, there may be a break between the two programs of study. The student only has to maintain continuous full-time studies during the program they are enrolled in at the time. The second program has to be completed within two years of completing the first program.
Questions: Can they be eligible for a 3-year PGWP if they take the two programs simultaneously, one being in full time basis during the day, and 2nd one being part time taking evening classes?
Answer: No. When combining two programs of study for the purposes of considering PGWP validity, the student has to maintain full-time status in each program they are enrolled in. In the abovementioned scenario, only the full-time program would be considered when determining the length of the PGWP.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

passport or towards the end of the initial PGWP that's given for 1.5 years?

Yours truly,
mmigration, Refugees
ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Apologies for the delay in responding.
You will find below in red answers to your questions.
1) Are there any specific financial/income requirements for applicants before they can be approved for permanent residence? When the Pilots were first announced, there was a requirement to demonstrate certain minimum “settlement funds” depending on the family size. It was posted on the IRCC website in late June-early July 2019, and it was reported in Canadian major media sources: i720[https://www.thestar.com/news/gta/2019/07/09/foreign-caregivers-say-changes-aimed-at-helping-them-](https://www.thestar.com/news/gta/2019/07/09/foreign-caregivers-say-changes-aimed-at-helping-them-) realize-their-immigration-dreams-come-with-a-costly-catch.html When I tried to locate that information again last Thursday (July 25), I could not find those details for minimum settlement funds anymore. Does it mean that the requirement for specific minimum income does not exist any longer for PR applicants under HCCP and HSW Pilots? Answer: There is no specific proof of settlement funds eligibility reguirement under the new Home Support Worker or Home Child Care Provider pilots. However, all applicants for permanent residence are subject to a financial admissibility requirement, including caregivers. Under the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker pilots the financial admissibility assessment is completed as part of the pre-assessment to permanent residence, before caregivers come to Canada. That being said, caregivers must continue to meet all admissibility requirements, including the financial admissibility requirement, at the time permanent residence is issued. For in-Canada caregiver applicants who have acquired the work experience before applying to one of the pilots, the caregiver applicant will be assessed for all criteria and all admissibility requirements when they apply to permanent residence. An officer will take several factors into consideration when assessing this requirement. Examples can include, but is not limited to: potential income of the caregivers and accompanying spouse/working age dependants and living arrangements.
2) Please clarify what categories of those applicants present in Canada are eligible to submit in-Canada WP applications. Are they the same as those listed under R199? The IRCC website does not make it fully clear. For example, the “How to apply” section states the following for in-Canada application eligibility: [...] have a valid study or work permit, are on implied status or eligible for restoration [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/child-care-home-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/caregivers/child-care-home-)
mmigration, Refugees
support-worker/no-experience-apply.html
Does it mean that only those that are on implied status or in restoration from SP/WP are eligible? What about those previously visitors and now in implied status or in restoration?
Answer: They are the same as those listed under R199 which means that someone on a visitor status (or on implied status or in restoration as a visitor) would not be eligible to apply for the work permit from within Canada. That does not mean they would not be eligible to apply for one of the pilots but they would need to use the outside of Canada form to apply for the work permit. On the page you provided, you would need to select outside Canada and get the instruction guide for applicants outside Canada.
Applicants who have a valid work permit or study permit or are on implied status or in restoration as a worker or a student would be able to use the package for inside of Canada applicants.
3) According to Ministerial Instructions #32 for the HCCP and HSW Pilots, applicants must demonstrate having attained a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies, or an equivalent “foreign diploma, certificate or credential”. Does this exclude those who completed 2+ years of post-secondary education abroad but did not attain a certificate or diploma? In other words, if the equivalency assessment equates their education to 1 or more years of post-secondary studies (again, not a diploma or à credential earned) – do such applicants meet the education requirement under MI #32? Answer: If an applicant has a foreign education credential, they will need an Education Credential Assessment (ECA) from a designated organization. In order to qualify, the ECA report must show that the applicants foreign education credential is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies. Only completed foreign education credentials can count towards meeting this requirement. See here for further information. If you have further questions on ECAs, you can contact a designated organization. We trust this information will assist you. Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox.

#### Canada ---REP-2019-2279-

Question 1: For minor students, if they come on a visitor visa and would like to stay and study, can they apply from within Canada? Mostly, these students come with their parents who are also visit visa holders. Answer 1: If the minor comes to Canada on a visitor visa and their parent only has a TRV and/or visitor record the minor would not be eligible to apply for a study permit within Canada. A minor child who comes to Canada on a visitor visa can apply for a study permit from within Canada pursuant to R215(2) of the IRPR which states:
Family members
(2) A family member of a foreign national may apply for a study permit after entering Canada if the foreign national resides in Canada and the foreign national
(a) holds a study permit;
(b) holds a work permit;
(c) holds a temporary resident permit issued under subsection 24(1) of the Act that is valid for at least six months;
(d) is subject to an unenforceable removal order;
(e) is a member of the armed forces of a country that is a designated state described in paragraph 186(d);
(f) is an officer of a foreign government described in paragraph 186(e);
(g) is a participant in sports activities or events, as described in paragraph 186(h);
(h) is an employee of a foreign news company as described in paragraph 186(i); or
(i) is a person who is responsible for assisting a congregation or group, as described in paragraph 186(l).

Au nom de l’Ordre des comptables professionnels agrées du Québec, nous souhaitons confirmer l’obligation d’un permis d’études à l’égard de certains candidats étrangers souhaitant obtenir le titre de Comptable Professionnel Agrée (CPA).
CANDIDAT QUI SUIT UNE ÉQUIVALENCE
Nous faisons référence au candidat détenteur d’un diplôme universitaire à l’étranger qui devra suivre des cours supplémentaires auprès d’une université québécoise.
L’équivalence du baccalauréat peut varier. Ainsi, un candidat formé à l’étranger pourrait avoir à réussir au Québec un minimum de trois cours (9 crédits) ou un maximum de 23 cours (environ 69 crédits). Dans le cas où le candidat n’a que 3 cours à réussir et qu’il n’obtient pas de diplôme, nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis.
Toutefois, dans le cas où le candidat aurait à faire 30 crédits et qu’il peut obtenir un certificat universitaire, nous comprenons qu’un permis d’études est requis.
Après son inscription à l'Ordre, le candidat dispose de 7 ans pour compléter son cheminement et obtenir son permis d’exercice CPA. À l’intérieur de cette période, le candidat doit réussir le Programme de Formation Professionnelle CPA (PFP –
nmigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés nd Citizenship Canada d under the Access to Information Ac
CPA).
Le PFP-CPA peut être complété suivant l’une des deux voies suivantes :
1. Compléter un programme national dispensé par l’Ordre d’une durée de 12 à 24 mois offert en ligne à temps partiel et avec un encadrement personnalisé par les partenaires universitaires de l’Ordre.
À noter que :
- Le programme est composé de 6 modules et il n’est pas un programme d’étude à temps plein. En effet, un étudiant doit consacrer en moyenne 13 à 17 heures par module par semaine);
- La durée de chaque module est de 8 semaines. Le contenu de la formation est en ligne et inclue un atelier en salle de classe ainsi qu’une évaluation finale.
- Les frais reliés à l’inscription aux modules sont payés à l’Ordre et non pas à l’Université;
- Les universités agissent à titre de partenaire de l’Ordre;
- Le programme ne mène pas à l’obtention d’un «diplôme»; Le contenu de la formation est en ligne o Le programme national permet à un candidat de travailler à temps plein.
Nous souhaitons confirmer l’obligation pour le candidat qui suit un programme national dispensé par l'Ordre d’obtenir un permis d’études.
2. Suivre un programme universitaire de 2e cycle d’une durée de 9 à 16 mois offert à temps plein par les universités accréditées par l’Ordre. Il est à noter que ceci est un programme universitaire diplômant (DESS). Par conséquent, nous comprenons que l’étudiant doit obtenir un permis d’études.
Pour votre information, une fois le programme de formation professionnelle CPA complété suivant l’un des deux parcours ci- dessus (le candidat peut aussi effectuer le stage en même temps que ces études s’il le souhaite), le candidat doit suivre un stage d’une durée de 24 mois. Ensuite, le candidat doit réussir l’examen final commun se déroulant sur une période de trois jours (4h/5h et 4h). Une fois toutes ces étapes terminées, une demande de permis CPA peut être faite.
CANDIDAT QUI BÉNÉFICIE D’UN ARRANGEMENT DE RECONNAISSANCE MUTUELLE QUÉBEC-FRANCE
L’Arrangement de reconnaissance mutuelle Québec-France s’applique aux membres de l’Ordre des experts-comptables de France ou qui détiennent un diplôme d’expertise comptable de France.
La première étape consiste à déposer une demande d’admissibilité auprès de l’Ordre. Ensuite, l’Ordre communique avec le candidat pour confirmer son admissibilité à l’arrangement de reconnaissance et il devra réussir la formation complémentaire. Cette formation complémentaire vise le CPA ou CPA Auditeur :
Formation CPA : composée des webinaires entre 15 à 20 heures de formation ainsi qu’une formation en éthique de 7 heures offerte à distance en ligne.
Nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis dans le cadre de la formation CPA d’un candidat qui bénéficie d’un arrangement de reconnaissance Québec-France
Formation CPA Auditeur : composée des webinaires entre 15 à 20 heures, d’une formation en éthique de 7 heures offerte à distance en ligne ainsi que d’une formation supplémentaire de 28 heures offerte à distance en ligne.
Nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis dans le cadre de la formation CPA-Auditeur d’un candidat qui bénéficie d’un arrangement de reconnaissance Québec-France.
Nous vous prions de bien vouloir confirmer l’obligation d’un permis d’études pour chaque situation précédemment décrite, ce qui facilitera l'accompagnement de l'Ordre aux participants et partenaires.
Si vous souhaitez des renseignements additionnels ou des clarifications à l’égard des programmes, n’hésitez pas à nous contacter.
Sincères salutations,
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Ce courriel est en réponse de votre correspondance datée du 29 août 2019.
Candidat qui suit une équivalence
Question : Nous faisons référence au candidat détenteur d’un diplôme universitaire à l’étranger qui devra suivre des cours supplémentaires auprès d’une université québécoise. L’équivalence du baccalauréat peut varier. Ainsi, un candidat formé à l’étranger pourrait avoir à réussir au Québec un minimum de trois cours (9 crédits) ou un maximum de 23 cours (environ 69 crédits). Dans le cas où le candidat n’a que 3 cours à réussir et qu’il n’obtient pas de diplôme, nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis.
Réponse : Pour déterminer si une personne est éligible à une dispense de permis d’études, c’est la durée prévue du programme qui importe plutôt que le nombre de crédits à compléter. En vertu de l’alinéa R1 88(1)( c) du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés un ressortissant étranger peut étudier au Canada sans permis d’études s’il suit un cours ou un programme de moins de six mois. Les étudiants étrangers qui ne possèdent pas de permis d’études ne peuvent pas obtenir de prolongation de leur séjour autorisé à titre de visiteur simplement pour terminer un cours de courte durée ou un programme de moins de 6 mois qui se poursuivrait au-delà de la période de séjour autorisée initiale. Il est donc recommandé que l’étranger présente une demande de permis d’études pour un cours ou un programme d’études de courte durée s’il prévoit de faire une demande pour un autre programme par la suite.
Question : (D)ans le cas où le candidat aurait à faire 30 crédits et qu’il peut obtenir un certificat universitaire, nous comprenons qu’un permis d’études est requis.
Réponse : En effet, un étudiant étranger doit obtenir un permis d’études pour entreprendre des études ou des cours de formation universitaire ou professionnelle ou d’autres cours lorsque la durée de ceux-ci est de plus de 6 mois et qu’ils sont donnés dans un établissement d'enseignement désigné (EED) au Canada.
Question : Nous souhaitons confirmer l’obligation pour le candidat qui suit un programme national dispensé par l’Ordre d’obtenir un permis d’études (programme national dispensé par l’Ordre d’une durée de 12 à 24 mois offert en ligne à temps partiel et avec un encadrement personnalisé par les partenaires universitaires de l’Ordre). (...) Le contenu de la formation est en ligne et inclue un atelier en salle de classe ainsi qu’une évaluation finale.
Réponse : Règle générale, comme l’apprentissage à distance ne requiert pas que le candidat soit physiquement présent au Canada, un permis d’études n’est habituellement pas requis. Par contre, certains cours à distance comprennent une partie du programme au Canada (p. ex. des séances spéciales de tutorat ou d’examen final). Si la totalité du programme d’études a une durée de plus de six mois, l’étudiant doit obtenir un permis d’études pour la partie du programme offerte au Canada, même si la
durée de la partie au Canada est de moins de six mois.
Candidat qui bénéficie d’un arrangement de reconnaissance MUTUELLE Québec-France
Question : Nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis dans le cadre de la formation CPA d’un candidat qui bénéficie d’un arrangement de reconnaissance Québec-France.
Réponse : Si la formation est exclusivement dispensée en ligne (sans séances en classe ni d’examen final qui exige une présence en personne) et est d’une durée de moins de six mois, un permis d’études n’est pas nécessaire.
Question : Nous comprenons qu’aucun permis d’études n’est requis dans le cadre de la formation CPA-Auditeur d’un candidat qui bénéficie d’un arrangement de reconnaissance Québec-France.
Réponse : Si la formation est exclusivement dispensée en ligne (sans séances en classe ni d’examen final qui exige une présence en personne) et est d’une durée de moins de six mois, un permis d’études n’est pas nécessaire.
J’espère que cette réponse vous sera utile. N’hésitez pas à envoyer toutes requêtes additionnelles à l’adresse suivante :
Cordialement, La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

threads.subject: Inside Canada applications for Study Permits/Study Permit Extensions-unusual delays -- REP-2018-1487
threads.question:
Good morning,
We have noticed unusually long delays this summer regarding the processing of inside Canada applications for:
First time Study Permit applicants – ie., for workers inside Canada applying for Study Permits; and
nmigration, Refugees
Lnfmn Study Permit Extensions for both returning students and for incoming international students from Canadian high schools.
We have seen a fair number of students who were admitted to the Fall 2018 term at who applied for their Study Permits in mid-July to early August, and who have still not received a decision on their applications.
While the returning university students can benefit from implied status and resume their studies while awaiting a decision, this is not the case for admitted students who are transitioning from inside Canada worker status or who are coming from high school. As far as we know, those students are not permitted to start engaging in study-related activities until their Study Permit applications have been approved. Many of these students have tried to contact IRCC to discuss their situation, but have been unable to get through due to the high volume of calls being received.
My questions are the following:
Is there anything that these students can do in order to have the processing of their applications expedited? In particular, the incoming high school students?
Are the unusually long processing times related to the closure of the Vegreville processing centre?
Can you provide any indication as to whether processing times for Study Permit Extensions and new Study Permit applications from inside Canada will shorten in the near future?
As you are aware, students in Quebec have the additional hurdle of first applying for their CAQ from Immigration Quebec, which also adds time to their overall application process. It is unfortunate that students who applied for their Study Permits in July/early August are now facing the difficult decision of whether or not to defer their studies – including all of the inconvenience, financial and otherwise, this may cause.
Any feedback you can provide regarding this issued would be greatly appreciated.
Best,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Ce:
Hello
We discovered this unanswered request for functional guidance from some time ago. We apologize that it has taken us this long to respond, and hope this information is still of use to you.
Processing times can fluctuate due to a number of factors, including higher than normal volumes and operational factors. While we strive to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times may sometimes increase due to these factors, and others.
Since you sent this request, we have introduced a facilitative measure which allows foreign nationals transitioning from one level of study (e.g. secondary to post-secondary) to begin studying immediately once they have submitted their application. This provision also applies to exchange students and those who have completed a prerequisite course or program.
In addition, as of April 11, 2019, students transitioning between levels of study (primary, secondary and post-secondary) are no longer required to apply for a new study permit, provided their current study permit is still valid. They should still update their DLI in their MyAccount, and may want to apply to change their study permit conditions to reflect that they are now eligible to work on or off campus or apply for an extension.
Applicants who were not previously studying must still wait to begin their studies. To ensure a decision is made on their application in time for the beginning of their studies, we recommend they ensure their application is complete and that it is submitted as soon as possible. We post current processing times on our website.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at Representantsimmigration.IRCC@.cic.gc.ca.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Work Permit Processing Question--REP-2019-2102
threads.question:
Hello,
My question is below:
A number of our clients previously filed work permit applications by paper under the Business Express Program in India and I appreciate that paper processing is no longer available.
Going forward is it possible for an employer to file an application online on behalf of an employee?
It is our understanding that in the online system only an authorized representative can file a work permit application on behalf of an employer/employee or alternatively an employee can create their own portal and file an application directly themselves. I don't believe an employee can set up a portal and then have an employer submit the application on their behalf (seems to contradicts section 91).
Thanks,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see updated response below in green.
Question:
Is it possible for an employer to file an application online on behalf of an employee?
Answer:
In order to provide immigration or citizenship advice or representation "for consideration" (i.e., some kind of benefit, including financial compensation such as a fee from the client or pay/salary from an organization) an individual must be authorized under section 91 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or section 21.1 of the Citizenship Act. This includes:
A lawyer who is a member in good standing of a law society of a province or a notary who is a member in good standing of the Chambre des notaires du Québec;
Any other member in good standing of a law society of a province or the Chambre des notaires du Québec, including a paralegal; or
À member in good standing of the body designated by the Minister of Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship to regulate consultants (the Immigration Consultants of Canada Regulatory Council or ICCRC).
An employer must be authorized under section 91 ofIRPA or section 21.1 of the Citizenship Act in order to provide immigration or citizenship advice or representation. An employer is not allowed to provide immigration or citizens hip advice or representation-including submitting an application online on behalf of a client-unless they are a member of a Canadian provincial/territorial law society, the Chambre des notaires du Quebec or the ICCRC.
While employers cannot provide immigration or citizenship advice, they can provide immigration or citizenship information, including administrative help. Immigration information includes: directing someone to the IRCC website to find information; helping someone to use a computer to view, upload, download and/or print electronic documents from the IRCC website; and providing administrative support in completing IRCC forms such as transcribing responses and information provided by an applicant into IRCC application forms (employers cannot guide clients on how to answer questions, including editing or making suggestions).
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

If a foreign national holds a 10 year multiple entry TRV, but did not include required
nmigration, Refugees
documentation toward a super visa when applying for that TRV, can they present evidence of super visa eligibility at the POE (ie. medical insurance, letter from child/grandchild, evidence of medical exam, and evidence of child/grandchild's income)? Will the border services officer hand write the expiry date in their passport for two years from date of entry?
Also, IRCC's operational manual indicates that if parents and grandparents who possess a super visa a stamp in their passport with no handwritten date, or if they have no stamp, then the period of authorized stay is 2 years from the date of entry (See: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/visitors/examination-admission-port-entry.html)
- Could you please clarify how IRCC determines when a holder of a super visa is required to extend their status within Canada, when they have exited and re-entered Canada before 2 years have elapsed since their initial entry? For example, if a foreign national has a handwritten expiry date of August 13, 2021 in their passport, and they leave and re-enter Canada on January 1, 2020 and no new expiry date is handwritten in their passport, would their permitted duration of stay still be August 13, 2021? Would it be January 1, 2022? Or would it be July 1, 2020?
- If no handwritten expiry date is entered in the passport, and the applicant has exited Canada while holding a super visa, how will IRCC confirm that that foreign national has valid status when applying to extend that status from inside Canada? For example, if the applicant entered Canada with a super visa on Jan 1, 2018 and has a handwritten stamp indicating an expiry date of Jan 1, 2020. They then leave and re-enter Canada on December 1, 2019, and their passport is not stamped upon re-entry. If they apply to extend their visitor status inside Canada in April 2020, how will CPC Edmonton confirm that they remain in valid status in Canada despite the handwritten date of January 1, 2020 in their passport?
Thank you very much in advance for your reply.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
If a foreign national is not issued a super visa (PG-1 visa) then they are not eligible for the period of authorized stay of up to two years. The evidence that they meet the requirements must be submitted with their visa application and cannot be
presented at the POE.
A foreign national's temporary resident status ends once they leave Canada. Each time they return to a port of entry and are admitted to Canada and their passport is either not stamped or stamped with no handwritten date, their period of authorized stay is 2 years.
Super visa holders who don't receive a stamp in their passport may request that CBSA stamp their passport or must be able to prove to IRCC when they entered the country. Please refer to the following link for information about travellers obtaining their travel history from CBSA:
[https://www.cbsa-asfc.gc.ca/agency-agence/reports-rapports/pia-efvp/atip-aiprp/thr-rav-eng.html](https://www.cbsa-asfc.gc.ca/agency-agence/reports-rapports/pia-efvp/atip-aiprp/thr-rav-eng.html)

threads.subject: Qualifying Hours for Teachers (FSWP)--REP-2019-2409--
threads.question:
E-delivered
September 05, 2019 (MST)
Good day! I am a RCIC and would like to ask if there is a specific guideline in calculating
full-time hours for teachers to qualify for the Federal Skilled Worker Program/Express Entry.
Would you be so kind to direct me where to find the information or provide me with the details, please.
- I understand that the skilled work experience hours must be at 1,560 hours per year to qualify, the question is, how can the at least 1 year of continuous work or 1,560 hours total (30 hours per week) be met if they are asked to take summer vacation (2 months) off? Would their work experience still be counted? If so, how and if not why.
Thank you!
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
I understand that the skilled work experience hours must be at 1,560 hours per year to qualify, the question is, how can the at least 1 year of continuous work or 1,560 hours total (30 hours per week) be met if they are asked to take summer vacation (2 months) off? Would their work experience still be counted? If so, how and if not why.
Answer:
To meet the minimum work experience criteria for the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program, the applicant must have accumulated at least one year of continuous full-time (or the equiv alent in continuous part- time) paid work experience in a skilled occupation listed in Skill Type 0, or Skill Level A or B of the National
Occupational Classification (NOC) [R75(2)(a)].
To answer your question, for a teacher, a period of time where they are not working during the summer months would constitute a break in employment and would not be counted towards the one-year work experience requirement set out in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
However, if a teacher could demonstrate that they were a permanent full-time teacher (not a contract
worker), where summer and winter breaks were considered paid vacation with full pay or income
averaging, and where they are returning to work in the coming school year, the work experience should be entered continuously for the number of years worked.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question: In a situation where there is a corporate reorganization and the foreign worker impacted holds an ICT work permit and he will no longer qualify for an ICT work permit after the corporate reorganization. Can he continue working on the ICT work permit after the corporate reorganization and while his new work permit application (under a different category) is pending?
Answer:
As per R185 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act Regulations (IRPR), a foreign worker is required to obtain a new work permit when the employer, work location or occupation changes.
The intra-company transferee category allows the transfer of certain employees to Canada from qualifying foreign entities for temporary periods. To be eligible in this category, the foreign employee must be employed by a foreign entity and be transferred to a position with the Canadian entity in an executive, senior managerial or specialized knowledge capacity. This requires a qualifying corporate relationship between the foreign and Canadian entity.
- Qualifying relationship between the Canadian and foreign employer
- Qualifying relationship between the employer and the foreign worker
If a qualifying relationship ceases to exist in the wake of a corporate restructuring, there is no basis for the Canadian entity to continue to employ a foreign worker as an intra-company transferee; in which case, a new work permit would be required, and possibly a Labout Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) (if the job position no longer fits the eligibility criteria of an LMIA exempt position, i.e. intra-company transferee). Or, if the new position was still LMIA-exempt, the new employer would need to create its own employer account in IRCC's Employer Portal and submit a new offer of employment to IRCC under the International Mobility Program, and with the LMIA-exemption number (A######) generated from that submission, the foreign worker would need to apply for a new work permit.
The employer is required [R209.2(1)(b)] to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for six years after the date of issuance of the work permit to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of a compliance inspection.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions [R209.2(1)] of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure option.

A30(1) says a foreign national may not study in Canada unless authorized. A30(2) says every minor in Canada, other than a child of a temporary resident not authorized to work or study, is authorized to study at the pre-school, primary, or secondary level.
R215(1)(f) states that a foreign national may apply for a study permit after entering Canada if he or she is a temporary resident studying at the preschool, primary or secondary level. R189 allows a SP holder to continue study on implied status "since the expiry of their study permit".
nmigration, Refugees
IRCC Website ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-) bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/making-application.html#InCanada) then states that foreign nationals with visitor status in Canada and who are authorized to apply for a study permit from within Canada under R215(1)(f) may begin studies once they submit their study permit applications (the Policy'").

Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on August 29, 2019 in regards to off-campus work and completion of a program of studies.
In order to work off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(y), students must hold full-time student status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break. They may work full-time off campus during a regular scheduled break until the first date they receive written confirmation of program completion from their educational institution (for instance, an email, a letter, a transcript or a diploma), provided their study permit remains valid during this period. Once they receive written confirmation of program completion of studies from their institution, they are no longer authorized to continue to work in Canada, as they no longer meet the eligibility criteria. To answer your question, the student can work full-time off-campus from May (i.e. following final exam) until June (i.e. obtains confirmation of study).
In regards to the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) Program, graduates who apply for a work permit, such as a post-graduation work permit, before the expiry of their study permit are eligible to work full time without a work permit while waiting for a decision on their application, provided they meet all other requirements listed under paragraph R186(w).

For caregivers already in Canada they may also be eligible for other economic streams such as Express Entry, the Atlantic Immigration Pilot or the Provincial Nominee Program in their respective province. Employers also have the option to continue hiring caregivers through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program by seeking an LMIA for applicants that are already in Canada and are eligible to apply for a work permit from within Canada.
