nmigration, Réfugiés nd Citizenship Canada e en vertu de la loi sur l'accès à l'informatior establish yourself and/or proof of funds to support family members joining the application?
All applicants for permanent residence are subject to financial admissibility under section 39 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Under the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker pilots the financial admissibility assessment is completed as part of the pre-assessment to permanent residence, before caregivers come to Canada. That being said, caregivers must continue to meet all admissibility requirements,
including the financial admissibility requirement, at the time permanent residence is issued. For in-Canada
caregiver applicants who have acquired the work experience before applying to one of the pilots, the caregiver applicant will be assessed for all criteria and all admissibility requirements when they apply to permanent residence.
The officer may obtain financial evidence by collecting a statutory declaration supported by evidence of statements made to an officer. This includes evidence of
●the person's current financial situation
the likelihood that they will have access to funds
- what arrangements, if any, have been made for their care and support
Proof of funds and information on the person's current financial situation can be provided with the initial application. Together with other relevant factors, the officer may consider the funds that applicants have available to them (for example, by way of a declaration or financial documentation, at an officer's discretion) in determining whether they are able to financially support themselves and their dependents (if applicable) in Canada.
3. In the section evaluating the ability to do the work, are there a minimum number of years of experience required or is the evaluation purely on a qualitative basis?
There is no set amount of years of previous work experience required to meet the ability to perform the work eligibility requirement. A combination of factors will be taken into account when an officer is assessing the applicant's ability to perform the work. Applicants to the Home Child Care Provider or Home Support Worker Pilot must prove that they are able to do the work as it is described in the NOC job descriptions under NOC 4411 and NOC 4412. To help satisfy an officer that the applicant is able to do the work, applicants can provide proof of relevant work experience, copies of relevant education credentials or training, a copy of their most recent work permit in Canada (if they've been working in Canada) or any other supporting documentation to prove they are able to do the work.
4. Regarding the initial work permit valid for 36 months, does the initial job offer have to be of the same length and/or is there a minimum length it must be to be valid?
Under the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker pilots, applicants must have an offer of employment for full-time work from an employer in Canada but outside the province of Quebec, in the eligible occupation under which the application is made. The offer must be genuine and valid when the applicant is issued their occupation-specific open work permit (i.e., when the caregiver start working in Canada), but there is no requirement that the offer be valid for a specific period of time.
5. What happens in the event that the 24 months of experience is not completed in the maximum time of 36 months?
If they don't obtain 24 months of qualifying work experience in 36 months, their permanent residence application will be refused.
6. Regarding the employer requirements, aside from the job offer made in the IMM 5983 form, does the employer have any financial requirements, such as proof of finances, NOA, and/or proof they have enough funds to pay the worker?

The job offer to the caregiver must be valid and genuine. To determine whether the job offer meets the criteria, the officer may use the employer's household income in combination with other information provided in the Offer of Employment form IMM 5983 (PDF, 2.33 MB).
i360There is no checklist provided, but when reviewing the job offer the officer may ask the employer for more information which can include proof of funds.
7. Regarding the salary of the employee, must the minimum wage be compared to the prevailing wage in the area of the employment and industry based or simply provincial standards?
To assess whether an offer of employment is genuine, officers may consider the fact that the wage specified in the offer is aligned with the prevailing wage for the same job (i.e., with similar skills and years of experience) in the province where the work will be carried out.

threads.subject: Question re: NAFTA--REP-2019-2321
threads.question:
Hi,
The IRCC NAFTA Professionals website states that:
Additionally, to be authorized to enter Canada under the Professionals category, a professional entering Canada to be a corporate executive must be coming to work in their field of qualification, i.e. an engineer, or the details of the position requirements and job duties of a specific profession are integral to the job.
In other words, a CEO of an engineering company can enter under NAFTA if their background as an engineer is integral to the job.
Does the same extend to universities? In other words, if someone was a University Professor for most of their life, can they qualify under NAFTA if the position in Canada is that of a Dean or Faculty Manager, so long as their experience as a university professor was integral to the job?
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees *
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
A CEO of an engineering company can enter under NAFTA if their background as an engineer is integral to the job.
Does the same extend to universities? In other words, if someone was a University Professor for most of their life, can they qualify under NAFTA if the position in Canada is that of a Dean or Faculty Manager, so long as their experience as a university professor was integral to the job?
ANSWER:
The NAFTA provides for any one of the 63 covered professionals to enter as a senior executive (despite not explicitly covering senior executives) provided that the position requires that the individual be one of the covered professionals (e.g. engineer becoming a chief engineering officer, or an accountant becoming a CFO, etc.).
Even though the occupation of University Dean or Faculty Manager (NOC 0421) are not listed in Appendix 1603.D.1, as they require several years of experience as a teacher, an officer assessing the NAFTA Professional work authorization request might determine at their discretion that the applicant meets the qualifying criteria.
However, it is also possible that an officer may challenge the applicant, if the job description in the Offer of Employment (submitted by the employer through the employer portal) is notably different to what is outlined in NOC 0421 (Dean) and under NOC 4011 (University Lecturer). Furthermore, an officer might determine that Dean or Faculty Manager duties are mainly administrative, and do not include teaching; and that the job duties must be teaching for the most part, with administrative duties playing a minor role.
We recommend, before the foreign worker arrives to Canada, you seek an opinion from an IRCC International Mobility Workers Unit (please open link for more information):
International Mobility Workers Unit: Help for employers

Question
R205(b) allows foreign worker to work in Canada on the basis of reciprocal opportunities abroad. IRCC online website states that coaches only need to show reciprocity in the particular occupation back home.
Does (online guidance) mean that the coaches only need to show that Canadian coaches are being hired in their home countries or that Canadian coaches in their particular field of sports are being hired in their home countries? threads.subject: CRS points for 2 or more credentials--REP-2019-2421-
threads.question:
Dear IMMReps,
If a foreign national holds both a Diploma and a Bachelors degree from the same DLI, can they be awarded CRS points for having two or more Canadian post-secondary credentials if the Bachelors degree was completed after only two years because transfer credits from the Diploma program were accepted to fast-track the second (bachelors) credential? Does it matter
whether the Diploma program and the Bachelors degree are completed in different disciplines?
Regards,
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee 's Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Pursuant to R73.1, a Canadian educational credential means any diploma, certificate or credential, issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions. In addition, the credential must meet the requirements stated in the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions -MI 11(3) and MI 30 (1)-(5). We would like to clarify that not all the educational credentials issued by a designated learning institution (DLI) meet the definition of R73.1 and/or the MIs.
As you may be aware, a candidate will be awarded education points under the Comprehensive Ranking System and the Federal Skilled Worker selection grid for having 'two or more post-secondary program credentials' if the educational credentials represent separate certificates, diplomas or degrees. To get points for having two or more credentials, at least one of the credentials must be for three or more years of study. There are no restrictions as far discipline of studies.
In order to make a determination, the officer will refer to the program description and program duration as confirmed by the
educational institution in the written confirmation of program completion (e.g., diploma/degree, transcripts, letter of
completion).
Pleases keep in mind that the onus remains on the applicant to provide all the documentary evidence to satisfy the officer that they meet all the requirements.
We hope this information is helpful.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The intent of the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) is to make permanent residence more accessible to skilled workers who have demonstrated an ability to integrate into the Canadian labour market. threads.subject: --REP-2019-2190-
threads.question:
Regarding international students taking authorized leaves from studies, IRCC specifies that authorized leaves must not be more than 150 days. Also, IRCC specifies that regularly scheduled breaks must not be more than 150 to a maximum of 180 days per calendar year cumulatively. If any of the two above breaks is more than 150 days a student must change their status to Visitor.
However, it does not appear that IRCC specifies what to do in a situation when a student studies full-time in, for example, a Winter semester preceding regularly scheduled summer break (no more than 150 days) and then goes on an authorized leave (no more than 150 days) due to pregnancy in a Fall semester right after a summer scheduled break.
Based on the above situation, the student is not required to change their status to Visitor because any of the two breaks from studies is more than 150 days.
Could you please advise if this is correct?
Best regards,
rmation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question regarding authorized leave.
Regularly scheduled academic breaks that occur in the winter and summer are not classified as "authorized leave" and as such would not be assessed as part of the 150 days.
For instance, if a student takes authorized leave for the winter semester (January to April) and their regular academic calendar provides for the summer semester to be off (May to August), the student would have been considered to have been on leave until April. In the example you provided, the regularly scheduled summer break would not be assessed as part of the 150 days and if the authorized leave is within 150 days from the late the leave commenced, they would not be required to change their status.
I hope this information assists you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:

Question:
Pourriez-vous confirmer si une personne peut posséder deux permis de travail valide simultanément émis sous la même dispense pour deux employeurs non reliés?
Réponse:
Oui, une personne pourrait détenir deux permis de travail sous la même dispense en autant qu’elle a une offre d’emploi, de chacun des employeurs, complétée dans le Portail des employeurs. La personne doit aussi démontrer qu’elle est en mesure de faire le travail, par exemple si les deux offres d’emploi sont pour un travail à temps plein, il est possible que l’agent ne soit pas satisfait que la personne puisse occuper les deux emplois.

threads.question:
Hello,
I am a lawyer in Edmonton, Alberta. I understand that a medical exam is required for work permit holders to perform certain jobs in the health care field-does this include Massage Therapist NOC 3236?
The client has been issued an open work permit valid until 2020 under the inland spousal sponsorship pilot program and would like to work in this occupation. In this case can the client still make the application to change conditions and retain the same validity of the OWP (valid until
2020)? I know the permit would ordinarily maintain validity just not sure about the change of conditions application in this scenario.
Best,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
QUESTION:
am a lawyer in Edmonton, Alberta. I understand that a medical exam is required for work permit holders to perform certain jobs in the health care field-does this include Massage Therapist NOC 3236?
The client has been issued an open work permit valid until 2020 under the inland spousal sponsorship pilot program and would like to work in this occupation. I understand that an application to change conditions of the work permit can be made online after the client completes a medical in order to remove the "must not work in health related field" notation but the sponsor recently passed away and we are waiting for the sponsored PR application to be refused as notice was sent to IRCC advising this earlier this summer.
n this case can the client still make the application to change conditions and retain the same validity of the OWP (valid until
2020)?I know the permit would ordinarily maintain validity just not sure about the change of conditions application in this scenario. RESPONSE:
Vassage Therapist NOC 3236 falls under the Health Care Field which would have the client working in close contact with people, therefore the client would need to do a medical exam: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents.html#needs](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/medical-police/medical-exams/requirements-temporary-residents.html#needs)
f the client was in status when they applied for the open work permit then they would have a received an open work permit that confers status. However, if they applied for the open work permit while they did not have valid status, and after they received their eligibility decision for their spousal application, then they would have received a work permit that 'does not confer status'. It will say this right on the document. If they do not have status then they are not eligible to apply for changes to the terms/conditions of their work permit.
f the client has a work permit that confers status, as mentioned above, they should be able to apply for a change to the terms/conditions of that work permit and the validity of the document should remain the same eg. 2020. However, in this case the sponsor has is now deceased, therefore the applicant no longer meets the requirements of the exemption. The client could apply for an LMIA or submit another type of permanent resident applicant, then the application could be assessed with the new information under new exemption
This mailbox is not intended to respond to case specific scenarios, you can call the Client Service Centre for details on your case.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: LMIA Exemption-Camp counsellor under the IMP---REP-2019-2417-
threads.question:
Hello,
I am requesting further information or clarification on the following information from IRCC website regarding LMIA exempt work permits for the International Mobility Program-Unique work situations-Camp Counsellors under R205b with exemption code C20.
Excerpt from the IRCC website states:
nmigration, Refugees
"As of March 1, 2017, camp counsellors going to residential camps during the summer season are exempt from the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) requirement pursuant to paragraph 205(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (reciprocal LMIA exemption C20)..."(emphasis mine)
"Work permit duration
\cbpat6Officers may issue an LMIA-exempt work permit that is valid for the duration of the offer of employment or until the expiry of the travel document, whichever is earlier."
\cbpat6[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/unique-situations/camp-counsellors-r205-b-exemption-code-c20.html
\cbpat6The situation is:
\cbpat6The applicant has been working for the employer on a seasonal basis and has been approved work permit for 6 months at a time. Now the client is being offered an all year (summer AND winter) round job as a Camp counsellor for at least 12 months by the same employer doing the same job.
\cbpat6The question is: Can this client then apply or request, under this provision, for at least 12 months or more (contingent to the duration of the job offer or the travel document) given that the wording of the first paragraph mentions "summer season"?
\cbpat6Does this provision also apply for Residential camps that operated ALL YEAR round with programs for summer, spring fall and winter seasons?
\cbpat6Please advise.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question:
Can Camp Counsellors going to residential camps apply under exemption code C20 to work for at least 12 months or more (contingent to the duration of the job offer or the travel document) even though the wording of the first paragraph of the guidance for Camp Counsellors mentions "summer season"?
Does this provision also apply for Residential camps that operate ALL YEAR round with programs for summer, spring, fall and winter seasons?
Answer:
The facilitation of camp counsellors under C20 is specific to seasonalcamps as there is a demonstrable and established international reciprocity for this type of time-limited situation. If a camp is running year round, the Foreign National (FN) needs an LMIA-required work permit. However, if the FN can demonstrate that there is a year-round opportunity for a Canadian camp counsellor to go abroad, then they may be eligible for C20. Please refer to the following guidance for more information regarding reciprocity.
We hope this information is of assistance.
Immigration Representatives Mailbox.

threads.subject: Implied status and study permit---REP-2019-2433-
threads.question:
Hello,
We have a question regarding the authorization to work for a student on implied status. While R189 allow them to continue studying, are they also allowed to work while they wait for their new study permit? Is there a difference between work on campus and off-campus?
Thank you,
Lnmanon
threads.answer:
Ce:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on September 10, 2019 regarding implied status and on/off campus work.
Question #1:
Are they also allowed to work while they wait for their new study permit?
Response #1:
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have implied status as a temporary resident during that period.
If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
In sum, if the international students are authorized to work on/off campus according to their study permit, they can continue to work under the same conditions while pending of their renewal application.
Question #2:
Is there a difference between work on campus and off-campus?
Response #2:
Yes. On and off campus work are different.
“On-campus” is defined as employment facilities within the boundaries of the campus. The students are only allowed to work on the campus of the educational institution at which they are registered in full-time studies. If an institution has more than one campus, the student can work at different locations on those campuses provided they are within the same municipality. If an institution has campuses in different cities, the student is restricted to working on the institution's campus where they are registered as a full-time student.
Students may work on campus as teaching or research assistants and may be located at a library, hospital, or research facility affiliated with the institution but located outside the physical boundaries of the institution's campus. This is allowed provided that the work is strictly related to the student's research grant.
The employer can be any of the following:
•the institution; •a faculty,
•a student organization;
•the students themselves (self-employment taking place on campus);
•a private business;
•a private contractor providing services to the institution on the campus.
Some universities and colleges are located in city centres. On-campus employers include those whose businesses serve the general public, as long as the place of business is located on the institution's campus.
“Off-campus” is defined as employment facilities at any location outside the boundaries of the campus of the educational institution at which the student is registered.

Thank you kindly

threads.subject: [CPD-2019-0878] DNA testing for a citizenship application--REP-2019-2445--
threads.question:
From Dear sir or madam:
When an applicant applying for proof of citizenship is unable to produce any documentation proving a parent-child relationship, will a DNA test between the parent and the child be acceptable as proof of the relationship? Are there any specific requirements relating to where this should be done and what steps must be taken?
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
The requirement for citizenship by descent is that a child born abroad in the first generation has a biological link to a Canadian parent who was either born in Canada or naturalized as a Canadian citizen before the child was born. As a result of a recent change in our policy, the biological connection now includes a genetic or gestational link—meaning that if a Canadian gives birth abroad to a child with whom they shares no genetic material, the child will still be considered a citizen under the Citizenship Act.
The law applies exactly the same way whether the child was conceived through Assisted Human Reproduction
(AHR)/InVitro Fertilization (IVF)/Surrogacy or not.
We would invite an applicant to apply on the following form, if the Canadian parent and child do in fact share a biological link.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-) guides/application-citizenship-certificate-adults-minors.html Once the application is assessed, a citizenship officer, may request additional information, such as hospital records
and/or contractual agreement with the lab, after the initial review of the application. Additionally, the citizenship officer, may request DNA, if necessary to establish genetic linkages.
Among other documents required for an application, an applicant must provide at least two documents to establish their identity. Both pieces of identification must show the applicant's name and date of birth, and at least one document must have a photograph of the applicant. Applicants residing outside Canada can provide foreign identity
documents that are equivalent to Canadian identity documents, such as a passport or government-issued identification
documents. Children of preschool age may not be able to provide two identity documents or an identity document that includes their photo. In such cases, an explanation letter must accompany their application.
If you are aware that there is not a biological link between the Canadian parent and the child, the family will be required to explore other options to bring the child to Canada including sponsorship or adoption.
Also, please find our link on DNA testing:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/standard-requirements/dna-testing.html
It is also important to note that IRCC will not accept DNA results unless and until IRCC requests such DNA reports.
Hoping this helps,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: General Inquiry--REP-2019-1959
threads.question:
Hello Immigration Representatives Team,
I have couple of questions in regards to eligibility of Spousal Open Work Permit application
Q1: Will a Spouse be eligible to apply for his/her SOWP if their sponsor is currently on International Student Visa but is on a Co-Op Work Term and will be going to back to school again to complete her studies. Co-Op term is part of her studies and is required for completion. Other eligibility factors are meeting as required.
Q2: Will a Spouse be eligible to apply for his/her SOWP if their sponsor is currently on a scheduled legal term break authorized by their college. They will be going back to college after completing their break and are eligible on other factors of the SOWP.
Q3: How many hours a Study Permit holder work off campus if they are on a Paid Co-Op full time Work Term If they cannot work in Paid Co-op term will be they be able to work off campus if they are on Unpaid Co-Op Work Term. In both cases Co-op Work Term is required for completion of program of the student.
Q4: Can a student work 20 hours off campus if they will be working on campus also 20 hours. Willif impact the number of hours they are working in total. In both cases they are getting paid for the work.
Regards,
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry regarding co-op work and spousal work permits. We apologize for the delay in responding.
Q1: Will a Spouse be eligible to apply for his/her SOWP if their sponsor is currently on International Student Visa but is on a Co-Op Work Term and will be going to back to school again to complete her studies. Co-Op term is part of her studies and is required for completion. Other eligibility factors are meeting as required.
If the student's DLI considers them to hold full-time status during their co-op work term, their spouse may be eligible to apply for a spousal work permit. If the student's DLl does not consider them to be full-time students during the work term (e.g. they are considered part-time), their spouse should wait until they resume full-time studies before applying, as enrollment in full-time studies is an eligibility requirement for spousal work permits, as per our PDI.
Q2: Will a Spouse be eligible to apply for his/her SOWP if their sponsor is currently on a scheduled legal term break authorized by their college. They will be going back to college after completing their break and are eligible on other factors of the SOWP.
If the study permit holder is on a regularly scheduled break (e.g. summer break, reading week, winter break) and will be returning to school in the following semester, their spouse may be eligible to apply for a spousal work permit.
If the study permit holder is on an authorized leave from studies (e.g. taking a semester off due to medical reasons) their spouse would not be eligible for a spousal work permit as they are not considered to be enrolled in studies during this period.
Q3: How many hours a Study Permit holder work off campus if they are on a Paid Co-Op full time Work Term. If they cannot work in Paid Co-op term will be they be able to work off campus if they are on Unpaid Co-Op Work Term. In both cases Co-op Work Term is required for completion of program of the student.
If a student is considered by their DLl to hold full-time status during their co-op work term, they may work on campus and up to 20 hours off campus in addition to their co-op work, as per our PDl on off-campus work.
Q4: Can a student work 20 hours off campus if they will be working on campus also 20 hours. Will if impact the number of hours they are working in total. In both cases they are getting paid for the work.
Yes, a study permit holder may combine work authorizations under R186(f) and (v) to work on campus in addition to 20 hours per week off campus. There is no limit on the number of hours study permit holders may work on campus.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Salary Increase--REP-2019-2532
threads.question:
Good afternoon,
Can you please confirm if there are any regulations regarding the amount of salary increase that a foreign worker who is currently on a 2 year work permit under the International Mobility Program? Is there a maximum salary increase that can be given for the same job, same position, same location (for example if a worker is making $50,000/year, could their salary be increased to $70,000/year as a merit increase due to excellent performance?). I have read that the salary must remain substantially the same, however, I cannot find mention of this in IRPA or on the IRCC website.
Can you please confirm if the employer is required to advise IRCC of the changes to the salary?
Many thanks,
migration, Refugees 1*1
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
L'nformaonduuedoislsinftion
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox,
Questions
a) Can you please confirm if there are any regulations regarding the amount of salary increase that a foreign worker who is currently on a 2 year work permit under the International Mobility Program?
Answer
No, under the International Mobility Program, there is no regulation specifically regarding the amount of a salary increase that is permitted. However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR [209.2] on issuance of a work permit based on the offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must:
- be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made;
- comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works;
- provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer;
- make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)
(a) if the IRPR.
b) Is there a maximum salary increase that can be given for the same job, same position, same location (for example if a worker is making $50,000/year, could their salary be increased to $70,000/year as a merit increase due to excellent performance?). Answer
See Answer c) below
c) I have read that the salary must remain substantially the same, however, I cannot find mention of this in IRPA or on the IRCC website.
nmigration, Réfugiés nd Citizenship Canada e en vertu de la loi sur l'accès à l'informatior Answer
See Answer a) above; and
Inspection guidance online states the following with respect to changes in wage:
“Substantially the same – but not less favourable – wages” means that:
- Wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the Offer of Employment provided as per R209.11
- Any unusual deductions (such as recovery of employer compliance fee, transportation costs, etc) should be stated in the Offer of Employment
Therefore, wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the LMIA letter and annexes, nor can they be substantially higher, as the employer may have been able to hire a Canadian or permanent resident if higher wages had been advertised in the first place.
For the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (Program led by Employment and Skills Development Canada and Service Canada for Labour Market Impact Assessment or LMIA-required job positions), “substantially higher" generally means higher than the rate of inflation or 2% per year, whichever is higher.
Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change and prior to the foreign worker taking on those new duties.
If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer.
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.
d) Can you please confirm if the employer is required to advise IRCC of the changes to the salary? Answer Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC. Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (recommended). Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the
nmigration, Refugees
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption.
General information:
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulat ions (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be flled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Under the International Mobility Program, providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer ofEmployment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Additional information can be found on our website using the following links:
International Mobility Program Resources
Regards,

threads.subject: QUESTIONS FROM LAWYER NAME: ·REP-2019-2379-
threads.question:
Hello IRCC,
We have two questions at this time that are of a general nature:
Can a person who has a study permit in canada be the owner of a business that would employ legal employees and where the study permit owner would not be working full time but only the allowed part time hours as per the study permit regulations? If a person completes a 3 yr program at a cdn college or university and they do not apply for a PGWP immediately (post graduate work permit), can that same person return to school and take another one or two year program, complete it and then apply for the PGWP after all of this attendance has been completed?

migration, Refugees 1*1 mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello,
This is in response to you August 30th enquiry regarding post-graduation work permits.
Question: Can a person who has a study permit in Canada be the owner of a business that would employ legal employees and where the study permit owner would not be working full time but only the allowed part time hours as per the study permit regulations?
Response: An international student with a valid study permit and authorization to work off-campus can perform the type of work as defined in the following instructions, including self-employment. There are no restrictions as to being an employer to others, as long as the international student adheres to the conditions set forth under R186(v).
Question: Can a person completes a 3 year program at a Canadian college or university and they do not apply for a PGWP immediately (post graduate work permit), can that same person return to school and take another one or two year program, complete it and then apply for the PGWP after all of this attendance has been completed?
Response: Yes. Post-graduation work permits are one time work permits that allow students who have graduated from a participating Canadian post-secondary institution to gain valuable Canadian work experience. It is possible to combine the length of two programs of study, providing that each program of study meets all PGWPP eligibility requirements and is at least 8 months in length. When combining two programs of study for the purposes of considering PGWP validity, there may be a break between the two programs of study, but the second program of study must be completed within 2 years of completing the first program. The student only has to maintain continuous full-time studies during the program they are enrolled in at the time. If the combined length is more than 2 years, the work permit may be valid for up to 3 years.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at

threads.subject: International students and self employment---REP-2019-2533
threads.question:
Hello,
I am an International Student Coordinator supporting students in a variety of Entertainment Arts programs. It is not uncommon for those training in entertainment arts programs to take on freelance work to support their studies, and while I understand that as long as they are eligible to work off campus and they work no more than 20 hrs/week it is not a problem, I was curious if the students performed this work for external clients while on the boundaries of the campus if that would count as "on campus" work? The PDI on On Campus Work makes reference to the employer being the student themselves (self-employment taking
place on campus)".
Thank you and I look forward to your reply.
Warm regards,
Page 3432
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Ce:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on September 18, 2019 regarding the definition of on-campus work.
“On-campus” is defined as employment facilities within the boundaries of the campus. The students are only allowed to work on the campus of the educational institution at which they are registered in full-time studies. To answer your question, self-employment taking place on campus is considered “on-campus work” when the students act as employers, not employees. In other words, for freelance work to be considered on-campus employment, the student must work for themselves, rather than for a company and their employment facility has to be leased by them and located on campus of their DLl (i.e. their dorm room, or apartment, etc.).

threads.subject: Caregiver Pilot--REP-2019-2322-
threads.question:
Hello,
Just wanted clarification on the IRCC infographic attached, it states prospective caregivers who want to immigrate under the new caregiver pilots only need 1 year post-secondary education/ Canadian equivalent.
Does this mean they need 1 year in any type of certificate or does it need to be related to the caregiving or healthcare field?
Regards
Lnmanon
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
To qualify for the Home Child Care Provider or Home Support Worker pilot, the applicant must hold a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies or an Education Credential Assessment and a foreign education credential that is equivalent to a Canadian educational credential of at least one year of post-secondary studies.
In order to qualify, the Canadian education credential must be issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institution. As long as the college is recognized by the provincial authorities, an education credential obtained from this college could count towards meeting the education requirements.
The educational credential does not need to be in the healthcare or caregiving field however the applicant must have one of the following:
- 2 years of full-time Canadian work experience in an eligible occupation within the preceding 3 years
- a valid full-time job offer from a Canadian employer in an eligible caregiver occupation
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: TFW works in 2 locations ---REP-2019-2519
threads.question:
Hello IRCC,
a foreign national worker obtained a Work Permit based on a positive LMIA issued by Service Canada. The type of position requires that foreign worker to work in 2 different branches/buildings of the SAME employer offered that employment. The employer asks FW to work (back and forth, almost everyday) in 2 different locations, both in the same street/ neighborhood, but different addresses.
The question is: is it acceptable on the eyes of IRCC? The employer would like to know/make sure that neither employer nor FW is not breaching the terms and conditions job offer and WP. As you know, on the WP, it says, FW not authorized to work in any location other than stated.
Just to add that there is no clear cut off how much of the employment (e.g. percentage) is performed in either locations. The employment is full time and same job title and same duties. The employer's name, legal business name, operating name are also the same for those 2 work locations.
We called Service Canada, LMIA department, as well, and we were told that this issue is of IRCC, that is whyI ask this question.
Please advise.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
QUESTION:
A foreign national worker obtained a Work Permit based on a positive LMIA issued by Service Canada. The type of position requires that foreign worker to work in 2 different branches/buildings of the SAME employer offered that employment. The employer asks FW to work (back and forth, almost every day) in 2 different locations, both in the same street/ neighborhood, but different addresses.
The question is: is it acceptable on the eyes of IRCC? The employer would like to know/make sure that neither employer nor FW is not breaching the terms and conditions job offer and WP. As you know, on the WP, it says, FW not authorized to workin any location other than stated.
Just to add that there is no clear cut off how much of the employment (e.g. percentage) is performed in either locations. The employment is full time and same job title and same duties. The employer's name, legal business name, operating name are also the same for those 2 work locations.
We called Service Canada, LMIA department, as well, and we were told that this issue is of IRCC, that is why I ask this question.
RESPONSE:
Based on this specific scenario, where the employer did provide both employment locations AND the work permit has the correct city named for location of work, there would be no need for a new work permit to be issued.
With respect to other locations, the employer has a regulatory obligation to provide accurate information, and so where work locations are known, they should indeed all be listed.
A foreign national holding a work permit must adhere to the conditions stated on the document. If no conditions on location were listed on the foreign nationals' work permit, a change in location would not be considered a violation of their conditions.
Work permits specify a location (currently as submitted by the foreign national in their application) which is the expected location of the job. The work permit may also specify the condition imposed under R185 that the foreign national is "Not authorized to work in any other location". A restriction may have been included by the immigration officer if the location of the position could have impacted the issuance of the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or the LMIA-exemption.
"Location" is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the "same working conditions". The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMIA exemption requirement or justification (for instance, provincial nominees). Immigration,
mmigration, Refugees Refugees (IRCC) does not require proactive notification of changes, but the employer is required to maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the voluntary disclosure process.
We trust this information is of assistance to you.
Kindly

threads.subject: Entry on spousal open work permit---REP-2019-2554
threads.question:
Recently a colleague received the following e-mail from you.
One additional issue I wish to clarify: can the person who holds the spousal open work permit leave and re enter Canada on the basis of that work permit during its validity even if the principal applicant is no longer working in Canada?
QUESTION: Can you please explain how a holder of a valid spousal work permit (WP) is impacted when they stop being eligible for such a WP? Instances of such change in eligibility are where the spouses separate, or where the principal spouse stops meeting any requirements which are necessary to entitle their spouse to a WP (e.g., the principal spouse is no longer employed in a skilled job, or no longer a full-time student). I understand that the dependent spouse's WP does not become invalid by itself in such cases, pursuant to R209. My specific questions are as follows:
1. Is the dependant spouse obligated to notify IRCC that they no longer meet the terms of the spousal WP, and proactively take steps to surrender this WP?
ANSWER: No.
2. Does the dependant spouse still retain their temporary-resident status even though they do not meet the terms of the spousal WP?
Answer: Yes, until expiry of the spousal permit.
3. If the dependant spouse continues working under the spousal WP after he/she no longer meets the terms of this WP (but the WP remains valid) – does IRCC consider such employment "unauthorized work" for the purposes of enforcement (inadmissible for unauthorized work) and eligibility for the Canadian Experience Class (under which unauthorized work does not count)?
Answer: No.
ANSWER: If the Principle Applicant (PA) is in possession of a valid work permit, and their spouse possesses a valid OPEN work permit, the spouse is eligible to work in Canada until the expiry date of the authorization. The status of the PA, even the marital status, does not affect the validity of the spouse's OPEN work permit.
The validity of the open work permit for the spouse is tied to the validity of the PA's work permit, however, if the PA is no longer employed in a skilled job, or no longer a full-time student, there is no provision to “cancel" or “relinquish” the OPEN work permit for the spouse. As you mentioned, as per R209, a work permit becomes invalid only when it expires or if a removal order becomes enforceable. Therefore the work permit will remain valid until the expiry date.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailboxly
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
QUESTION:
Can the person who holds the spousal open work permit leave and re-enter Canada on the basis of that work permit
during its validity even if the principal applicant is no longer working in Canada?
RESPONSE:
The client on the spousal open work permit still holds a valid in-status document, then they should be able to re-enter with that document (and a visa, unless they are from a visa-exempt country), however they will still be subject to a port of entry examination by a Border Services Officer who will make the final determination on whether to allow entry or not based on the individual circumstances.

threads.subject: Caregiver Path--REP-2019-2381
threads.question:
From Dear Sir/Madam,
If an international student (at a private Canadian DLl, holding a valid study permit) wants to work as a caregiver right after their studies, are they eligible to be hired by a Canadian employer through the TFWP considering they're an "inside the country" applicant? Assuming LMIA is required in this case?
It would seem they'd be eligible to apply for the Home Child Care Provider Pilot once they meet the education and language requirements. Considering the acceptance processing time for the pilot being up to 12 months, can the applicant continue to work under their TFWP as a caregiver and take this work experience into count when applying for the PR (if accepted into the pilot)?
Last question, can the dependent of the applicant study at a Canadian university under domestic tuition fee rates, given the applicant holding a valid work permit under either the TFWP or the Open Work permit from the caregiver pilot?
Thank you.
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please find the answers to your questions below:
If an international student (at a private Canadian DLl, holding a valid study permit) wants to work as a caregiver right after their studies, are they eligible to be hired by a Canadian employer through the TFWP considering they're an "inside the country" applicant? Assuming LMIA is required in this case? Yes they would be eligible to apply from inside Canada under the TFWP as long as their employer gets an LMIA. If they want to apply for PR under the new pilots, they would need to wait until they got their 2 years work experience with their TFWP work permit before they can apply for PR. If they want to apply right away for PR without the work experience, they would need to transition to an occupation-restricted open work permit. Work experience under both work permits can be taken into account as long as it's under the same NOC. As for the spouse, they would have to apply on their own to study in Canada if the caregiver has a work permit under TFWP, no special measure for them. If the caregiver gets an occupation-restricted open work permit, the spouse can also submit a study permit as part of the PR application (not sure about the domestic fee and they would still be required to submit an LOA).
It would seem they'd be eligible to apply for the Home Child Care Provider Pilot once they meet the education and language requirements. Considering the acceptance processing time for the pilot being up to 12 months, can the applicant continue to work under their TFWP as a caregiver and take this work experience into count when applying for the PR (if accepted into the pilot)? If a home child care provider or home support worker has recent qualifying Canadian work experience (this includes work experience obtained under their TWFP WP), it may count toward the requirements of the pilots. Caregivers can apply immediately to the pilot relevant to their occupation without having the total of 24 months' work experience however, in this case, they must submit an application for the occupation-specific work permit. If approved, they cannot continue to work under their Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) caregiver work permit. After completing their work experience, they would then submit proof that they have completed the work experience requirement to . A combination of qualifying work experience obtained on a TFWP (LMIA) work permit and occupation-specific work permit can count towards meeting this requirement.
Alternately, the caregiver could complete the required work experience on their existing TFWP LMIA supported work permit and apply through one of the pilots after reaching two years of eligible work experience. In that situation, their application would be processed through to a final decision on their permanent residence right away. See here for further information on the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker Pilots.
Last question, can the dependent of the applicant study at a Canadian university under domestic tuition fee rates, given the applicant holding a valid work permit under either the TFWP or the Open Work permit from the caregiver pilot? Dependants of caregivers are eligible to apply for an open study permit from outside Canada only if the caregiver's work permit has been approved in writing before they entered Canada. Please note that tuition fees are regulated by the universities.
Thank you
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

When a business operates from a dwelling-house where the foreign worker performs work, employer consent to enter the premises is required. As per section 209.8 (1), an investigator may enter and inspect any premises or place in which a foreign worker performs work.

Un étranger qui est autorisé à entrer au Canada en tant que titulaire d'un permis de travail a le statut de résident temporaire et est autorisé à travailler. He then decides to go back to school for a post graduate certificate in January and applies for a study permit. Assuming he is approved. threads.answer:
Ce:
Good morning,
This is in response to your July 19 enquiry regarding holding a post graduate work permit and study permit concurrently.
Post-graduation work permits are one time work permits that are issued for the length of the study program, for a maximum of three years. The Post-Graduation Work Permit acts as an open work permit to allow students who have graduated from a participating Canadian post-secondary institution to gain valuable Canadian work experience. In case where the student reenrolls to continue their studies, they may continue to utilize their open work permit from the Post-Graduation Work Permit Program (PGWPP) to work, as the new Study permit will not invalidate their existing PGWP.

threads.subject: Clarification: On and Off Campus Work Eligibility for Distance Learning Programs--REP-2019-2499--
threads.question:
Greetings from
Context
As the Canadian education landscape continues to evolve, distance learning programs, both in blended and solely distance formats, continues to rise.
We recognize that distance learning is not defined as studies according to Canadian immigration regulations; however, some students chose to come to Canada or are already in Canada at the time they choose to pursue a distance learning program. Such students have been able to secure study permits for a portion or entire program. Furthermore most distance learning programs fit the criteria of an academic program, professional training or in some cases, vocational training. They also lead to a degree, diploma or certification that can be defined by Designated Learning Institutions (DLIs) as full-time for immigration purposes.
Pursuant to R186(f) and R186(v), on and off-campus work is permitted for full-time students holding a study permit and in eligible programs (particularly for off-campus work) from DLIs.
Given that the regulations or the program delivery instructions do not distinguish a difference between distance learning and face- to-face programs; both of which are viewed with high academic integrity and rigor at our institution as well as many others, we would like to know the following:
Are students in 100% distance learning programs that lead to a degree, diploma or certificate eligible to work on campus as well as off-campus?
Would the above differ if the distance learning program was a blend of online and in-person in terms of %s?
Input
Thank you for making information accessible and publicly-available. Three recommendations would continue to deliver on this strength:
- Include this clarification as a scenario in the help centre question bank
- Include the above direction in the on campus and off-campus work PDIs-[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html) and [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/working-on-campus.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/working-on-campus.html)
Many thanks for your response.
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Good morning,
This is in response to your September 17th enquiry regarding distance learning.
Question: Are students in 100% distance learning programs that lead to a degree, diploma or certificate eligible to work on campus as well as off-campus?
Answer: No. In order to be eligible to work on and off-campus, an international student must hold a valid study permit, amongst other requirements. Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place. Since the definition of distance learning does not require one to be in Canada, a study permit cannot be issued for this type of course. As such, students enrolled in 100% distance learning programs are not eligible to work on and off campus.
Question: Would the above differ if the distance learning program was a blend of online and in-person in terms of%s?
Answer: If the distance learning courses include an in-Canada portion to the program and the overall course of study is greater than six months, then the student requires a study permit for the in-Canada portion of the program, even if the in-Canada portion is less than six months. The duration of the study permit should be for the duration of the in-Canada portion only. As such, they may be eligible to work on-campus and off-campus during the period covered by their study permit, providing that they meet the all the other program requirements.
Additional information on on-campus and off-campus requirements, please consult our website.

Minor children already in Canada are authorized to study without a study permit at the pre-school, primary or secondary level if
they are either accompanying parents claiming refugee status or are claimants themselves;
•one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident;
•one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is authorized to work or study in Canada; this includes temporary residents who
are owork permit holders, ostudy permit holders,
visitor status holders (e.g., visitor record holders) who are either authorized to work without a permit, as per section 186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), or authorized to study without a permit, as per section R188; or
•neither parent is physically in Canada.
Therefore, if a minor was studying in Canada already (without a study permit) based on one of the criteria mentioned above they would be eligible to apply for a study permit from within Canada pursuant to R215(1)(f)(i).

Merci de l’attention portée à la présente question.
Sincères salutations.
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Voici la réponse à votre demande envoyée le 25 septembre 2019 concernant le travail hors campus.
Oui, un étudiant étranger qui détient un permis d’études valide et qui satisfait aux conditions de l’article R186 v) ou w), il peut travailler hors campus. Toutefois, c'est necessary d'une des conditions suivantes doit être imprimée sur son permis d’études :
- Peut travailler 20 heures par semaine hors campus ou à temps plein durant les congés réguliers s’il respecte les critères décrits à l'alinéa 186v) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés.
- Peut accepter un emploi sur le campus ou hors du campus s’il répond aux critères d’admissibilité aux termes des alinéas 186f). v) ou w) du Règlement sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés. Doit cesser de travailler s’il ne respecte plus ces critères.

nmigration, Refugees

threads.question:
Dear ImmReps
Can you kindly clarify a student's eligibility for PGWP in the following scenarios?
Scenario A
A student attends a PGWP-eligible program (e.g. 4 year bachelor degree from an eligible DLI) and completes that program. The student then goes on to complete another one-year post-secondary program at a DLI that is not eligible for PGWP (e.g. one-year certificate program). Can the student apply for a PGWP based on his initial PGWP-eligible program when he completes the non-PGWP program? At this point in time, it would have been more than 180 days since he completed his PGWP-eligible program, however, he would still be a holder of a valid study permit (albeit the study permit would be for the non-PGWP program).
Scenario B
nmigration, Refugees
Following Scenario A and assuming that the student does not apply for PGWP after completing the non-PGWP program, the student goes on to complete another PGWP-eligible program (e.g. a 1-year Master degree at an eligible DLI). The student then applies for PGWP upon obtaining the Master degree. So at this point in time, the student has a four-year Bachelor degree (PGWP eligible), one-year certificate (non-PGWP), and one-year Master degree (PGWP eligible). Can the student use his four-year Bachelor degree toward the PGWP duration calculation now, such that the PGWP can be issued for three years instead of one year?
Scenario C
A student completes a PGWP-eligible program (e.g. four-year Bachelor degree from an eligible DLI), and then goes on to complete another PGWP-eligible program (e.g. one-year Master degree from an eligible DLI). Upon completing the second PGWP-eligible program (with no credit transfers between the two programs), the student applies for PGWP. threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry sent on September 6 regarding PGWP application and validity
To be eligible for PGWP, graduates must apply within 180 days of completing an eligible program. Enrolling in another program of study does not extend this period.
As per our PDI, programs may be combined when determining PGWP validity duration if they are completed within two years of each other. If more than two years have elapsed between completion of the programs, only the duration of the most recently completed program will be considered when determining validity duration of the PGWP.

or,

threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
If an foreign national holding a lEC Working Holiday work permit valid for one year had to leave Canada due to medical emergency and spent a significant period of that one year (e.g. 8 or 9 months) outside of Canada, can that applicant:
- apply to recapture time on the current work permit? or,
- be eligible for a new IEC Working Holiday work permit given that the previous participation was not a full participation inside Canada? Kindly clarify whether working as a personal support worker (NOC 4412) at an agency that provides care to the elderly, would qualify an applicant under NOC 4412 for the purpose of that pilot program, or whether the qualified and eligible experience as a Home support worker must be provided at the elderly's home or the caregiver's home only.
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act

threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
In order to qualify for the Home Support Worker Pilot, the applicant must have cared for someone who needs help from a home support worker either in their own home or in their employer's home.
- The applicant doesn't need to have lived in their employer's home to qualify
- Only home support workers are eligible under NOC 4412
- Experience as a housekeeper doesn't count

- The applicant must show that the job matches the NOC 4412 job description and the applicant must have done most of the main duties
- 24 months of work experience must be gained in a 36 month period
- Full-time work means at least 30 hours of paid work each week
- Any work experience the applicant gained while a full-time student doesn't count

Does an applicant applying under the intra-company transferee (ICT) category of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) have to be currently employed by the foreign entity of the multi-national company at the time of application? threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Question:
Does an applicant applying under the intra-company transferee (ICT) category of the Comprehensive and Progressive
Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) have to be currently employed by the foreign entity of the multi-national company at the time of application?
Answer:
Yes. In order for a foreign entity to transfer’ a foreign national to a Canadian subsidiary/affiliate's payrofll, the foreign national must be employed (i.e. be on the payroll of) at the foreign entity.
Intra-corporate transferees R204(a) – T51 (CPTPP)
The intra-corporate transferees category is comprised of business persons who are employed by an enterprise in the territory of a party and who are seeking to render services to one of the following of that enterprise:
- the parent entity
- a subsidiary
- an affiliate
Criteria for intra-corporate transferees
All intra-corporate transferees must follow these conditions:
- be a citizen of a Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) signatory
- have been employed by an enterprise of or have been partners in an enterprise of a CPTPP signatory continuously for at least 1 year within the previous 3 years at the time of submitting the application o includes citizens of CPTPP countries who are employed by an enterprise in another CPTPP country
- be transferred to an enterprise (that must be a parent entity, subsidiary or affiliate company of the enterprise) in Canada

threads.subject: Sponsorship & rent-geared-to-income units--REP-2019-2363
threads.question:
Thanks for writing back. This is for a spousal sponsorship.
If a sponsor wants to sponsor a spouse, but lives in a rent-geared-to-income unit that is managed by the City of Toronto – is that considered by IRCC to be “social assistance" that renders someone ineligible to sponsor?
In addition, what if a sponsor is receiving Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP) payments due to a disability and also lives
migration, Refugees
L'nmanon in a rent-geared-to-income unit? My understanding is that if the sponsor is receiving social assistance due to a disability, that will not render them ineligible to sponsor.
Thanks,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry.
The Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (R2) define social assistance in broad terms, but render someone who is in receipt of social assistance for a reason other than a disability ineligible to be a sponsor under the family class [R133(1)(k)]. The intent of R133(1)(k) is to bar persons whose primary or sole source of income is “social assistance” benefits from sponsoring a relative under the family class.
There are various programs and services provided by provinces and territories which confer benefits that IRCC does not consider to be social assistance for the purposes of imposing a bar on sponsorship.
Examples of these would include, but are not limited to:
- subsidized housing
- tax credits
- child care subsidies
- other benefits which would be widely available to residents of a province or territory, including persons who are employed
Please be advised that officers processing family class sponsorship applications do not treat subsidized housing as social assistance. You may find this and other useful information in the IRCC website under Applications under family classes: Assessing the sponsor.

threads.question:
Dear officer,
Thank you. Please kindly see below.
FN holds and ICT work permit with ABC Canada Co. ABC Canada Co. will spin off one part of its business to XYZ Canada Co. We can show that XYZ Canada Co. is the successor in interest for the part of the business that was spun off by ABC Canada Co. There is no corporate relationship between ABC Canada Co. and XYZ Canada Co. They are not part of the same group of companies.
Company XYZ Canada Co. is part of a larger group of companies that have operations outside of Canada. Said companies share common ownership and control.
Question:
Does the FN qualify for an ICT work permit in the name ofXYZ Canada Co.? We can prove successor in interest and that XYZ Canada Co. belongs to a larger group of companies with operations outside of Canada.
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question:
Does the FN qualify for an ICT work permit in the name of XYZ Canada Co.? We can prove successor in interest and that XYZ Canada Co. belongs to a larger group of companies with operations outside of Canada.
Answer:
We have consulted with our Immigration Policy (temporary workers) colleagues who have provided the following confirmation:
If the WP is under the name of the former enterprise, then the applicant would have to submit a change of conditions as the qualifying relationship, between the two initial entities of which the work authorization was based, has changed.
Rationale: As per the requestor's submission, the initial company the foreign worker came to work for has not gone out of business, but is jettisoning a part of its business to another Canadian business that isn't related. If this is the case, and the employee is working for the part of the business that is leaving, then the employee would need a change of conditions; this scenario is quite different to a business being wholly taken over.
It would not affect the workers' eligibility to remain at the enterprise while the new application is being processed, as this would be the equivalent of implied status, until the change of conditions is approved.
It does mean, though, that if the new enterprise doesn't have the same qualifying relationship with the foreign entity, then they may not be eligible to extend. Furthermore, they may not qualify for a new ICT work permit because they haven't been able to meet the requirement of working for one year for the foreign branch/subsidiary of the new company they are working for.
Please note: Applications to change conditions must be submitted to the Edmonton Case Processing Centre. The Canadian employer MUST submit a new Offer of Employment through the Employer Portal – which includes the $230 compliance fee payment – to obtain a new offer of employment number (i.e. A0000001) before the foreign worker can apply.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox.

For this reason, we recommend new Offers of Employment and new work permit applications.

threads.subject: Restoration-PGWP refused---REP-2019-2474
threads.question:
If a student applied within 90 days of graduation for Post Graduate Work Permit (PGWP):
1. His study permit document is still valid at the time of application and at the time of PGWP application decision (i.e. the date of expiry on the Study Permit is beyond the date of decision).
2. The study permit becomes invalid after 90 days of completion of studies, even though the study permit has a date of validity beyond the decision date.
Informatn od eAomtinAct In such a case, what is the correct status ofthe applicant in case the PGWP application is refused after 90-days have elapsed since study permit completion. Is the study permit considered invalid or the rules of implied status up until the point of decision would render the study permit still valid.
1. We need to know if the applicants are required to apply for restoration in that case?
2. At what point in this scenario does the study permit become invalid?
3. A restoration ofjust the work permit is sufficient in this case or do we need to also restore study permit as well?
Thank you,
nmigration, Refugees mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your September 13 enquiry regarding restoration and PGWP applications. We apologize for the delay in responding to your request.
As per R222 (1), a study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies,
(b) the day on which a removal order made against the permit holder becomes enforceable, or
(c) the day on which the permit expires.
In the situation where a graduate applies for a PGWP while holding a valid study permit and the study permit becomes invalid for one of the reasons listed above before a decision is rendered on their application, the applicant is considered in status until the day the decision is made on their application
In the situation described in your email, if a person applies for a PGWP 90 days after the completion of their studies, their study permit would be considered invalid as per R222(1)(a). The applicant would need to apply for restoration prior to submitting a PGWP application from inside Canada. In this situation, they may submit an application to restore status as a student at the same time as an application for a PGWP, with a note explaining that they are restoring their status for the sole purpose of applying for a PGWP.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at

Question : We have had students who for various reasons were refused their initial PGWP application. By the time the decision was made on their application, the 90 days has passed or their study permit has expired.
Since February 14 a valid study permit is not required to apply for PGWP. Could students in that situation apply to restore as a visitor through an online account and after generate a separate application and apply for PGWP? The paragraph seems to indicate that in order to enjoy the provision to work part-time off-campus students MUST have enrolled full-time EVERY single term throughout their studies.
Question #1 – Can you clarify if “maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study" refers to the program type i.e. full-time / part-time?

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on September 24, 2019 regarding eligibility for off-campus work authorization.
Question #1
Can you clarify if “maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study” refers to the program type
i.e. full-time / part-time?
Response #1
Students must maintain full-time course load to have access to off-campus work authorizations. Students who have maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and who only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, may work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session.
Full-time status: DLls set the number of hours and credits toward a degree, diploma or certificate that are required for a student to hold full-time status. Officers will defer to DLls on the determination of a student's status. Students must stop working off campus as soon as their full-time status becomes part-time during a regular academic session (for instance, a student may begin a regular academic session on a full-time basis and become part-time during the same session as they drop courses). In this case, they are no longer authorized to undertake off-campus work.
Question #2
If it refers to each term enrolment, then, can students work if they have taken part-time terms during their scheduled breaks?
Response #2
Students who are enrolled full time during the academic sessions before and after a regularly scheduled break and who decide to undertake a full-time or part-time course load during that regularly scheduled break are eligible to work off campus on a full-time basis. Please note, each regularly scheduled break (must be part of the DLl's academic calendar; for instance, winter and summer holidays, reading week) should not be longer than 150 days. The maximum cumulative duration of scheduled breaks is 180 days per calendar year.
I hope that this information is helpful to you.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Can you please clarify:
