In instances where a Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) application is submitted pending a pending PR application, and the BOWP is approved and the work permit issued, what happens to the BOWP if the PR application in process receives a refusal after the BOWP has been issued. Does the BOWP automatically become null, or does it remain valid until the date of expiry printed on it's
face?
2. If the BOWP remains valid, is the foreign national at risk of losing their BOWP if they exit and reenter Canada upon inspection, or can they treat the BOWP as a fully valid work permit as if the PR application did not get refused?

threads.answer:
Hello,
n instances where a Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) application is submitted pending a pending PR application, and the BOwP is approved and the work permit issued, what happens to the BOwP if the PR application in process receives a refusal after the BOwP has been issued. Does the BOWP automatically become null, or does it remain valid until the date of expiry printed on it's face?
Pursuant to section 209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations a work permit becomes invalid when it expires or when a removal order that is made against the permit holder becomes enforceable. Similar to any other type of work permit, once the bridging open work permit (BOwP) has been issued, the client can work until the work permit validity expires even if the circumstances have changed from when he/she initially obtained the BOWP.
f the BOWP remains valid, is the foreign national at risk of losing their BOwP if they exit and reenter Canada upon inspection, or can they treat the BOwP as a fully valid work permit as if the PR application did not get refused?
No, a bridging open work permit will not be revoked or nullified upon exit and re-entry to Canada. The bridging open work permit is a valid document and provides the bearer with temporary resident status in Canada for the duration of the work permit.
We hope this information is helpful.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
QUESTIONS:
Seeking clarification as to the requirements of the CPTPP theoretical knowledge requirement. Questions are as follows:
1. If a candidate qualifies for a NOC 0 management position in an industry (food services/restaurant management) that allows for advancement to senior management with work experience in lieu of education, can that applicant apply for a work permit under CPTPP with an explanation as to why there is no theoretical component?
2. Does a provincial licensing requirement such as Serving it Right (BC) or ProServe (AB) count as a theoretical component?
3. Is there any situations where an applicant can apply for a CPTPP without education?
RESPONSES:
The agreement specifies that a professional must have "theoretical and practical application of a body of specialized knowledge and either of the following:
where the occupation is regulated by the province or territory of the applicant's intended destination, evidence of licensing or certification in their occupation from the applicable Canadian or foreign regulatory body
where the occupation is not regulated by the province or territory of the applicant's intended destination, or where licensing or certification is not required to fulfill the offer of employment, evidence of study in a field of study related to the specialty occupation (theoretical) and evidence of paid work experience in the specialty occupation (practical)"
i720Professionals require both of the following:
a post-secondary degree of 4 or more years of study, unless otherwise specified in the country-specific occupation list, and any additional requirements defined in the National Occupational Classification (NOC)
paid work experience for a length of 2 years in the sector of activity of the contract
Any qualification would count towards the theoretical component, however if a license is required to serve alcohol then this would be what an officer would be assessing.
Depending on the country and the category for which they are applying for, the criteria may be different. threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Voici la réponse à votre question envoyée le 13 septembre 2019 concernant le stage coop international au titre du programme Expérience internationale Canada (EIC).
La catégorie de Stage coop à l’étranger est conçue pour les ressortissants étrangers qui sont inscrits dans un
établissement d'enseignement postsecondaire. Les participants doivent vouloir compléter un placement ou un
stage au Canada afin de respecter une partie de leur programme scolaire ou universitaire (jusqu'à 12 mois).
Aux termes de l’accord EIC conclu entre la France et le Canada, les ressortissants français sont éligibles pour participer au volet Stage coop à l’étranger tant qu'ils sont «des étudiants ou des jeunes en formation, inscrits dans un établissement secondaire, d’enseignement supérieur ou d’un centre de formation et qui souhaitent effectuer, dans le pays dont ils ne sont pas ressortissants, un stage qui leur permet d’acquérir une expérience pertinente dans leur domaine d’études, conformément à la législation en vigueur dans ce pays ».
Si, dans le cas en question, l'étudiant satisfait à l'exigence ci-dessus, il pourra peut-être demander un permis sous la catégorie de Stage coop à l’étranger dans le cadre du programme EIC. L'étudiant doit également satisfaire à d'autres exigences du volet.
Il est à noter que la demande en ligne est la seule façon de présenter une demande de permis de travail au titre du programme EIC, et les étudiants devront attendre que la nouvelle saison lEC s'ouvre pour pouvoir postuler.
Pour plus d’informaiton, veuillez vous référer au lien ci-dessous:
[https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/services/travailler-canada/eic.html](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/services/travailler-canada/eic.html)

threads.answer:

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
In order to obtain additional points for arranged employment under Express Entry LMIA-exempt Work Permit holders need to satisfy the following requirements:
if you have a valid work permit for a NOC 0, A or B job that is exempt from needing an LMIA, and you:
are currently working for an employer specified on the work permit have one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) for that employer

If an applicant provides a job offer with indeterminate duration only, would it suffice the last requirement of " have a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after we issue your permanent resident visa"?

In order to be awarded CRS points, the officer must be satisfied that the applicant has a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after we issue the permanent resident visa. An "indeterminate" offer can meet this requirement.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.question:
Hi there,
I wanted to kindly request some clarification on a matter pertaining to criminal inadmissibility inside Canada.
My client's Canadian criminal record check is showing outstanding charges: assault sec. 266 CC from investigating agency Edmonton Police Service. The court judgement pursuant to this matter reads as follows: "ordered to enter into a Peace Bond pursuant to provisions of sec 810(1) CC." "Crown proceed summarily." "The condition of the above written recognizance is that ifperson keeps peace and is of good behaviour for the term of 12 months, the said recognizance is void, otherwise it
stands in full force and effect (810)." The period referred ends on January 2020.
We inquired with the Alberta Provincial Nominee program which answered that they would process an application for nomination regardless of the peace bond and that he may face problems at the federal level when applying for permanent residence as a provincial nominee (paper application).
I have two questions:
1. since the peace bond is not a conviction and charges will be dropped within 6 months, if he remains of good behaviour, (registered as summary not indictable offence), is there criminal inadmissibility that needs to be addressed?
2. if we apply to the province of Alberta for nomination now, and receive nomination in 6 months, by the time a federal application is received and logged, the disposition of the charges should be clear so at that point, if there was criminal inadmissibility, or is it gone? Thank you kindly and hope to get some clarification on this delicate matter.
Best regards,
Lnmanon
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
A peace bond is not a conviction but a judicial measure imposed to ensure an individual keeps the peace during a certain period of time. If the individual complies with its conditions and keeps the peace, there will not be criminal inadmissibility that needs to be addressed. However, should they not comply with its conditions, it may result in a criminal charge. Breaching any condition of a peace pond is a criminal offence. At this time, there will not be criminal admissibility if he successfully complies with the peace bond conditions.
If you apply at this time, an officer will review the application and use their discretion as the peace bond has not been carried out successfully in full. However, if there is no conviction or disposition on his record, he will not be criminally inadmissible.
We trust that this information will be of assistance.

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on September 18, 2019.
Scenario 1:
The student has been a full time student for two semesters and one semester did not do well and became a part time student. Will his wife who is a holder of an open work permit (because she accompanies this student, her husband), one of their children is a holder of a study permit and another is a holder of a visitor record will not be allowed to work and study that period of time when the student is not a full time student?
Response 1:
If the spouse or common-law partner of a full-time student is issued a work permit under C42 (Spouses or common-law partners of full-time students [C42]), the work permit (C42) of the spouse or common-law partner remains valid until it expires or becomes invalid.
If the spouse of a full-time student still holds a valid work permit, issued under Labour Market Impact Assessment exemption code C42, the children continue to be authorized to study at the pre-school, primary or secondary level without a study permit. Minors studying in Canada at the preschool, primary or secondary level without a study permit, pursuant to subsection A30(2), can apply for a study permit from within Canada, pursuant to subparagraph R215(1)(f)(i).
Scenario 2:
A pregnant student got authorized leave from school for one term. Will her husband, a holder of an open work permit, is not allowed to work while his wife, a student, is taking an authorized leave for that period of time? A husband's open work permit remark states: Accompanying spouse's work permit is valid if spouse is enrolled as a full time student at a DLl. What is he does not have this condition or remark on his open work permit?
Response 2:
A student on leave who begins or resumes their studies within 150 days from the date the leave commenced (that is, the date the leave was granted by the institution) is considered to be actively pursuing studies during their leave. In this case, the open work permit of the spouse or common-law partner of full-time student remains valid until it expires or becomes invalid.
Scenario 3:
A student's study permit has a following condition:
mmigration, Refugees
Attendance at the university, college or other institution specified by the immigration officer. Does this mean that the student is not allowed to study at any other institution-only in the one specified by the officer? What if this statement is under remarks section? Does it make a difference if it is under conditions or remarks section? For r example:
a) Conditions: Attendance at the university, college or other institution specified by the immigration officer. Remarks: Must leave Canada by 2020/04/05 Or
b) Conditions: Must leave Canada by 2020/04/05 Remarks: Attendance at the university, college or other institution specified by the immigration officer. Response 3: Officers may also recommend the imposition of conditions when issuing study permits in accordance with section R185. As such, the student permit holder is only authorized to study in the specific studies/courses, educational institution, locations of studies and periods of studies as per the imposed conditions. If a specific DLI name is printed on a study permit, the permit hold must apply for an amendment (with fees) when changing school. Thank you for your inquiry, with respect to your questions:
1. Does the term "temporary resident" in R193(3)(f) include PGWP applicants awaiting a decision on their PGWP applications?
2. Is a PGWP applicant who is awaiting a decision on his/her PGWP application and whose Canadian TRV has expired, eligible to re-enter Canada from the US without having to apply for new TRV? A client who is in the possession of a valid study permit in Canada who applies for a PGWP prior to the expiry date of their permit would be able to remain in Canada and considered a temporary resident until we make a decision on the new permit. Further, if the client leaves Canada while the decision for the PGWP is pending the applicant must be in the possession of a valid TRV, when they are from a country whose nationals require a visa or an eTA, when they are from a country whose nationals are visa-exempt, and they are travelling to Canada by Air. Thus, if the client's TRV or eTA is expired, they must apply for a new one. However, if the same client is seeking to re-enter Canada following a visit solely to the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon then under R193(3)(f) the client would not be required to apply for a new TRV. We hope this clarifies the information you provided. The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Seeking Clarification Regarding Biometrics for In-Canada Applications--REP-2019-2610
threads.question:
* Lmon
Dear Immigration Representative,
I m seeking clarification on the requirements for biometrics for in-Canada applicants.
Context
Certain individuals are able to apply for a study permit from within Canada pursuant to R215(1)(f)(ii); such as exchange and visiting students.
We have a sizable number of exchange and visiting students whose initial intentions are to study in Canada for less than six months. As a result, they enter and are admitted to Canada as visitors. However, there are times when their intentions shift and they would like to study for more than six months. Given R215, such students can apply for a study permit from within Canada. However, they must provide biometrics before their application can be approved.
Currently, applicants have the option of providing biometrics at the port of entry (only if they have been authorized to do so, or have been directed by an officer to do so, pursuant to R12(13)) or outside of Canada at a Visa Application Centre or Application Support Centre. There are no in-land collections centres, to date.
As a result, in-Canada applications, such as those submitted by exchange or visiting students must provide biometrics outside of Canada as the temporary public policy exemption for biometrics does not apply to them even though they are applying from within Canada:
© Note: There is a temporary public policy exemption for in-Canada applicants. More specifically, foreign nationals who are eligible to apply from within Canada would normally provide their biometrics as part of an application or request for •a temporary resident visa (TRV) •a work permit or study permit
- a temporary resident permit
- permanent residence
However, since there is currently no biometric service delivery network within Canada, these applicants are exempt from the biometrics requirement until such time as the public policy is lifted. Applicants who apply from within Canada, but whose applications are not eligible to be processed from within Canada, are not covered under this public policy exemption. Those applicants are required to leave Canada in order to submit their biometrics as part of their application.
By virtue of proximity, most individuals will travel to the US to provide biometrics to full-fill this requirement; however, we noticed the following discouragement on IRCC s website:
If you're already in Canada and need to leave the country to give
biometrics If you're in Canada and you apply for an initial study or work permit, and you received a biometrics instruction letter from us, you may need to leave Canada to give biometrics. Do NOT travel to the United States (U.S.) to give your biometrics. You must already be legally in the U.S. or an overseas territory of the U.S. to go to an Application Support Center. Instead, go to a visa application centre (VAC) in any other country that you can legally enter, such as your home country, to give your biometrics.
Questions
Given the above, please clarify the following:
Since R215 allows certain individuals, such as exchange and visiting students, to apply for a study permit from within Canada, is the above discouragement to visit the US not applicable to them?
If the discouragement is applicable, where should exchange and visiting students provide biometrics to facilitate procedural fairness within the regulations? Would the POE be best place to redirect students to?
Input
We sincerely appreciate the ability of exchange and visiting students to submit initial study permit applications from within Canada pursuant to R215. This facilitative measure strengthens Canada s educational brand. To ensure immigration processes are clear and accessible, updated information on both public facing website (similar to the link above) as well as the biometrics pages would be helpful for this specific group of individuals.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day
Thank you for your question. Below are our responses to your questions.
Since R215 allows certain individuals, such as exchange and visiting students, to apply for a study permit from within Canada, is the above discouragement to visit the US not applicable to them?
The above discouragement to visit the United States solely to have biometrics collected at a U.S. Application Support Centre (USASC) applies to all foreign nationals that require biometrics in support of an application for temporary or permanent residence. Applicants who plan on attending/scheduling a biometric collection appointment in the U.S. should already be legally in (i.e. physically present in) the United States or an overseas territory of the U.S. Clients need to understand the entry requirements for the U.S. before travelling, as U.S. border agents can refuse entry to travellers from Canada if their sole reason for entering the
U.S. is to enrol their biometrics. In the case you have described, pursuant to R215 of the IRPR; these study permit applications are allowed to be made from within Canada, and would therefore qualify for the in-Canada biometric public policy exemption until the in-Canada biometric collection service is up and running in December 2019. We would also like to note that if students gave biometrics in the past as part of an application for a visitor visa, work or study permit and they are still valid, they do not need to provide them again in support of the study permit application.
If the discouragement is applicable, where should exchange and visiting students provide biometrics to facilitate procedural fairness within the regulations? Please see previous answer. These applications are considered exempt from the biometric requirement until the in-Canada biometric collection service is up and running in December 2019.
Would the POE be best place to redirect students to? Clients who have been issued a Biometric Instruction Letter may travel to any country that they can legally enter to enrol their biometrics. A complete list can be found here [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/where-to-give-biometrics.asphttp:/www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/where-to-give-biometrics.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/where-to-give-biometrics.asphttp:/www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/where-to-give-biometrics.asp)
We hope this proves helpful. Feel free to contact us if you require further clarification.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: [CPD-2019-0939] military exchange officers-Citizenship fast track--REP-2019-2597-
threads.question:
Dear ImmReps officer:
I have 2 general questions about the fast-track citizenship grant process pursuant to s.5(1.3) of the Citizenship Act
Foreign military officers who seconded to the CAF, and who have completed 3 years of service, can apply for citizenship without satisfying the PR residency obligation.
(a) Are such an applicant's spouse and dependent children eligible to apply for citizenship as well, or are they required to satisfy the s.5(1)(c) residency obligation?
(b) Does "fast track" also refer to processing times, or are such applications subject to normal IRCC average processing times for citizenship applications?
Thank you for your help. Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good Day M.
Thank you for your query.
As you note, an applicant under s.5(1.3) would not be a permanent resident but would have completed three years of service with the Canadian Armed Forces within the six years immediately before the date of his or her application.
In response to your question (a), the spouse or adult children of an applicant under s.5(1.3), unless eligible under another section of the Citizenship Act, would have to meet all of the regular requirements for a grant of citizenship under s.5(1), including having PR status. Any minor child of the applicant could apply under s.5(2) concurrently, or after the principle applicant (parent) becomes a Canadian citizen.
As to your question (b) on the use of the term “fast-track”. This term does not refer to processing times, but rather was used when applicants under s.5(1) were required to be physically present in Canada for the equivalent of four years in the six years preceding the application, whereas applicants under s5(1.3) only require 3 years of service within the six years preceding the application. Please note that following the implementation of Bill C-6, the physical presence requirement under s.5(1) is now the equivalent of three years in the five years preceding the application
I hope these clarifications have been helpful.
Salutations,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

All officers assessing applications submitted under Federal economic immigration programs are required to assess the intent of the applicant to reside outside Quebec as a permanent resident, under terms ofjurisdiction governing selection of economic immigrants outlined in the Canada-Quebec Accord.
For this reason, immigrants applying under the federal Economic Class programs must intend to establish in Canada outside Quebec, and must satisfy an officer regarding that intent. Assessing the genuineness of Intent to reside can depend on a range of evidence, including but not limited to the applicant's own declaration or affidavit of intent.
The fact of an applicant currently residing in Quebec at time of application does not, conclusively, suggest that the applicant does not intend to establish in another Province or Territory as a permanent resident. Similarly, the applicant's declaration and/or affidavit of intent to reside in another province other than the province of Quebec may not be sufficient for an officer to be satisfied that the applicant intends to relocate outside Quebec, and the onus is on the applicant to satisfy an officer, usually in the form of other evidence to demonstrate their intent.
For the Caring for Children class and the Interim Pathway for Caregivers, proof that applicants intend to reside outside of Quebec can include, but is not limited to, job offers, affidavit, rental agreements, home purchases, utility bills from outside of Quebec. It is up to the applicant to provide sufficient proof to satisfy the officer that they intend to reside outside of Quebec as a permanent resident.
An applicant who applies for permanent residence under a federal economic immigration program is assessed for their ability to economically establish in Canada, outside Quebec. This requirement applies across all federal economic immigration programs, and is not limited to the Caregiver Ministerial Instruction classes or the Interim Pathway for Caregivers public policies.

threads.answer:
Hello
Thank you for your inquiry.
Without specific details we cannot comment on a specific case, however, those admitted with temporary resident status in Canada applying under the in-Canada Spouse or Common-law Partner class are exempt from biometrics.

threads.question:
Good afternoon,
I have a question regarding the validity of an ICT work permit if the foreign employer is sold off and therefore no longer related to the Canadian employer.
If the work permit is valid for another two years, can the foreign worker keep using it until it expires? What action, if any, is required?
Appendix I of the FW1 Manual (version 2014-01-10) states that the original foreign entity can cease to exist in an ICT situation, as long as there is another entity with a qualifying relationship to the Canadian entity. The terms and conditions of the intra- company transferee's work permit will continue to be valid if the Canadian employer is still doing business either directly or through a parent, branch, affiliate or subsidiary in another country to which the employee can reasonably be expected to be transferred at the end of their assignment in Canada. I cannot locate this guidance on the IRCC website so I would like to confirm if this has changed since the manual was last updated.
In our situation, the employer is a Canadian multinational corporation with operations in Canada, Country A, Country B, and Country C. The foreign worker has been transferred to Canada from Country C and holds an ICT work permit that is valid for another two years. The operations in Country C are being sold off The operations in Canada, Country A and Country B will all continue to exist.
Can the worker from Country C continue using the ICT work permit? What is the definition of“reasonably be expected to be transferred"– does the worker have to have the ability to work in Countries A or B without restriction (e.g., citizenship) in order for this to apply? Or does there simply need to be a position in Countries A or B that the worker could qualify for at the end of the assignment in Canada?
Thanks,
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Ce:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question
(Regarding) the validity of an ICT work permit if the foreign employer is sold off and therefore no longer related to the Canadian employer. If the work permit is valid for another two years, can the foreign worker keep using it until it expires? What action, if any, is required?
Ans wer
The F1 (Temporary Foreign Worker) Manual is no longer in use; guidance has been modernized to web content.
ICT guidance can now be found at the following links:
International Mobility Program: Canadian interests – Significant benefit — Intra-company transferees [R205(a)] (exemption code C12)
Program delivery update: Intra-company transferees
Doing business means regularly, systematically, and continuously providing goods and/or services by a parent, branch, subsidiary, or affiliate in Canada and the foreign country, as the case may be. It does not include the mere presence of an agent or office in Canada. For instance, a company with no employees which exists in name only and is established for the sole purpose of facilitating the entry of intra-company transferees would not qualify. Evidence of the fact that a company is actively doing business such as annual reports (for public companies), articles of incorporation, profit/loss statements, partnership agreements, license to do business, business tax returns and registration with Canada Customs and Revenue Agency as an employer, may be useful.Both the Canadian and the foreign branches of the company must be doing business for the duration of the intended stay in Canada of the intra-company transferee. The foreign national employee must be able to transfer back to the foreign company at the end of their assignment in Canada.
That said, as the International Mobility Program aims to be as facilitative as possible for business people coming to work in Canada, especially where the job positions bring an element of benefit to Canada, a foreign national holding an ICT work authorization and where the foreign entity that transferred the foreign national initially is sold off, may continue working for the Canadian employer until the date of expiry for the current work permit. If the Canadian employer wishes to extend the employment of the foreign national, ICT eligibility criteria no longer being met, that employer will need to apply to Service Canada (under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program) for a Labour Market Impact Assessment before the foreign national can apply for a new work permit.
Regards,

threads.subject: QUESTION: 187(2)(c) "foreign business"---REP-2019-2566
threads.question:
From ## Good afternoon,
What is the definition offoreign business" and “principal place of business" for R187(2)(c)? Can a foreign national that works for the U.S. subsidiary of a Canadian software company sell the company's software in Canada to clients without a work permit (assuming of course this it would be done in a way that would not be considered sales to the general public)? The foreign national is not paid in Canada, only in the U.S. Does the fact that the U.S. subsidiary is owned by a Canadian company disqualify a
R187(2)(c) argument?
Thanks,
* Lnfomn
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question 1:
What is the definition offoreign business" and “principal place of business" for R187(2)(c)?
Answer:
Foreign business" in R187(2)(c) refers to a corporate entity that primarily conducts business in a country other than Canada.
Principal place of business" in R187(3)(b) refers to the primary location where a corporate entity's business is performed.
Question 2:
Can a foreign national that works for the U.S. subsidiary of a Canadian software company sell the company's software in Canada to clients* without a work permit (assuming of course this it would be done in a way that would not be considered sales to the general public)?
*Clients of the company (clients the company has an existing relationship with or ones that are referred to the company through the company's various marketing channels).
The foreign national is not paid in Canada, only in the U.S. Does the fact that the U.S. subsidiary is owned by a Canadian company disqualify a R187(2)(c) argument?
Answer:
The foreign national's employment relationship with the U.S. subsidiary does not disqualify him/her from accessing R186(a) as they would meet the criteria of R187(3); that is, the primary source of remuneration, principal place of business and accrual of profits are outside Canada. However, the fact is that the foreign national is essentially coming to Canada for the express purpose of selling proprietary software of a Canadian company to the Canadian company's own clients, so the end beneficiary of that work is the Canadian company. This appears no different than a contract for services through a third party, so a work permit would be required.
It is not just the wages paid that must be examined but all the factors laid out in R187 must be met. That being said, perhaps this individual can benefit from the GSS short-term work permit exemption if he/she is in NOC 0 or A, and if this is a one-time activity.
Lnformon We hope this information is of assistance.

threads.subject: ICT-no Canadian physical company office location --REP-2019-2742
threads.question:
Dear officer,
In a situation where a FN holds and ICT work permit and his Canadian employer will continue to have active operations in Canada but is wishing to close its Canadian office location and have the employees work from home, is the ICT work permit still valid?
Is a physical company office location required in order to obtain an ICT work permit? Or, is proof of active Canadian business
operations sufficient enough to obtain an ICT work permit?
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question
Is a physical company office location required in order to obtain an ICT work permit? Or, is proof of active Canadian business operations sufficient enough to obtain an ICT work permit?
Answer
Actively engaged
We have consulted with our temporary immigration policy, and the result is that a physical presence in some capacity is required under all LMIA-exempt employer specific work permits (International Mobility Program) as it is a requirement when assessing the genuineness of the offer of employment which mandates that businesses should be 'actively engaged'. Under the definition of 'actively engaged' it lists 'have a physical work location in Canada where
the temporary worker will work' as a requirement.
The one exception to this is start-ups under ICTs where we state in our guidance online that ‘it would be acceptable that the address of the new start-up not yet be secured; for example, the company may use its counsel's address until
the executive can purchase or lease a premise.'
New work permit required
If the employer is changing the job location, then a new work permit will be required for the worker. This means, also, that the employer will need to submit a new Offer of Employment (through their account in the Employer Portal) along with a new $230 compliance fee payment, before the worker may submit an 'Application to change conditions on a work permit in Canada' (IMM 5710).
This ensures that the employer has the correct conditions imposed on them under the Employer Compliance regime and that the worker has the correct conditions imposed on their work permit.
Teleworking vs significant benefit to Canada
However, the assessing officer may have concerns about why an intra-company transferee is apparently needed in Canada and will provide significant economic benefit... but can complete at least a portion of the work via telework.
Under the C12 provision, the foreign national is transferring here because the position in Canada requires their specialized knowledge. IF they can provide the specialized knowledge by telework, then why do they need to come to
migration, Refugees Canada? What is the benefit of having them here?
On the other hand, it is the work of the foreign national that should be assessed when considering whether there is a significant benefit to Canada. threads.answer:
Good day
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
You will find in red answers to your questions.
1. The one-year work experience has to be continuous employment with ONE employer, or can be cumulative experiences with more than one employer?
Answer: Work experience does not need to be continuous to qualify and can be obtained with more than one employer, as long as the applicant has obtained a total of 12 months qualifying work experience within the 3 years prior to the time of application.
2. If it is allowed with more than one employer, is it OK if there are a few months gap between jobs?
Answer: As mentioned above, work experience does not need to be contimuous to qualify and can be accumulated within the last 3 years. When calculating the period of 12 months ofrequired employment, it cannot include any extended breaks in employment, periods ofunemployment, prolonged sick leave or parental leave. However, a reasonable period of vacation time will be counted towards meeting the work experience requirement (for example, a 2-week period of paid vacation leave within a given 52-week period in which the applicant was engaged in qualifying work).
3. or it does not matter with one employer or with more than one employers, as long as the applicant has accumulated 12 months full time (or equivalent part time) experience within the immediate three years before he/she applies?
Answer: This is correct.
4. for the AIPP High Skilled category, the 12-month experience has to be in the same NOC (same occupation) or can be in different NOC (s) as long as they all fall under NOC 0, A, or B?
Answer: To meet the requirements of the Atlantic High-Skilled Program, work experience must be in a NOC 0, A, or B position and the job offer must be at the NOC 0, A or B level. Work experience does not need to be in the exact same NOC level as the job offer (ie. can be different NOCs) so long as both are at the NOC 0, A or B level.
5. for the AIPP Intermediate Skilled category, the 12-month experience has to be in the same NOC or can be in different NOC (s) as long as they all fall under NOC C?
Answer: To meet the requirements of the Atlantic Intermediate-Skilled Program, work experience must be in a NOC C position and the job offer must be at the NOC 0, A, B or C level.
Note however, the candidate must demonstrate that they performed the actions and main duties described in the occupation for which they are claiming work experience. Furthermore, they must demonstrate that they are able to perform and likely to accept

and cary out the duties of the job being offered and that they meet the relevant employment requirements of the occupation. Part TWO: One of the eligibility requirements for International graduates to qualify is to graduate from an eligible two-year program. Many of the potential applicants for AIPP has already had post-secondary education from their home country, so post-graduate programs offered by public colleges would be more appropriate programs for them to choose, and most of the post-graduate programs offered by public colleges are one-year in length, results in a certificate, so potential applicants who complete two of the one-year post-graduate certificate programs, total in 2 years, should be counted as meeting the education requirements. Answer: The intention of the Atlantic International Graduate Program is for students who have studied at an Atlantic Institution for 2 years. threads.answer:

Does this mean that the 12 months is cumulative and that only 12 months can be issued in total within a 24 month period for a CETA Independent Professional or would an Independent Professional be able to extend for an additional 12 month period within the 24 month period (assuming that in all other respects she is qualified – further contract provided by Canadian company, employer Offer of Employment filed, etc).

threads.question:
This is a follow up on my prior email regarding PGWP and Restoration.
If an applicant is outside of the 90 days after completing their studies and they want to apply for a PGWP. Can they apply for a PGWP + restoration or must they apply for a PGWP + a Study Permit + Restoration or do they have to apply for PGWP + Visitor Ext + Restoration.
migration, Refugees If they apply for a Study Permit + Restoration followed by a PGWP would they then be eligible to begin working full-time as of the date of approval of their study permit + restoration application?
If they are no longer a student, what is the basis for the restoration to a study permit?
Work authorization after submitting a post-graduation work permit
application
Per paragraph R186(w), graduates who apply for a work permit, such as a post-graduation work permit, before the expiry of their study permit are eligible to work full time without a work permit while waiting for a decision on their application if all of the following apply:
- They are or were the holders of a valid study permit at the time of the post-graduation work permit application.
- They have completed their program of study.
- They met the requirements for working off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v) (that is, they were a full-time student enrolled at a DLI in a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program of at least 6 months in duration that led to a degree, diploma or certificate).
- They did not exceed the allowable hours of work under paragraph R186(v).
Applicants must stop working as soon as they are notified by IRCC (for example, via their MyAccount, by email or by mailed letter) that their application for a work permit is refused.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/post-graduation-work-permit-program/permit.html
The applicant may apply for a post-graduation work permit from within Canada if their study permit is still valid. If the applicant's study permit is no longer valid, and they wish to remain in Canada, they must apply for visitor status before their study permit expires.
Former international students who change their status to visitor status before their study permit expires, while waiting for their notice of graduation from their institution, may also apply for a post-graduation work permit from within Canada.
Foreign nationals who do not apply for a post-graduation work permit, and whose study permit becomes invalid or expires, must either leave Canada or submit an application to change their status in Canada. They may also be subject to Restoration of temporary resident status.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/post-graduation-work-permit-program/permit.html
The phrase “initial requirements for their stay" should not be read too literally when it is being applied in the context of a restoration application, and the requirements of section
R179 should not be applied rigidly in that regard. The preferred interpretation in this
context would be that the person seeking restoration must meet the requirements of the class under which they are currently applying to be restored as a temporary resident. The desired approach to the restoration provision of section R182 is to be facilitative and consistent with the current approach to extension applications of the provision in section R181, since the two provisions are similar in nature and section R181 actually refers specifically to the requirements of section R179.
Possible restoration scenarios
A foreign student who is still in status can apply in Canada for a work permit under certain conditions. By inference, the foreign student can apply for a work permit when restoring status.
- A temporary foreign worker who is still in status can apply in Canada for a study permit if they meet certain conditions. By inference, they can also apply for a study permit when restoring status.
- A temporary resident who is eligible to apply in Canada for a work or study permit would be allowed to do so when restoring their status.
Note: The person must still satisfy the officer that they are a genuine temporary resident
and meet all the requirements of the Act, in order to qualify for restoration.

The backgrounder:
The spouse who successfully submitted the Family Spousal Sponsorship application from overseas and now travelled to Canada to be with her husband, was admitted as a visitor for 6 months(has an active TRV). formation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
R124 does not prohibit this and is not attached to the place ofPR application: R124 A foreign national is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class if they
- (a) are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with that sponsor in Canada;
- (b) have temporary resident status in Canada; and
- (c) are the subject of a sponsorship application.
Applicants in Canada-Open Work Permit provision
R207 A work permit may be issued under section 200 to a foreign national in Canada who
(b) is a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class set out in Division 2 of Part 7;- R124 However, the IRPR and IRPA is unclear on the place of the PR application. If we look into the IP8, it seems to initiate the LMIA exemption for spouses inside Canada Class PR applicants only(section
5.37 of[https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/ip/ip08-eng.pdf](https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/ip/ip08-eng.pdf)). Could you please clarify whether A70 LMIA exemption code is applicable only for Spouses who have submitted the PR application from inside Canada? Very best,
threads.answer:
Hello Ms
Please note that IP8 has been converted in the electronic Program Delivery Instructions and is no longer valid. Please see : Active manuals (PDF format). For updated Program Delivery Instructions on this topic please see: Determining membership in the class: Spouse or common-law partners
QUESTiON: Could you please clarify whether A70 LMIA exemption code is applicable only for Spouses who have submitted the PR application from inside Canada?
RESPoNSE: Yes. An application as a member of the family class (ie: spouse) submitted outside of Canada is submitted under R70 (1) (Part 5 - Division 6). The applicant must meet the definition of Family Class found in section R117 (Part 7 Division 1).
An application as a Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada Class must meet the following requirements, at the time of application:
(a) are the spouse or common-law partner of a sponsor and cohabit with that sponsor in Canada;
(b) have temporary resident status in Canada; and
(c) are the subject of a sponsorship application.
If a foreign national is residing outside of Canada and submits their application as the spouse or common-law partner of a Canadian sponsor and then enters Canada to reside with their sponsor as a temporary resident, they do not meet the requirements of the 'in-Canada' spouse or common-law partner class instead they are Family Class under Part 7, Division 1. They were not cohabitating with their sponsor in Canada at the time of application and they did not have temporary resident
status in Canada.
Only those who meet the requirements of the Spouse or Common-law Partner in Canada class fall within the LMIA-exemption of section R207. A person who submitted their family class application outside of Canada does not meet the requirements of R207.

threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry and suggestion. In response to your question: it is currently not possible to sign the IMM 5476 Use of Representative form or other forms through signnow.com or other such digital-signature software. There are two sets of circumstances under which an IMM 5476 Use of a Representative form is submitted.
1. When an applicant has not yet submitted an immigration or citizenship application, the IMM 5476 must be included with the application to the office listed in the guide of the application.
a. If the application is submitted on paper, the IMM 5476 must carry the original signature of the applicant;
b. if the application is submitted electronically, a scanned signature of the applicant is acceptable.
2. When an immigration or citizenship application has already been submitted, the IMM 5476 can be submitted
a. through the Web form ([http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp));
b. or via your Authorized Paid Representatives Portal account in response to a request from the processing office.
When submitted electronically (Web form or upload via account), a scanned signature is acceptable. If a hard copy IMM 5476 is sent in, the signature of the client must be original.
Regards.

Hello -
QUESTloN: Mexican citizens are not required to obtain a visitor visa but only an ETA. Does this mean that it would be possible for them to apply for a work permit (LMIA based-high wage or low wage) at the port of entry, if he presents a job offer, the employers LMIA confirmation, CAQ, work contract, and other necessary supporting documents?
RESPoNSE: Section 198 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) specifies who may apply for a work permit at the port of entry. You will also find information who may apply at the port of entry in our publically available Program Delivery Instruction: Temporary Foreign Worker Program and International Mobility Program: Persons who may apply at a port of entry.
The response to your question is in the Program Delivery Instruction, copied below for ease of reference:
Most foreign workers must apply for a work permit outside of Canada. Foreign nationals may apply for a work permit on arrival at a port of entry (POE) in Canada if the following applies:
- they are exempt from the requirement for a temporary resident visa and their job falls within the International Mobility Program (i.e., they are not required to obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment [LMIA]);
- they are exempt from the requirement for a temporary resident visa and their job falls within the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (i.e., they are required to obtain an LMIA) and a positive or neutral LMIA has been issued by the time they arrive
- they are a national or permanent resident of the U.S., Greenland or Saint-Pierre and Miquelon regardless of whether their job falls with the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or the International Mobility Program
- they will not be working as a live-in caregiver or as a seasonal agricultural worker

threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry sent on November 8 regarding work authorizations for study permit holders.
As per our PDI on off-campus work, study permit holders may work on campus in addition to up to 20 hours per week off-campus during academic sessions, provided they continue to meet all eligibility requirements and comply with the conditions of their study permit. There is no limit to the number of hours a study permit holder may work on campus.
Study permits with the condition "Unless authorized, prohibited from engaging in employment in Canada" do not authorize its holder to work in Canada. They may only work if they obtain another form of authorization (e.g. a work permit).

May accept employment on or off campus if meeting eligibility criteria per paragraph R186(f), (v) or (w); must cease working if no longer meeting these criteria
May accept employment only on campus if meeting eligibility criteria per paragraph R186(f); must cease working if no longer meeting these criteria
May not accept off-campus employment, unless prerequisite course or program has been completed; may accept employment once meeting paragraph R186(v)
If the study permit is issued without one of the above conditions, or the one prohibiting work, the study permit holder should apply to have it amended.

Let us say a foreign national has a VR approved, with the expiration day in one year in the future, i.e. Oct. 31, 2020, and then after he/she obtains the VR document, he/she has to travel outside of Canada in the following 2 different scenarios:
1. travel to USA only
2. travel to other countries, for example, China. Let us say he comes back to Canada from the travelling on Dec. 15, 2019.

2. If the VR document is not valid anymore, then he will have legal temp status for six months from the date of new entering? (the entering date is Dec. 15, 2019). Correct? In this question, does it matter travelling to USA only or traveling to other countries,

threads.answer:

A foreign national’s temporary resident status ends when they leave Canada or when the Visitor Record expires.

threads.question:
Good afternoon,
A Canadian employer has a foreign national employee on Canadian payroll. The foreign national's work permit extension application is pending and the foreign national is outside Canada working remotely for the Canadian employer.
QUESTION: Can the foreign national continue working remotely for the employer without a valid work permit and no implied status while being paid from Canadian payroll? Does IRCC have juris diction over individuals who are working outside Canada?
I have reviewed the definition of work at R2 and this site:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/what-is-work.html
Canadian wages are paid from a Canadian payroll, and the activity does compete with the activities of Canadians in the Canadian labour market. However, the activity is taking place OUTSIDE Canada. threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION: Can the foreign national continue working remotely for the employer without a valid work permit and no implied status while being paid from Canadian payroll? Does IRCC have jurisdiction over individuals who are working outside Canada?
RESPONSE: The first relevant provision for work in Canada is subsection 30 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), which states that: A foreign national may not work or study in Canada unless authorized to do so under this Act.
The interpretation of this clause means that IRPA and its provisions do not apply to work situations outside the country; as such, even though the work being performed may meet the definition of work, it is irrelevant as IRPA does not apply to work being performed outside our borders.

threads.subject: Foreign work experience for self-employed applicant under EE--REP-2019-2856
threads.question:
Hello,
Express entry points for foreign work experience (self-employed)
Is it possible for a self-employed applicant to be awarded 1 year foreign work experience based on the fact that they have over 1,560 over a period of 2 years though the hours were accumulated and recorded as monthly hours and not weekly? I.e. for month of May 90 hours in total as opposed to 15 hours per week. Please let me know.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Ce:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Express entry points for foreign work experience (self-employed)
Is it possible for a self-employed applicant to be awarded 1 year foreign work experience based on the fact that they have over 1,560 over a period of2 years though the hours were accumulated and recorded as monthly hours and not weekly? I.e. for month of May 90 hours in total as opposed to 15 hours per week. Please let me know.
Answer:
To meet the minimum requirements of the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) Class, the work experience must be continuous. Monthly hourly totals do not satisfactorily demonstrate that the work was continuous because there is no proof that work was performed each week. Work in excess of 30 hours a week cannot compensate for no work another week. So if the 90 hours in May was acquired over the course of two weeks, and the applicant did not work the last two weeks, this would not be continuous and would not count for FSW.
Your skilled work experience must be:
- in the same type of job (have the same NOC) as the job you want to use for your immigration application (called your primary occupation) within the last 10 years
- paid work (This means you must have been paid wages or earned commission. Volunteer work or unpaid internships don't count.)
- at least 1 year of continuous work or 1,560 hours total (30 hours per week). You can meet this in a few different ways: full-time at 1 job: 30 hours/week for 12 months = 1 year full time (1,560 hours) o equal amount in part-time: 15 hours/week for 24 months = 1 year full time (1,560 hours)
For part-time work, you can work more or less than 15 hours/week as long as it adds up to 1,560 hours and as long as it is continuous.
In all cases, the onus is on the applicant to establish that they meet the program criteria at the time of their application
We trust that this information will assist you.
Lnformon
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Medical Fellowship-Ability to do Rotation at Another Location not Named on Work Permit --REP-2019-2911-
threads.question:
Good Evening,
Can you please confirm whether a person who is currently doing a medical fellowship, pursuant to a work permit with a Canadian university named as the employer on their work permit, can do a one month rotation in another area of medicine at another university?
Typically, a person would be restricted to the employer/location named on their work permit. Is there any exception to this restriction when they are looking to do a short-term (one month) rotation at another university as part of their fellowship, and they will continue to be paid by the university named on their work permit? Would the work permit exemption detailed here ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/work-without-permit/authorization-work-without-work-permit-health-care- students.html) apply in a circumstance where the person has a work permit and is not a currently enrolled student?
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
QUESTION: Can you please confirm whether a person who is currently doing a medical fellowship, pursuant to a work permit with a Canadian university named as the employer on their work permit, can do a one month rotation in another area of medicine at another university?
RESPONSE: Since Medical Residents and Fellows are no longer considered students, as they have completed their M.D., they are required to obtain a work permit to complete their residence or fellowship periods. Since they are no longer students, subsection 186(p) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) do not apply to them.
They can apply under paragraph 205(c)(ii) of the IRPR for an exemption from a Labour Market Impact Assessment. However, a LMIA-exempt offer of employment submitted by their prospective employer, usually the training institute, is required. When the work permit is approved and issued, the employer is then liable for specific conditions in regards to working conditions including location, wages, etc.
If the employer (Canadian training institute) has indicated in the LMIA-exempt Offer of employment that the foreign worker will be working at various locations or institutions in Canada, then the work permit holder could then do electives in their occupation at different locations in Canada. If the various locations’ is listed in the offer of employment then the employer does not violate their conditions of they allow the foreign worker to complete electives outside of their location and the foreign worker should not be limited to a single location on their work permit.
If however, the employer has indicated only one work location in the offer of employment and the foreign worker wants to work at a different location, then a new offer of employment and work permit are required as this would be a change of conditions under the Employer Compliance regime.

[mailto: ] # Good Day,

Question:
Express entry points for foreign work experience (self-employed)
Is it possible for a self-employed applicant to be awarded 1 year foreign work experience based on the fact that they have over 1,560 over a period of2 years though the hours were accumulated and recorded as monthly hours and not weekly? Answer:
To meet the minimum requirements of the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) Class, the work experience must be continuous. Monthly hourly totals do not satisfactorily demonstrate that the work was continuous because there is no proof that work was performed each week. Work in excess of 30 hours a week cannot compensate for no work another week. So if the 90 hours in May was acquired over the course of two weeks, and the applicant did not work the last two weeks, this would not be continuous and would not count for FSW.

Inmn
- in the same type ofjob (have the same NOC) as the job you want to use for your immigration application (called your primary occupation) within the last 10 years
- paid work (This means you must have been paid wages or earned commission. Volunteer work or unpaid internships don't count.)

For part-time work, you can work more or less than 15 hours/week as long as it adds up to 1,560 hours and as long as it is continuous.
In all cases, the onus is on the applicant to establish that they meet the program criteria at the time of their application.

Greetings,

pears that in order to qualify for permanent residence under the LCP, you must gain (approximately) 24 months of Canadian work experience under a LCP work permit within the first 4 years of arriving in Canada. If a worker did not gain 24 months under a LCP work permit within the first 4 years of arriving in Canada, is it correct that the worker is not eligible for permanent residence under the LCP?
As indicated in our Program Delivery Instructions on permanent residence applications from live-in caregivers under the Live-in Caregiver Program (LCP), Live-in caregivers may apply for permanent residence after they have worked full time for at least 24 months (or for a total of 3,900 hours within a minimum of 22 months, which may include a maximum of 390 hours of overtime) within the four years immediately following their entry into Canada under the Live-in Caregiver Program. en does a person lose worker status under a LCP work permit? Does a person lose worker status under a LCP work permit when the person no longer qualifies for permanent residence under the LCP?

person ineligible to qualify for permanent residence under the IPCP on the basis that they hold a LCP work permit, notwithstanding the fact that they are also ineligible to qualify for permanent residence under the LCP for the reasons mentioned above?

s the Canadian work experience for the IPCP have to be under 2011 NOC code 4412 or can it also be achieved using the previous equivalent 2006 NOC code 6474?
The Interim Pathway for Caregivers closed to new applications on October 8, 2019. threads.subject: Study Permit invalid after 90 days--REP-2019-2775
threads.question:
Hello, A study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the day the student completes their course or program of study (e.g., notification in writing of program completion).
I'm wondering how IRCC is enforcing this requirement. A student can apply for a post-grad work permit up until 180 days after graduating so how does the above get enforced?
Thank you
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question.
Under R222(1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies,
(b) the day on which a removal order made against the permit holder becomes enforceable, or
(c) the day on which the permit expires
Non-compliance with study permit conditions may result in enforcement action; that is, an exclusion order can be issued for non-compliance, per subparagraph R228(1)(c)(v). Non-compliance with study permit conditions or engaging in unauthorized work or study may also negatively affect future applications that are made under the IRPA and IRPR.
With respect to a student who has completed their studies from an eligible Designated Learning Institution (DLI), they may apply for a Post-Grad Work Permit (PGWP). As noted, an applicant has within 180 days to apply after their school issues final marks. As part of the eligibility an applicant must provide a transcript and official letter from the DLI confirming completion of the
program of study.
We hope this information assists you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Dear Sir/Madam,
I am seeking your guidance as to whether a PR applicant who resided in a particular country for more than six months in a row as a diplomatic passport holder in a NATO mission, and on that basis was in fact considered not to have been a resident of the country in question, is required to provide a police certificate from said country? I searched for guidance on the impact of diplomatic status on the police certificate requirements for PR applicants prior to submitting this request but could not locate any guidance on the website or in the operational manuals or guidance. If this guidance is published, I would be most obliged if you could kindly direct me to it when providing your reply. I look forward to hearing from you at your convenience.
Many thanks.
Kind regards,
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry regarding your client's application to and Citizenship (IRCC).
In processing an application, an IRCC officer must be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible to Canada. For countries where an applicant has spent a total of six months or longer, a Permanent Resident applicant must submit a police certificate (unless otherwise specified). This includes time where the applicant is not a resident in that country, as well as diplomatic status.
If, for any reason, the applicant is unable to obtain a police certificate, they should submit their own written explanation as to why they could not obtain one, and any associated supporting documentation (such as the completed application for a police certificate, any response from the organisation that issues police certificates, etc.).
If the officer reviewing the file requires further documentation or information at any point while processing the file, they may request it.
We trust that this information has been helpful

threads.answer:
Ce:
Good day,
To answer your question, we refer you to paragraph 42(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act which specifies the following:
42 (1) A foreign national, other than a protected person, is inadmissible on grounds of an inadmissible family member if
i720(a) their accompanying family member or, in prescribed circumstances, their non-accompanying family member is inadmissible;
Section 23 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations specifies what the prescribed circumstances mentioned in A42(1)(a) are:
Prescribed circumstances — family members
23 For the purposes of paragraph 42(1)(a) of the Act, the prescribed circumstances in which the foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of an inadmissible non-accompanying family member are that
•(a) the foreign national is a temporary resident or has made an application for temporary resident status, an application for a permanent resident visa or an application to remain in Canada as a temporary or permanent resident; and
•(b) the non-accompanying family member is
(i) the spouse of the foreign national, except where the relationship between the spouse and foreign national has broken down in law or in fact,
As a result, in the example you provided, a wife and children who apply for permanent residence will be found inadmissible under A42(1)(a) on the grounds of having an inadmissible spouse if the spouse, whether accompanying or not, is inadmissible due to misrepresentation under A40.
Our Family Class Program Delivery Instructions provide instructions on the situation where a family member was examined and found to be inadmissible.

Subject: FW: CLARIFICATION of your response re Query regarding intra company transferee work permits for "start ups" - how does IRCC define "start up" in the intra company transferee situation?---REP-2019-2613------REP-2019-2842---
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Question:
In the intra-company transferee work permit context, newly formed Canadian subsidiaries or branches of established companies outside of Canada are not considered to meet the start-up guidelines under the ICT policy? For example, a software company in has been operating for many years there and it incorporates a subsidiary in Canada and it wants to transfer some manager and senior software engineers to the new Canadian subsidiary. In that case, is it reviewed by IRCC as a regular ICT and not a start-up, so things like having premises and only being able to get a 12 month work permit instead of a 3 year work permit are things that are applied to the situation?
Answer:
As indicated in the previous response, start-ups’ are newly emerging companies; therefore, subsidiaries are not ‘start-ups’ as they are using funding and assets from the parent company. If the newly opened Canadian subsidiary fails in the first year, they can receive support from the international parent whereas a truly new company is on its own to establish in that first year.
In the scenario described, does the new subsidiary meet the genuineness requirements ofR200(5) (e.g., business is active, can pay wages, meets all provincial and federal laws related to employment)? If they do, they could ask for more than one year work permit.
Thank you/Merci,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Mail received time: Thu, 28Nov 2019 12:23:37
Good day,
Thanks very much for your inquiry and apologies for the delay in getting back to you. You have pointed to an important gap that we are aware of, that is that there are some situations where leaving an abusive employer may change or delay the pathway to permanent residence. When designing the new authority the primary focus was on providing workers with the means of leaving an employer, remaining in status, and regaining some momentum in the Canadian job market. We are looking closely at these situations from a policy perspective.
For the time being, however, with respect to the case you’ve brought to our attention, we are bound by the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions which dictate that the applicant is no longer entitled to the points for arranged employment if they are unable or unlikely to agree to perform the job duties. I have copied the relevant provision below. Even if an applicant indicates that they meet this criteria in their initial application, they must provide proof of such and continue to satisfy these conditions until the application is approved.
MI29(3) If the offer referred to in subsection (1) is revoked or ceases to be a qualifying offer of arranged employment or if the foreign national is unable to perform the duties of the employment or is unlikely to agree to perform them, the foreign national is no longer entitled to the points assigned under subsection (1) in respect of that offer and the total number of points assigned to the foreign national under the Comprehensive Ranking System is to be adjusted accordingly. (emphasis mine)
Unfortunately, we do not have the authority at this time to provide flexibility or facilitation in Express Entry to applicants who have been issued the open work permit for vulnerable workers. That said, we would strongly encourage workers who are facing abuse to exercise the mobility of the open work permit and seek out a better employment situation, despite the impacts to their permanent residence application. While we recognize that it is not an ideal alternative, there is nothing preventing a client from re- applying for permanent residence, through Express Entry or any other pathway, if and when they meet the criteria of that program.
Apologies for not being able to provide more facilitation in the case you have described. We appreciate you bringing this situation to our attention and we will be keeping this gap in mind as we continue to improve the program.
\f0Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The worker is eligible for a cumulative total of 12 months within a 24 month period. They would not be eligible for another 12 month period within the 24 months. Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Question 1: Does a foreign worker in Canada pursuant to a CETA Independent Professional work permit (R204(a), T43) need to be self-employed in Canada as a condition ofthat work permit? Or is it enough that they are self-employed in their home country, but then they are permitted to enter into an employer-employee relationship with the company in Canada that they are providing services to and that is named on the CETA Independent Professional work permit?
Answer 1: Please note that Independent professional means a self-employed professional who has a contract to supply a
service to a Canadian consumer.".
Follow up Question to Answer 1: Based on this definition, it is clear that the foreign national must be self-employed in their home country; however, it is not clear whether they must also be self-employed inside Canada as a condition of their CETA Independent Professional work permit. As an example: You could have a scenario where an applicant is self-employed in their home country providing professional services to various companies. That individual could be contracted to provide professional services to a Canadian company, and during the course of that contract, the individual enters into an employer-employee relationship with the Canadian company. Would this be permitted while on a CETA Independent Professional work permit, as the individual was self-employed prior to arriving in Canada?
Question 2: Can work in Canada while on a CETA Independent Professional work permit be counted towards Human Capital points for Canadian work experience under Express Entry?
Answer 2: Work in Canada may be counted towards points for Core Human Capital Factors provided the employment meets the requirements of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system (MI) for Canadian work experience. Please note that as per subsection 15(7)(b) of the MI, a period of self-employment or unauthorized work is not to be included in calculating a period of work experience
Follow up Question to Answer2: While it is understood that a period of self-employment cannot count towards points for Canadian work experience, is it a condition of a CETA Independent Professional work permit that all work done in Canada while on that work permit is done while the foreign national is self-employed, or is it possible to be in an employer-employee relationship while on a CETA Independent Professional work permit ?
Question 3: Can one year of work in Canada pursuant to a CETA Independent Professional work permit be counted towards arranged employment points where the employer named on the Work Permit is providing an offer of indeterminate employment?
Lnmion Answer 3: CRS points may be assigned for a job offer if it meets the definition of a, "qualifying offer of arranged employment." The offer must be made by an employer, and meet the requirements of subsection 29(2)(a)(i),(ii), or (ii), of the MI.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Yes the rule of 150 days would apply to students who do not start their program or withdraw from classes. If a student does not begin their studies within 150 days of receiving their study permit, they should do either of the following:

•leave Canada

Good Day
All foreign nationals, including American citizens, are required to provide biometrics when applying for permanent residence (PR) in Canada. It was decided that PR should be a checkpoint in the immigration stream to confirm a client's identity and ensure there are no security or criminality concerns, since Permanent Residence is part of the pathway to Citizenship in Canada.
American citizens are exempt from providing biometrics for temporary resident applications (i.e. study permit, work permit or temporary resident visas). In these cases, a Nexus card will help simplify and expedite their travel process.
Therefore, American clients with Nexus cards would be required to pay for and provide their biometrics, if they wish to immigrate to Canada.
