threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Can you please elaborate the below Note under the below link:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5772-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5772-) application-sponsor-parents-grandparents.html
Note: Check "proceed with the application for permanent residence" if you submit an
undertaking of assistance to support the permanent residence application of a family member or
close relative on Humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
As per the above words, in case a Child is not eligible to sponsor his parent for not meeting the income requirements for Parent Sponsorship, should the child/the sponsor still apply for the parent sponsorship package? and if the application is refused then proceed with H&C if there is merit. I am inclined to say "no" since the child as a sponsor is not eligible to apply for parent sponsorship in the first place.
But what about if the PA/parent has H&C grounds in their case!
In this case the Child/Sponsor should not use the sponsorship package as per guide 5772 - Application to Sponsor Parent but should then apply for H&C as per guide 5291 - Humanitarian and Compassionate Grounds if valid basis and merit exist?
Please advise.
Thank you for your co-operation and understanding.
threads.answer:
Ce:
Hello,
Potential sponsors who successfully submit an interest to sponsor form and are invited to submit a complete application may request humanitarian and compassionate considerations if they do not meet the sponsorship eligibility requirements, including the minimum necessary income.
**They can do so by checking the "proceed with the application for permanent residence" box on the application to sponsor, sponsorship agreement and undertaking [IMM 1344] form. This will indicate that they wish to proceed with the application for permanent residence if they are found ineligible to sponsor. If found ineligible, the application and supporting documents will be sent to the appropriate visa office for processing and the request for humanitarian and compassionate consideration will be assessed.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5772-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5772-) application-sponsor-parents-grandparents.html
**Note: Check "proceed with the application for permanent residence" if you submit an undertaking of assistance to support the permanent residence application of a family member or close relative on Humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
Under R133 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, a sponsorship application can be approved only if there is evidence that the sponsor:
is not subject to a removal order is not detained in any penitentiary, reformatory or prison has not been convicted of an offence of a sexual nature, a violent criminal offence, an offence against a specific group of people that results in bodily harm, or an attempt or threat to commit any such offences—depending on circumstances such as the nature of the offence, how long ago it occurred and whether a pardon was issued (please refer to R133[1][e] for complete details) is not in default of a previous sponsorship, family support payments (e.g. alimony, child support) or immigration debt is not an undischarged bankrupt is not in receipt of social assistance for a reason other than disability
With regard to the income requirements, immigration officers assess whether or not the sponsor meets the requirement of R133 (1) (j) i.e. has a total income that is equal to or greater than the minimum necessary income (MNI) that sponsors and a co-signer (where applicable) must meet to satisfy IRCC that they are able to provide the basic requirements, e.g. food, clothing, and shelter for the family member.
In addition, please note that as per R130 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, for the sponsor to be considered, he must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who is at least 18 years of age and reside in Canada.
With respect to your second question; yes, submitting an H&C application only under A25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee
mmigration, Refugees
Protection Act (IRPA) is an option.
If the applicant is in Canada
request for an exemption based on humanitarian and compassionate or public policy considerations (IMM 5283) must accompany an application for permanent residence in Canada (IMM 0008). The application must be submitted in accordance with the requirements specified in section R10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
If the applicant is outside Canada:
he applicant must use one of the existing departmental application forms for the three immigration classes (family, economic or refugee) and provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1)
Furthermore, please note that as per the Ministerial Instructions with respect to the processing of applications for permanent resident visa made by parents or grandparents, a request made under subsection 25(1) of the Act from outside Canada and that accompanies an application that was not accepted for processing under the Ministerial Instructions, will not be processed. In other words, requests for humanitarian and compassionate consideration (H&C) for persons outside of Canada will not be accepted unless the request for H&C consideration under A25(1) submitted outside Canada is made by a sponsor who successfully submitted an interest to sponsor form and was invited by IRCC to submit a complete sponsorship application. PR status will be granted if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by H&C considerations relating to the foreign national, taking into account the best interest of the child directly affected. Therefore, in the event that a minor is listed as a sponsor of a parent overseas, given the Ministerial Instructions referred to above, a request made by the parent overseas to consider the sponsorship application in spite of the sponsor being under 18 would not be considered.
Please do not hesitate to contact us should you have further questions.
Thank you,

Hi IRCC officer,
Following up on your answer to question 4, can you please confirm the eligibility to work you were saying is for summer break or last semester? I was asking you the work eligibility for summer semester, but I do not see a clear answer whether you refer to summer or last semester.
Thanks for your reply in advance.
For students who are part-time studying to finish the rest of course requirements in their last academic semester, we will report them as a part-time student because we report status by the number of credits they take. 9 and above is considered a full-time student. We cannot report this group of students as full-time because we would have to check whether they are in their last semester and we do not have the information when we report them. Also, if a student cannot complete the part-time course load in the last semester for some reason and needs to take another semester to complete, we would give the inaccurate information by reporting the student full-time twice although the student was part-time in two semesters.
Therefore, if a student who is part-time studying to finish the rest of course requirements in the Fall semester, which is also the last semester, can student work in the Summer semester, which is their scheduled break? I do not think the current IRCC PDI mentioned this. It only says students need to be full-time in the semester before and after the scheduled breaks to be able to work off-campus on a full-time basis. However, what about students who are finishing in the semester after their scheduled break? Any instructions? The outreach officer said students can work off-campus on a full-time basis. However, I am not sure if we can advise students to do so as I do not see any supporting resources.
Response
Study permit holders who are studying part time in their last semester because it is all they require to complete their program requirements are granted an exemption from the requirement to hold full-time student status in order to work. Schools are not required to grant these students full-time status so that they can benefit from this exemption, and should report on their status as normal. It is the study permit holder's responsibility to demonstrate that they are in this situation should an immigration officer request evidence of compliance with study permit conditions.

Therefore, if a student who is part-time studying to finish the rest of course requirements in the Fall semester, which is also the last semester, can student work in the Summer semester, which is their scheduled break? I do not think the current IRCC PDI mentioned this. It only says students need to be full-time in the semester before and after the scheduled breaks to be able to work off-campus on a full-time basis. However, what about students who are finishing in the semester after their scheduled break? Any instructions?I would feel it is just like a regular scheduled break and the student is part-time just because he only has part-time course load left. Students are panicked and they are thinking if they need to take extra courses in the Fall semester to meet the full-time requirement so as to work in the Summer semester.
The outreach officer said students can work off-campus on a full-time basis. However, I am not sure if we can advise students to do so as I do not see any supporting resources.
Response:
DLls set the number of hours and credits toward a degree, diploma or certificate that are required for a student to hold full-time status. Students who have maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and who only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, may work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session. In order to work off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v), students must hold full-time status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break.
Students must stop working off campus as soon as their full-time status becomes part-time during a regular academic session (for instance, a student may begin a regular academic session on a full-time basis and become part-time during the same session as they drop courses). In this case, they are no longer authorized to undertake off-campus work. Thus, a part-time student in their last academic semester will not be eligibility for off-campus work during the scheduled summer break as student must hold a full-time status during the length of the program of studies.
Hope you will find this information useful.

threads.answer:

Students cannot work off campus if they participate in a prerequisite such as English as a second language (ESL) or French as a second language (FSL) program before the start of the academic, professional or vocational program regardless the duration of the prerequisite.
The provisions for the off-campus work can be found:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html#who-cant](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html#who-cant)
With respect to the open work permits under C42, there is no program of studies requirement that the spouse or common-law partner who is the study permit holder must be taking. If the study permit holders engages in full-time studies at one of the eligible Canadian institutions listed below, the spouse or common-law partner of the study permit holder would be eligible for an open work permit under C42, provided that they meet all eligibility requirements.
Eligibility
Applicants must provide evidence that they are the spouse or common-law partner of a study permit holder who is a full-time student at either
a public post-secondary institution, such as:
o a college
o trade/technical school
o university
CEGEP in Quebec
a private post-secondary institution that operates under the same rules and regulations as a public post-secondary institution in Quebec
a private or public secondary or post-secondary institution (in Quebec) offering qualifying programs of 900 hours or longer leading to a diploma of vocational studies or an attestation of vocational specialization
a Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees (for example, a bachelor's degree, master's or doctorate) but only if the student is enrolled in one of the programs of study leading to a degree, as authorized by the province and not in just any program of study offered by the private institution.
The provisions for the open work permit under C42 can be found:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-) residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes/public-policy-competitiveness-economy.html#fulltime-students

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on October 30, 2019, regarding the validity of study permits.
As per R222 (1)(a) a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies. However, the study permit does not become invalid when a study permit holder drops out of school permanently, without finishing their studies first.
That being said, as per R220.1(1), the study permit holder in Canada is still subject to the following conditions:
rey shall enroll at a designated learning institution and remain enrolled at a designated learning institution until they complete their studies; and
rey shall actively pursue their course or program of study.
\foTherefore, when a study permit holder has dropped out permanently, does not plan on continuing to pursue their studies and they plan on remaining in Canada, they should change their status (e.g., change to a visitor status) or leave Canada.
Otherwíse, they will be considered as non-complaint with their study permit conditions.
Non-compliance with study permit conditions may result in enforcement action (i.e. an exclusion order can be issued for non-compliance as per R228(1)(c)(v)) and may also negatively affect future applications made under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and its Regulations.

threads.question:
Good day:
If a student is required to complete an internship as part of their program, and the internship will account for 20 hours or less during the academic session, is the student required to obtain a co-op work permit, or can they complete the internship/ co-op off campus using their existing authorization to work off campus?

mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on November 5, 2019 regarding co-op work permit.
The co-op work permit and the off-campus work authorization listed on the study permit serve different purposes and are not interchangeable. In other word, international students must obtain their valid co-op work permit prior to starting their work terms. The designated learning institution (DLl) should clearly establish that the work is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. If students won't exceed 20 hours of off-campus work per week during a regular academic session, they may use the work authorizations of their study permit to complete co-op work while waiting for the decision of their co-op work permit application. Please note, in order to use their study permit work authorizations to work in health or early childhood program, the study permit must not include the restriction to work in in such fields: “Not authorized to work in 1) child care, 2) primary or secondary school teaching, 3) health services field occupations”. However, if their co-op work permit application is refused, the students would not be allowed to continue their co-op program without authorization.
I hope that this information is helpful to you.

threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION 1: If an application was sent before the status expired and the application is rejected later, when does the person lose his status?
RESPONSE 1: If an application is rejected under section 12 of of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) as being incomplete, it is considered that no application has been received. Therefore, the provisions of subsection 183(5) to automatically extend status do not apply. The foreign national would have lost temporary resident status at the end of their authorized period – in this case, when their initial document expired. For example, if the person had a valid permit until February 15 and submitted an incomplete application for an extension, if the application is rejected on March 1, the person's status would have expired on February 15th. An application must be complete as per section 10 of the IRPA for the provisions of subsection 183(5) of the IRPA to apply.
QUESTION 2: if the application is refused in the same scenario, Will the applicant lose status on the date of the refusal?
RESPONSE 2: An application that is refused, was a complete application, if it was submitted prior to the expiry of the person's present status, the person would benefit from the provisions of 183(5) to an automatic extension of status until decision on their application. The refusal would be that decision and therefore the end of their authorized period of stay.
QUESTION 3: Can a work permit and a study permit can exist at the same time?
RESPONSE 3: There is no legislative or regulatory bar to a foreign national holding both a study and work permit. However, the person would still be required to meet the conditions of studying in Canada (ie: full time studies) and the hours of work specified in the offer of employment or LMIA.
QUESTION 4a: Can a person have two status at the same time, like both a visitor and a student?
QUESTION 4a A foreign national who has been authorized to enter Canada has Temporary Resident Status. A temporary resident may also be authorized to study or work either by Regulation or by holding the appropriate permit.
QUESTION 4b: I know a person who was on a Graduate Work permit after graduating from an University in Ontario -. She went to Australia and did her master right after. When she was trying to come back from Australia, she could not find the option to apply online for a TRV, so instead she applied for a visitor visa and was approved!
QUESTION 4b: A TRV or Temporary Resident Visa is the legal term for what is commonly known as a 'visitor visa'. The application forms use the term 'visitor visa' as it is more generally known and understood.
L'information divulguée en QUESTION 4c: She came back to Canada to work on a visit visa! Now she has two statuses – worker and visitor. A year later, she applied for PR under Canadian Experience Class online while in China and in the meantime her 3-year work permit expired.
QUESTION 4c: There is only status as a temporary resident, if authorized to enter Canada, and authorization to work. Visitors, students and workers are usually all have temporary resident status. However, students and workers also have authorization to study or work.
For a better understanding of Temporary resident status, you can review the Program Delivery Instructions available to the public at : Temporary residents

current job in Canada? " but there are only 3 possible answers:
Yes,
No-job does not require WP, and
No, WP is required but I do not have one.

Answer:
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have implied status as a temporary resident during that period.
If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
If the above applies to the applicant, and they are on implied status, and you may select: Yes
If the subsequent application for extension of status is refused, you must update your profile.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Professional Training Courses at Non-DLI's-REP-2019-2836-
threads.question:
Dear Immreps,
I am hoping that you can address a question I have about professional training. There are institutions in Canada who offer vocational and professional training programs that are essential for particular occupations. Often these institutions are not DLI's and will never qualify as a DLI but their programs and courses are vital to the improvement of workplace skills and benefit employers and industries across Canada. My question is how a foreign worker, whether here in Canada on an employer specific work permit or an open work permit, can take advantage of professional training courses without compromising their work permit.
Most work permits will contain the following condition: "Unless authorized, prohibited from attending any educational institution, or taking any academic, professional or vocational training course"
I know that they cannot apply for a study permit to counteract that condition as the institutions are not DLI's but is there any policy which willallow them to take advantage of short term courses (less than 6 months) without breaching the aforementioned condition.
Thank you for your advice and assistance.
threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on September 18, 2019 regarding to short-term courses.
Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less at a non-DLI as per [R188(1)(c)]. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry for up to 6 months. That being said, the duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study.
It should also be noted that R188(1)(c) was not put in place to allow foreign nationals to take short-term courses, one after the other, simply by extending their temporary resident status—in effect, making it possible for them to complete a whole certificate, diploma or degree without ever having a study permit. (IRCC) recognizes that long-term visitors and foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting 6 months or less at any time during their stay in Canada.
Thank you kindly

Question:
Pursuant to s.11(3) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, in order for a foreign national to be assigned points for the level of education they are claiming, they must have an educational credential equivalency assessment completed by an organization or institution designated under subsection 75(4) of the Regulations. threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
QUESTION 1: If the employer needs to change NOC code for an ICT employee, who is on LMIA exempt work permit, what shall be the process for the same?
RESPONSE 1: Temporary Workers who have received their work permit in the Intra-company transferee (ICT) category (LMIA-exemption code C12) can not change their occupation from within Canada unless they continue to meet the ICT requirements.
To be LMIA-exempt under the ICT category, the foreign national must have been employed continuously (via payroll or by contract directly with the company), by the company that plans to transfer them outside Canada in a similar full-time position (not accumulated part-time) for at least one year in the three-year period immediately preceding the date of initial application. If the foreign national has already transferred to Canada and is working for the Canadian entity, then they are not transferring' from an international company into Canada. For further information you may review the relevant program delivery instructions at : International Mobility Program: Canadian interests-Significant benefit – Intra-company transferees-General requirements [R205(a)] (exemption code C12)
QUESTION 2: What could be the most appropriate option from the following?
1.The employer Changes the employee NOC code through Employer portal and share the information through web form with IRCC to update the information?
2.The employer Changes the employee NOC code through Employer portal and employee needs to reapply for work permit?
3.The employer Changes the employee NOC code through Employer portal and employee could go to POE and get the work permit updated?
4.OR if there is any other way to address the above process, shall request to share the same.
RESPONSE 2:In order to meet the ICT requirements, the foreign national would have to leave Canada and work in the new NOC occupation for a minimum of 12 months before they can apply to transfer back to Canada or the employer may obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment for the new occupation, and the foreign national would have to obtain a new work permit under the LMIA or the employer may determine if their situation meets the requirements of a different LMIA-exemption category and submit a new offer of employment and the foreign national must then obtain a new work permit in the new occupation.

threads.subject: Conjugal Partner-Martial Status IMM 5406 --REP-2019-2583-
threads.question:
Lnmn # Hello ImmRep,
What is the best option for conjugal partner to select under marital status on the IMM5406 Additional Family Information form? My client and his conjugal partner are not legally married, and they have never lived together. What would the best option be?
The current options include: annuled marriage, common-law, divorced, legally separated, married-physically present, married- not physically present, single, widowed, and unknown.
member of the Law Society of Manitoba Member # I am writing on behalf of my principal,
Thanks,
nmigration, Refugees ation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry.
For immigration purposes, it is recognized that a conjugal partnership occurs when neither common-law status nor marriage is possible. Furthermore, a person's marital status is not affected by being in a conjugal relationship. For example, a person who is single and then enters into a conjugal relationship should still indicate single as the marital status. Likewise, a person who is widowed should indicate widowed, divorced as divorced, and so on.
As per the instructions in the Guide IMM 5289, a conjugal partner is a person who is living outside Canada and in a conjugal relationship with the sponsor for at least one year. Additionally, please find below the definition of each marital status as found in the Guide:
Annulled Marriage: This is a marriage that is legally declared as not valid. An annulment can also be a declaration by the Catholic Church that the marriage union did not have a binding force.
Common-Law: This means that you have lived continuously with your partner in a marital-type relationship for a minimum of one (1) year.
Divorced: This means that you are officially separated and have legally ended your marriage.
Legally Separated: This means that you are married, but no longer living with your spouse.
Married: This means that you and your spouse have had a ceremony that legally binds you to each other. Your marriage must be legally recognized in the country where it was performed and in Canada.
Single: This means that you have never been married and are not in a common-law relationship.
Widowed: This means that your spouse has died and that you have not re-married or entered into a common-law relationship.
Trusting this addresses your question.

threads.answer:
Mail received time: Mon, 9 Dec :12:48
Good day,
This is in response to your November 5th enquiry regarding overlapping coursework.
To clarify, the overlapping credits earned from two programs of study cannot be counted twice to determine the length of a PGWP.
If an officer observes that the applicant's time spent studying is shorter than the duration of the programs as indicated by the letters of program completion, and it is apparent that the student did not accelerate their studies, the post-graduation work permit may be issued with a validity duration based on the time spent studying rather than overall programs length.
On the other hand, the officer will also consider the length of the programs as indicated on the letter of completion to ensure that a student is not slowing down their academic progress for the purpose of getting a longer PGWP.

threads.subject: Exchange students and implied status--REP-2019-2910
threads.question:
Hello,
We have 3 exchange students who originally applied to do a 4-month exchange and do not have study permits (program under 6 months). They all came with eTA and have visitor status until mid or late February. They have enjoyed their exchange so much that they are applying through our university and their home universities to extend their exchange and complete 8 months in Canada. They will now require study permits and are in the process of applying for them online from within Canada. Applications are currently taking 73 days to process, so they wouldn't receive their study permits until the end of January. The second 4- month term starts January 6, 2019.
Question: Do these students have implied status while they wait for their study permits? If not, when do they need to stop studying?
Some of them are considering going home for the winter break in December and their applications are unlikely to be processed before they leave – does that change their status and their ability to study upon return?
We would appreciate your help in this matter so that we can advise the students correctly.
Sincerely,
Page 2884
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please find the responses to your questions below:
Question: Do these students have implied status while they wait for their study permits? If not, when do they need to stop studying?
No, students in this situation would not have implied status while they wait for their study permits. As per section 189 of the IRPR, a foreign national who has made an application under subsection 217(1) is authorized to study without a study permit until a decision is made on the application if they have remained in Canada since the expiry of their study permit and continue to comply with the conditions, other than the expiry date, set out on the expired study permit. Therefore, a foreign national who has temporary status in Canada as a visitor and applies for a study permit would not have implied status as a student.
They would have to stop studying after the expiry of their original visitor status. In order to remain in Canada legally while they await their study permit applications to be processed they would have to apply for visitor records to extend their stay in Canada. Applying for a visitor record would (before the expiry of their temporary resident status as visitors) would give them implied status as visitors, however they would still need to wait until they received their study permit applications in order to continue studying in Canada.
Some of them are considering going home for the winter break in December and their applications are unlikely to be processed before they leave – does that change their status and their ability to study upon return?
Please note that as soon as a foreign national leaves Canada they will lose their implied status (if they applied to extend their status as visitors in Canada). The foreign national may also be required to apply for a new temporary resident visa in order to re- enter Canada if they are from a visa requiring country.
It will be up to the discretion of the border officer whether to allow the foreign nationals back into Canada if they left before a final decision on their study permits were made. The students also have the option of applying for a study permit from overseas if they decide to return home OR if they are eligible they may apply at the port of entry (POE). Information on applying at the POE can be found below:
Applying at a POE
The foreign nationals who may apply for a study permit when entering Canada [R214] are any
•national or permanent resident of the United States (U.S.)
•person who has lawfully been admitted to the U.S. for perimanent residence
•resident of Greenland or St. Pierre and Miquelon
Note: To apply for a study permit at an air POE, a lawful permanent resident of the U.S. who is travelling to Canada must apply
for and obtain an eTA before boarding their flight to Canada.

threads.answer:

Question:
My question is this. How are CRS points assessed for a foreign national who has consecutively completed, over the course of 1 year, 6 months of full-time work experience outside of Canada and 6 months of full-time work experience inside Canada? All work was done at the NOC B level.
Also, does this scenario meet the Express Entry threshold requirement of 1 year of work experience?
Answer:
To be awarded CRS points, the minimum requirements are 1 year or more of foreign experience or 1 year or more of Canadian experience. You cannot combine the two.
To meet the requirements of the Express Entry Federal Skilled Worker (FSW), the work needs to be continuous (no break in service) and in the same NOC/occupation.
This experience would not qualify for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) as it did not take place solely in Canada.

threads.subject: Points for Job Offer for LMIA exempt Work Permit--REP-2019-2963
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Religious workers are exempt and can work in Canada with LMIA exempt employer specific work permit (R205d). They do not need an LMIA so can they get 50 additional points for a job offer in Express Entry System? Can the job offer be just a written offer from an employer-LMIA is not needed?
Warm Regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Religious workers are exempt and can work in Canada with LMIA exempt employer specific work permit (R205d). They do not need an LMIA so can they get 50 additional points for a job offer in Express Entry System? Can the job offer be just a written offer from an employer-LMIA is not needed?
Answer:
If the applicant has a valid work permit for a NOC 0. A or B job that is exempt from needing an LMIA, and they:
- are currently working for an employer specified on the work permit
- have one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) for that employer
- have a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after we issue the permanent resident visa
Then the might have a valid offer of arranged employment provided they meet all other requirements.
A valid job offer has to be:
- made by one employer
- continuous
- paid
- full-time (at least 30 hours a week)
- for at least one year after we issue your permanent resident visa o not seasonal
- in a job that is NOC: Skill Type 0 or Skill Levels A or B
Details about arranged employment is on our website.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Request information on transfer schools and holding WP and SP at the same time--REP-2019-1359--
threads.question:
Dear IRCC Policy Analyst,
Q1: According to the information from IRCC website ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-) citizenship/services/study-canada/change-schools.html ), the post-secondary students do not need to apply to change the study permit when they are changing schools.
We recently encountered a situation that the student's study permit indicated that “Attendance at the University, College, or other Institution specified by the immigration officer" under the condition. In this case, does the student requirement to change the condition of their study permit? Or change DLI number only?
To expend this question, if the study permit limited the student to study in a specific field under Field of Stud," do the students need to change the study permit when they transfer schools?
Q2: Can the foreigner national (FN) holds a study permit and work permit at the same time? For example, can an open work holder apply for a study permit giving that the FN meet the eligibility of the study permit and vice versa?

Best Regards,
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Response:
Hi
We apologize for the delay. Please see our response to your questions below in blue.
Question 1:
Question: We recently encountered a situation that the student's study permit indicated that “Attendance at the University, College, or other Institution specified by the immigration officer" under the condition. In this case, does the student requirement to change the condition of their study permit? Or change DLI number only?
Response: As per R185(c)(ii), officers may impose, vary, or cancel conditions on the studies a foreign national is permitted or prohibited from engaging in while in Canada. One condition that may be imposed is on the educational institution an international student may attend. In the situation where a foreign national is seeking to change schools and has a condition on their study permit, the foreign national must notify IRCC of the change in DLI by changing their DLI number in MyAccount.
Question: If the study permit limited the student to study in a specific field under Field of Stud," do the students need to change the study permit when they transfer schools?
Response: If an international student has conditions on their study permit specifying the type of studies or course they are permitted to engage in, they must apply to change the conditions on their study permit if they would like to change programs to one outside the field of study specified in their conditions. If the international student is seeking to change schools but remain in the same field of studies as specified in their study permit conditions, they would only need to update their DLI number.
Question 2:
Question: Can the foreigner national (FN) holds a study permit and work permit at the same time? For example, can an open work holder apply for a study permit giving that the FN meet the eligibility of the study permit and vice versa?
Response: Foreign nationals may hold both a study permit and work permit at the same time. Foreign nationals who possess a valid open work permit may apply for a study permit so long as they meet the eligibility requirements.
Question: Can I understand that if the FNs hold a work permit and study permit at the same time, they could study and work full-time?
Res ponse: That's correct. An international student that holds an open work permit is given the authorization to work full-time
via their open work permit. Thus, they can study and work full-time.
I hope that you find this information helpful. If you have any further enquiries, please contact us at .
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: marital status in conjugal partner sponsorship applications--REP-2019-3007--
threads.question:
Hi
This is a general question regarding to the marital status in conjugal partner family sponsorship applications.
What marital status should I use when filling the forms?
Most application forms list the following options:
1. Annulled Marriage
2. Common-Law
3. Divorced
4. Legally Separated
5. Married
6. Single
7. Unknown
8. Widowed
IMM 5406 Additional Family Information has a slightly different list:
1. Annulled marriage
2. Common-law
3. Divorced
4. Legally Separated
5. Married-physically present
6. Married-not physically present
7. Single
8. Windowed
9. Unknown
Conjugal partner is not in the lists.
So which option should I use when filling the forms?
Thanks for the clarification!
Lnfomn
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry.
For immigration purposes, it is recognized that a conjugal partnership occurs when neither common-law status nor marriage is possible. Furthermore, a person's marital status is not affected by being in a conjugal relationship. For example, a person who is single and then enters into a conjugal relationship should still indicate single as the marital status. Likewise, a person who is widowed should indicate widowed, divorced as divorced, and so on.
As per the instructions in the Guide IMM 5289, a conjugal partner is a person who is living outside Canada and in a conjugal relationship with the sponsor for at least one year. Additionally, please find below the definition of each marital status as found in the Guide:
Annulled Marriage: This is a marriage that is legally declared as not valid. An annulment can also be a declaration by the Catholic Church that the marriage union did not have a binding force.
Common-Law: This means that you have lived continuously with your partner in a marital-type relationship for a minimum of one (1) year.
Divorced: This means that you are officially separated and have legally ended your marriage.
Legally Separated: This means that you are married, but no longer living with your spouse.
Married: This means that you and your spouse have had a ceremony that legally binds you to each other. Your marriage must be legally recognized in the country where it was performed and in Canada.
Single: This means that you have never been married and are not in a common-law relationship
Widowed: This means that your spouse has died and that you have not re-married or entered into a common-law relationship.
Trusting this addresses your question.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Study Permit Exemption Under R188(1)(d)--REP-2019-2582---------REP-2019-2889
threads.question:
Greetings,
Thank you for your response, it's very helpful
in the below questions? I appreciate your time and assistance.
Lnmdion
Could you please clarify how students are deemed to be Indians entitled to be registered' for the purposes of confirming their eligibility for a study permit exemption as per the PDI? Furthermore, how would 'Indians entitled to be registered' be addressed
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Immigraton Kepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Hello,
Registration under the Indian Act is completed by Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada. Once the foreign national can provide proof of registration, then they fall within the study permit exemption section of R188(d). Therefore, registered Indians or Indians entitled to be registered as defined under the Indian Act both qualify for the study permit exemption. As IRCC does not determine who meets the requirements of the Indian Act students may confirm their status with Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada if necessary and provide confirmation to IRCC that they are Indians entitled to be registered as defined under the Indian Act. For more information please refer to the following links:
[https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1461766373625/1556203056093](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1461766373625/1556203056093) [https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1540405608208/1568898474141](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1540405608208/1568898474141) \f0 \fOThank you/Merci, \f0 The Immigration Representatives Mailbox La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Good morning,
Please find the responses to your questions below :
•How does IRCC determine who falls under the Indian Act to be eligible for a study permit exemption, particularly students who are entitled to be registered?
RESPONSE: IRCC does not determine who meets the requirements of the Indian Act. Registration under the Indian Act, is completed by Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada. Once the foreign national can provide proof of registration, then they fall within the study permit exemption section of R188(d).
•What documents are viewed as acceptable proof for the above?
RESPONSE: Acceptable documents establishing one's status as registered under the terms of the Indian Act include the certificate of Indian status and the secure certificate of Indian status cards. Both are commonly referred to as the status card and are produced by ISC. The paper-laminate certificate ofIndian status card is issued in partnership with First Nations in 500 communities across Canada through ISC's Indian Registration Administrator Program. The secure certificate of Indian status card is an identity card with enhanced security features.
Inmn Subject to an application process, the certificate of Indian status and the secure certificate ofIndian status cards are issued to adults, children and dependent adults listed in the Indian Register. The Indian Register, which is maintained by Indigenous Services Canada is the official record identifying people who are registered under the Indian Act.
•What documents could accompanying family members who are also Indian/Indigenous be eligible for? E.g. would a spouse/partner be eligible for an open work permit?
RESPONSE: If the spouse is also a registered Indian they would meet requirements of the study or work permit exemptions. If the spouse is not a registered Indian then, it would depend on the studies or occupation of the Registered Indian status holder. If the Registered Indian is enrolled in full-time studies at a Designated Learning Institute their spouse may be eligible for the open work permit under Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption code C42. Further information can be found in Who can get a work permit as the spouse or common-law partner of a student?
If the Registered Indian is in an occupation designated under the National Classification Code (NOC) in skill levels 0,A or B, and they are working for longer than 6 months, their spouse may be eligible for an open work permit under the LMIA exemption code C41. Further information can be found in You're a spouse or family member of someone working or studying temporarily in
Canada.
•When should/could an Indian/Indigenous student apply for proof of their status in Canada
RESPONSE: In order to fall within the study permit exemption section ofR188(d) this should be done before they decide to attend school in Canada
•If an Indian/Indigenous student were eligible for the study permit exemption, what work authorization would they have?
RESPONSE: Per paragraph 186(x) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, registered Indians, as defined under the Indian Act, are exempt from having to apply for a work permit.
Thank you
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
We are looking for guidance regarding after-sales services provisions under IRPR 186(a) and 187(1). As we understand it, after-sales the regulations allow for entry as a business visitor to perform work for people seeking to repair, service, set up, test or supervise work on specialized commercial or industrial equipment purchased or leased outside of Canada.
nmigration, Refugees
Can you clarify whether commercial/industrial equipment purchased outside of Canada that is to be installed into other machinery already in Canada qualifies for this exemption. For instance, equipment is purchased outside of Canada and as part of the purchase agreement, this equipment is to be set-up and serviced within an MRI machine already in Canada. The MRI machine was not purchased outside of Canada and does not form part of the agreement at hand. However, the equipment purchased outside of Canada is essential to the optimization of the imaging technologies of the MRI machine. In other words, the equipment is not meant to simply fix parts of the MRI machine, but the equipment is required to increase performance outcomes in patient screening, diagnosis and treatment management.

mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Question:
As per IRPR 186(a) and 187(1), with respect to after-sales services, people seeking entry to repair, service, set up, test or supervise work on specialized commercial or industrial equipment purchased or leased outside of Canada are eligible to enter Canada as a business visitor.
Can you clarify whether commercial/industrial equipment purchased outside of Canada that is to be installed into other machinery already in Canada qualifies for this exemption?
Answer:
Since this is a new equipment purchase order (even though it is for the optimization of an existing machinery), this is a new contract for a new product and, therefore, it would qualify for this exemption.
Note that it is important to ensure that the applicant is able to provide documentation outlining the relationship between the purchaser and the seller, as well as the contractual obligation for installing the product.

threads.subject: Urgent-basic question-is study permit needed for a course under 6 months long--REP-2019-2929
threads.question:
mmigration, Refugees
Dear ImmReps,
I am a lawyer in Ontario -Thank you in advance for your assistance.
R188(1)(c) allows a FN to study in Canada without a study permit if the duration of their course of study is 6 months or less and will be completed within the period for their stay authorized upon entry into Canada.
A FN has applications for spousal sponsorship and an open work permit under the pilot program in process. FN's current study permit expires on Dec 31, 2019. Since she applied for the open work permit before her study permit expired, she will go on implied status on January 1.
Question 1: FN wants to take a 5 week/30 hour course at a DLI that runs from mid-Jan to mid-Feb. Can she take this course without extending her SP? I think so, since the course is less than 6 months. I'm just unsure about the the requirement that the course be "completed within the period for her stay authorized upon entry into Canada." She is on implied status, which is not "authorized upon entry" / has no clear end date.
Question 2: If FN not only wants to take the course mentioned above, but also decides to take another course that is 5 weeks long/30 hours from May-June 2020 and another course that is 4 weeks long/30 hours from June-July, 2020, does she need a study permit for these courses? If yes, based on what section of the act/regs?
Thank you so much,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on November 19, 2019. Please note that this service is to give general functional guidance, thus we are not able to provide case-specific advice.
Question 1:
FN wants to take a 5 week/30 hour course at a DLI that runs from mid-Jan to mid-Feb. Can she take this course without extending her SP? I think so, since the course is less than 6 months. I'm just unsure about the requirement that the course be "completed within the period for her stay authorized upon entry into Canada." She is on implied status, which is not "authorized upon entry" / has no clear end date.
Answer 1:
Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months). As per R183(5), if a temporary resident has applied for an extension of the period authorized for their stay and a decision is not made on the application by the end of the period authorized for their stay, the period is extended until (a) the day on which a decision is made, if the application is refused; or (b) the end of the new period authorized for their stay, if the application is allowed. Thus, a temporary resident on implied status may take a short-term course.
Question 2:
If FN not only wants to take the course mentioned above, but also decides to take another course that is 5 weeks long/30 hours from May-June 2020 and another course that is 4 weeks long/30 hours from June-July, 2020, does she need a study permit for these courses? If yes, based on what section of the act/regs
Answer 2:
Paragraph R188(1)(c) was not put in place to allow foreign nationals to take short-term courses, one after the other, simply by extending their temporary resident status—in effect, making it possible for them to complete a whole certificate, diploma or degree without ever having a study permit. (IRCC) recognizes that long-term visitors and foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting 6 months or less at any time during their stay in Canada. It is therefore recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards or work on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student. Section R215 provides an exemption to allow certain foreign nationals to apply for a study permit after entry to Canada.
I hope you will find this information useful.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The qualifying experience for this program does not need to have been acquired under a Home Child Care Provider pilot work permit. If an applicant has 2 years of full-time work experience as a Home Child Care Provider (NOC 4411) on a post- graduation work permit, it can be counted as eligible experience to apply for PR under this program. For applicants with at least 24 months of qualifying Canadian work experience at the time of application, they will submit their proof of qualifying work experience upfront in their application for permanent residence. (b) must only involve work that was authorized under a work permit;
(c) must be acquired while the foreign national had temporary resident status; and

threads.answer:
Hello,
Question
Do we need an amendment of a work permit if the duties and title are changing but not the NOC?
Response
Although the job title is listed on the work permit, the National Occupational Code (NOC) is used for the assessment of the work permit and inspections. Therefore, if the duties, educational requirements etc. of the new position continue to match the NOC code, a new work permit is not required. Also, as outlined in the instructions related to employer compliance inspections, "The employer must provide the foreign worker with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as, but not less favourable than, those in the same offer [R209.2(1)(a)(iii)]."
In addition, the employer should retain all documents related to the position changes to ensure they can be provided if an inspection is conducted.

threads.question:

2for the new pilot programs- is a calculation and proof of income of the employer, as it was with the low -skilled LMIA, required? What is the calculation?

threads.answer:
Greetings,
Please accept our apologies for the delay in responding to your enquiry. You will find the answers under your questions below
As I did not see a detailed guide for those pilot programs, please be so kind and answer my questions:
You may find more information on the Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot on 4 different sections of our website:
- Information on the pilots for the applicants (process, eligibility, how to apply, etc.)
- Information for employers to hire a home child care provider or home support worker Help Centre questions and answers related to caregivers
- Program Delivery Instructions for IRCC officers
1. for the new pilot programs- is the employment contract as it was with the low-skilled LMIA required, a must?
Note: The employer was supposed to pay the airfare, free room to live, health insurance etc
Employers must make an offer of employment using the Offer of Employment (IMM 5983) form. For your question on airfare and room & board, please refer to the following Help Centre questions and answers:
- Do I have to pay for the caregiver's travel costs ifI'm hiring them through the caregiver pilots?
- I want to hire a caregiver with a live-in arrangement. What's the maximum amount I can charge for room and board?
For health insurance, similar to the airfare and consistent with the situation for other International Mobility Program foreign workers, it is not a requirement, though it can be offered to the employee and outlined in the Offer of Employment form.
2. for the new pilot programs- is a calculation and proof of income of the employer, as it was with the low -skilled LMIA, required? What is the calculation? An employer's household income, in combination with other information provided in the job offer, may be used by an officer to assess whether the job offer is valid and genuine. The assessment is made on a case-by-case
nmigration, Refugees Inmn basis, but officers may use the LICO (Low income cut-offs) to inform their decision and request additional documentation from the employer.
Acceptable forms ofproof are:
- Notice of Assessment (NOA) from Canada Revenue Agency or T4/T1 for the most recent tax year,
- Employment Insurance stubs
- Employment letter including salary and date of hiring
- Pay stubs
- Bank statements
3. for the new pilot programs- can the employer charge for room and board/food ? if yes, how much?
Please refer to the following Help Centre question: I want to hire a caregiver with a live-in arrangement. What's the maximum amount I can charge for room and board?
4. is the prevailing wages required?
Wages offered is an element of a job offer assessment when a reviewing officer considers the genuineness of the job offer. If the job offer meets minimum wage for caregivers, but does not meet the prevailing wages, this may raise concerns when assessing the genuineness of the job offer. In some localities, prevailing wages may not be available and officers may compare the wage offered to the applicable minimum wage as a guideline. Caregivers under the new pilots should not experience lower wages and working conditions than caregivers under previous programs, so officers will assess all information provided to ensure that the offer to the foreign national worker is reasonable and genuine.
5. for employer with high medical needs or terminal sickness, is it possible to hire the worker from out of country " fast", less than 6-12 months?
Is there an option LMIA as "hiring only" from out of country workers and apply for PR when the worker has gathered work experience in Canada?
NOTE: In the past the LMIA dealing with this special group could get the caregiver in as fast as in 2-3 months.
It is not possible to hire out of country in-home caregivers or home support workers without their also applying for permanent residence under one of the pilots, for the duration of the new caregiver pilot programs and as long as the "refusal to process" is in place. For more details and legislative references, please refer to the Program Delivery Instructions Refusal to process Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)-required work permit applications for caregivers received on or after June 18. 2019.
There is no expedited processing procedures in place for work permit applications under the Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot. However, families continue to have the option to hire a foreign worker as a caregiver if this person is already in Canada and eligible to apply for a work permit from within Canada.
Regards,

threads.subject: Exemption de permis d'étude pour semestrés--REP-2019-3042-
threads.question:
From Bonjour,
Les guides opérationnels d'IRCC disent ici [https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/organisation/publications-) guides/bulletins-guides-operationnels/residents-temporaires/permis-etudes/doit-obtenir-permis-etudes.html que:
La durée du cours ou du programme d’études est souvent un facteur plus important que le nombre de mois que l'étranger compte passer à étudier. À l'exception des programmes d’échange, lorsque l'étranger prévoit d’étudier pendant une période maximale de 6 mois, mais que le cours ou le programme choisi est d’une durée supérieure à 6 mois, il doit avoir un permis d’études.
Plus tard, un exemple donné est que :
\cbpat7Un étudiant prévoit venir au Canada pour un semestre (quatre mois) dans le cadre d'un programme d'échange de la 12e année.
\cbpat7Non. Même si, en principe, la 12e année dure 10 mois, si le programme d'échange précise que sa durée est d'un semestre, l'étudiant n'a pas besoin d'un permis d'études, car le programme sera achevé en moins de six mois. Toutefois, les
étrangers en provenance de pays visés par l'obligation de visa doivent présenter une demande de VRT.
Dans ce contexte, nous nous demandons si un étudiant étranger dont le pays d’origine divise son année scolaire en semestre et qui viendrait compléter l’entièreté de sa 12 année au Canada (donc 10 mois ou 2 semestre) dans le cadre d’un programme d’échange étudiant aurait besoin d’un permis d’étude dès son arrivée au Canada ou s’il lui est possible de compléter le premier semestre de
moins de 6 mois avant qu’un permis d’étude ne sois requis?
Nous vous remercions d’avance pour votre assistance.
Au plaisir,
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Ce courriel est en réponse à votre correspondance datée du 4 décembre 2019, concernant l’exemption de permis d’étude pour un programme d’échange étudiant.
L’article 188(1)(c) du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés prévoit que les étrangers séjourner au Canada sans permis d’études afin d’y suivre un cours ou un programme d’études d’une durée maximale de 6 mois se terminant à l’intérieur de la période de séjour autorisée lors de l’entrée. Dans la situation décrite ci-dessous, comme le programme d’échange est de plus de 6 mois, soit deux semestres, l’étudiant devra obtenir un permis d’études d’emblée.
J’espère que cette réponse vous sera utile. N’hésitez pas à envoyer toutes requêtes additionnelles à l’adresse suivante :
Cordialement,

threads.subject: Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot Project--REP-2019-3054--
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
In order to qualify for the Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot Project an applicant must have a job offer in one of the rural communities. If a company makes a job offer what accountability (if any) would that company have? For instance if the employee were to be terminated or if the office of the company that made the job offer were to be permanently closed in that community? Would the company have to declare any of this to IRCC or would that be the employee's obligation to do so?
Are you able to comment on this in 2 instances:
1. When the PR application is in progress
2. After the PR application is approved
Thank you,
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Thank you very much for reaching out to IRCC regarding the termination of job offers within the Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot. The onus is always on the applicant to inform the department of any change that could impact the processing of their application, including changes to their mandatory job offer.
1. When the PR application is in progress
Employer obligations:
Employers must inform the applicant (employee) of any changes to their job offer, including a changes in duties, compensation, hours of work, or the complete withdrawal of the offer. The employee will then be responsible for informing the department.
As part of the participation in the pilot, employers will agree to inform the community-based economic development organization of any changes to the job offer that they issued, this includes informing them of the employee start date, the withdrawal of the job offer or termination of the employee/employer relationship.
Economic Development Organization obligations:
It is the designated Economic Development Organizations' responsibility to verify that the offer of employment is valid and genuine (as well as verify other eligibility criteria required) before issuing a recommendation, and to inform IRCC of any known changes to the offer of employment. Should a job offer be withdrawn, the EDO must revoke their recommendation and inform IRCC of the change.
An applicant who has a permanent residence application in process may obtain a new genuine offer of employment only under certain circumstances which are listed in section 11 of the Mls with respect to the Rural and Northern Community Immigration Class. For further information, you can review the Mls at the following link:
Ministerial Instructions with respect to the Rural and Northern Community Immigration Class
Applicant's (employee) obligations:
The applicant (employee) must inform IRCC of any changes during the processing of their application and up until granting of Permanent residence (changes such as marital status, changes to your job offer, etc.)
Failure to advise IRCC of any changes in circumstance may render the applicant and family members inadmissible to Canada.
2. After the PR application is approved
If the PR application is approved but PR status not granted yet: As explained above, both the applicant and the EDO must advise IRCC of any changes (including changes to the job offer) up until the applicant is granted Permanent
Residence status.
After permanent residence has been granted: Once permanent residence status has been granted, the applicant is no longer required to inform IRCC of changes to their employment situation. IRCC will solicit information regarding employment status from both Economic Development Organizations and employers through voluntary surveys to evaluate the success of the program.
If IRCC determines that the applicant was aware of the change to their job offer before becoming a Permanent Resident and did not declare it, it may result in a misrepresentation investigation and removal from Canada.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Dear Representative,
With respect to your questions below, please note that a protected person in Canada who applies for permanent residence may include any of their dependent family members in their application in accordance with Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and its Regulations.

threads.answer:
Mail received time: Mon, 23 Dec :57:36 Ce:
Good day,
This is in response to your November 27 enquiry regarding authorized leave from studies.
Per paragraph R186(w) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, graduates who apply for a work permit, such as a post-graduation work permit, before the expiry of their study permit are eligible to work full time without a work permit while waiting for a decision on their application if all of the following apply:
- They are or were the holders of a valid study permit at the time of the post-graduation work permit application. They have completed their program of study. They met the requirements for working off-campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
- They did not exceed the allowable hours of work under paragraph R186(v) Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
In cases where a student has taken multiple periods of leave in Canada during their program of study, the officer should consider the student's reasons for the various periods of leave. If the multiple periods of leave do not appear to support the expectation that the student is making reasonable progress toward the completion of their course or program of study in the time allotted by the course or program of study, the officer may determine that the study permit holder has not fulfilled the condition to actively pursue their course or program of study. As such, the processing officer still retains a certain level of discretion in determining if the applicant was actively pursuing their studies and if based on the facts of the case they could be exempt from the PGWPP eligibility requirement of having to maintain "full-time student status in Canada during each academic session of the program or programs of study they have completed.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at
Thank you/Merci,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
This is in response to your October 3rd enquiry regarding part-time studies and PGWP eligibility.
In order to be eligible to work full time without a work permit while waiting for a decision on their application, the applicant must meet the requirements for working off campus without a work permit under paragraph R186(v) (that is, they were a full-time student enrolled at a DLl in a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program of at least 6 months in duration that led to a degree, diploma or certificate). The applicant must have maintained full-time student status in Canada during each academic session of the program or programs of study they have completed and submitted as part of their post-graduation work permit application. Exceptions can be made only for authorized leave from studies and final academic session.
Thus, an applicant who were registered part time for any other semester other than the final academic session would not be eligible to work under R186(w), whereas an applicant who had an authorized leave from study would be eligible.

threads.subject: Priest Work--REP-2019-2960-
threads.answer:
Good day,
A foreign national would only be able to continue working on an work permit exemption under section 186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulation (IRPR) if they had applied to extend their temporary resident status under section 181 of the IRPR prior to the expiration of their visitor record. Since the extension of status as per operation of law (implied status) under R183(5) and conditions extended under R183(6) are not triggered, the priest in question would be in breach of both 185(a) and 185(b)(iv) if they continued to work after their status expired., The priest would have 90 days to apply for restoration of status from the day their visitor record expired and they would be unable to work while awaiting a decision regarding whether their status will be restored.
Regards,

threads.subject: International Students' eligibility to work off campus as Self-employed--REP-2019-2721-
threads.question:
Dear IRCC,
This is to request clarification on the International Students' eligibility to work off campus as Self-employed.
We find that although this type of employment is allowed (not restricted), it is really hard to monitor the number of hours they students are self-employed.
Also, if you could provide any direction as to the types of legal business formation or registration (such as Ontario Master business license) are allowed for Temporary residents?
In other words, can we assume that international students on valid SP can operate as Sole proprietors and self-report earnings to CRA under their Social Insurance Numbers.
Any guidance will be greatly appreciated as both our staff and international students.
Thank you in advance!
nmigration, Refugees mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Ce:
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry sent on October 17, 2019 in regards to monitoring the number of work hours for students who are self-employed.
First of all, students need to meet the requirements for on and/or off campus employment in order to engage in any type of employment (e.g. self-employed). If the person is doing work, and the work takes place on campus (in his leased dorm room/apartment or in the cafeteria or any location which is located on the campus of the school), they would need to fulfill the requirement for on campus work to do so. If the person does the work off campus, then he would need to fulfill the requirements for off campus work. It's about where the "work” is undertaken. Off-campus employment has to be limited to 20 hours a week. While on- campus employment is not limited in hours.
Students who are self-employed should keep track of their hours worked and provide proof of work and/or payment. If the officer has reason to believe the permit holder is not complying or has not complied with one or more of the conditions of their study permit, study permit holders must provide evidence of their compliance with their study permit conditions as per R220.1(4).

I am an RCIC. My number is
I am requesting clarification on the Education Criteria for the Home Support Worker Pilot Program. The
criteria states that 1 year of post secondary education is required.
Informationdisclosed under theAccessto IformationAct

threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representative Mailbox.
As indicated in the Program Delivery Instructions:
An applicant must provide evidence that they have either of the following completed: a Canadian one-year post-secondary educational credential or a foreign educational credential and an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) report issued by an organization designated by IRCC.
For applicants with a foreign educational credential, the ECA report must:
- indicate that the credential is equivalent to a completed Canadian one-year post-secondary (or higher) educational credential
- be less than 5 years old on the date of application receipt
- have been issued on or after the date the ECA organization was designated by IRCC
As per subsection 73(1) of the Regulations, “Canadian educational credential” is defined as, “any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions." Therefore, the applicant would need to provide evidence of a one year post-secondary credential, such as a post-secondary diploma or certificate.
We hope this information is useful.
Sincerely,

threads.question:
Dear ImmReps,
We've been having some debate within our firm regarding the interpretation of some wording within the CETA guidelines and I was wondering if you could perhaps shed some light for us? Specifically, can you please confirm if contract service suppliers/professionals under CETA are eligible for work permits beyond 1 year?
The guidelines state that extensions are at the discretion of the officer but then go on to state the following: "Extensions for contractual service suppliers and independent professionals may be extended only up to 12 months from the start of the initial work permit and must fall within the overall 24-month window permitted for these categories."
Does this mean that a professional who was issued a work permit from Jan 1, 2019 to Dec 31, 2019 can apply for up to 12 more months (so long as it's within the initial 24-month period) or does it mean that because they've already held it for 12 months from the date it was issued, they've maxed out?

Thanks and happy holidays,
ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTIoN: Does this mean that a professional who was issued a work permit from Jan 1, 2019 to Dec 31, 2019 can apply for up to 12 more months (so long as it's within the initial 24-month period) or does it mean that because they've already held it for 12 months from the date it was issued, they've maxed out?
RESPoNSE: As per the instruction found in Canada-European Union (EU) Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement
(CETA) - Contractual service suppliers and independent professionals (work permit required/LMIA exemption codes T47 and
T43) the period of 12 months is cumulative.
Length of stay: A cumulative period of no more than 12 months in any 24-month period or for the duration of the contract, whichever is less. Extensions are possible at the officer’s discretion. For more information, see:
• Extending CETA work permits
On review of the instruction in the hyperlink : Extending CETA work permits, the line : Extensions for contractual service suppliers and independent professionals may be extended only up to 12 months from the start of the initial work permit and must
fall within the overall 24-month window permitted for these categories.
It become clear that it can only be a maximum of 12 months work in a 24 month period. In your example of the person who has already worked for 12 months, they have earned the cumulative maximum and can not be extended. If they had only worked 6 months in that first year, then they could work up to an additional 6 months during the second year.
